The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda: Organisational Dynamics in Egypt and Tunisia since 2011 examines the organisational dynamics and capacity for change of the Arab world’s two most influential Islamist movements.
Rather than foregrounding external political pressures, the book explores the internal organisational worlds of Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood and Tunisia’s Ennahda, treating them as long-standing institutions shaped by their own cultures, structures, and internal debates. Drawing on a framework that places organisational culture and intra-party politics at the centre of the analysis, it investigates how each movement confronted the pressures of governing, adapting, and redefining its political role and identity after 2011. The book argues that the capacity for change within these organisations was shaped by internal dynamics: the Brotherhood’s strong commitment to preserving its long-standing mission and organisational vision often constrained reform, while Ennahda struggled with a weak conceptualisation of how and why change should occur. By comparing their contrasting trajectories of party formation and institutional reconfiguration, the book highlights how each movement came to understand organisational change differently – as variation or replication, and as an opportunity or a threat to itstheir foundational identity.
This book will be of interest to students and scholars of Middle East politics, political Islam, and comparative politics, as well as to readers seeking a deeper understanding of the evolution of Islamist movements in the post-Arab Spring era.
Carmen Fulco is a Lecturer in International Relations in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and a Research Fellow at Demos Tunisia. She is a scholar of Middle East politics whose research explores contemporary Islamist movements, authoritarian populism, and youth politics., with a focus on Tunisia..
Routledge Studies in Middle Eastern Democratization and Government
Edited by:
Larbi Sadiki, Qatar University
This series examines new ways of understanding democratization and government in the Middle East. The varied and uneven processes of change, occurring in the Middle Eastern region, can no longer be read and interpreted solely through the prism of Euro-American transitology. Seeking to frame critical parameters in light of these new horizons, this series instigates reinterpretations of democracy and propagates formerly ‘subaltern,’ narratives of democratization. Reinvigorating discussion on how Arab and Middle Eastern peoples and societies seek good government, Routledge Studies in Middle Eastern Democratization and Government provides tests and contests of old and new assumptions.

Notes on Transliteration and Translation
Notes on Transliteration and Translation
Notes on transliteration and translation
In this book, the transliteration of Arabic words generally follows the IJMES guidelines,0 with some simplifications. Most diacritical marks are omitted, including underdots indicating emphatic consonants and overbars for long vowels, in line with conventions commonly used in Middle Eastern studies. Only diacritics indicating the presence of ʿayn [ʿ] and hamza [ʾ] are retained infor concepts and in the titles of books and articles available exclusively in Arabic.
The Arabic-to-English transliteration of organisations, parties, and movements omits all diacritics. The transliteration of the proper names of politicians and high-profile members of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda follows conventional English and French spellings to enhance readability for non-Arabic speakers. Similarly, Arabic words commonly used in English follow standard English spelling.
All translations of interview material extracted from Arabic sources and presented in this book are the author’s own, and any errors or inaccuracies remain the sole responsibility of the author.

Introduction
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Introduction
More than a decade after the Arab Uprisings that shook regimes across the Middle East, the echoes of protest chants have still not faded. They continue to reverberate across the region, as images of jubilant crowds in Tahrir Square and on Avenue Habib Bourguiba resurface on social media with each anniversary. Although some have sought to reduce the 2011 Uprisings to a mere electoral slogan,0 an inconvenient chapter to be erased from history,0 or even a curse,0 such detractors have struggled to silence the voices of those who dared to challenge authoritarian rule.0
Amid widespread and embittered disillusionment over the fate of revolutionary demands for freedom, justice, and dignity, the spectre of the Uprisings continues to haunt both the leaders and supporters of the Islamist movements that appeared to benefit most from their electoral aftermath. Within these movements, individuals of different ages and social backgrounds continue to discuss, debate, and reassess mistakes, responsibilities, and miscalculations. In 2019, I joined this conversation and embarked on the research journey that culminates in this book.0
Following the ousting of Hosni Mubarak in Egypt and Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in Tunisia, the strong performance of the Muslim Brothers and Ennahda in the first free elections generated mixed reactions. While some Western commentators hastily labelled the episode an ‘Islamist winter’,0 other observers focused on assessing these movements’ democratic credentials and the extent of their ideological moderation once in power.0
Yet the more intriguing puzzle lies elsewhere. How could a complex, nearly century-old organisation such as the Brotherhood, illegal for most of its existence, suddenly transform its structures, abandon a clandestine mindset, and enter institutional politics? What did this transformation mean for the organisation itself? Similarly, in Tunisia, how smooth or fraught was the process through which the long-banned Ennahda Movement reconstructed its base and structures, engaged in party politics, and gained acceptance as a political party?0
This book, therefore, examines the intra-organisational dynamics experienced by the Muslim Brothers and Ennahda during the decade following the Arab Uprisings. It explores how these dynamics inform the movements’ capacity for change and the cumulative imprint that internal developments have left on their organisations. A decade on, these questions have become particularly pressing. Much of the scholarship that has focused on Islamist movements engaged in institutional politics has relied heavily on Social Movement Theory (SMT) and its variants. Through this lens, scholars have examined ideological transformation, mobilisation capacity, and political behaviour, often overlooking internal developments.0 Consequently, the field has become saturated with structure- and incentive-centred analyses and fixated on a narrow and relativistic conception of ‘change’.0 Change has typically been understood as a reactive and mechanistic linear process, either progressive or regressive, to be completed or avoided, and thus largely stripped of complexity and deviation. It has also been treated as a relational reconfiguration requiring a second term of comparison, whereby Islamist actors’ ideology, conduct, and discourse are assessed primarily in relation to the ‘state, the army, liberal democratic concepts, and other political contenders’, that is, vis-� -vis, or at times against, the ‘other’.0
The passage of time calls for renewed efforts to move beyond the epistemic impasse into which the study of Islamist movements has fallen. It is in this spirit that I approached the post-Uprisings decade as an opportunity to rethink how change is conceptualised and explained. While searching for an alternative analytical lens to understand how a long-standing institution such as the Muslim Brotherhood could conceive and implement organisational change, I encountered a research participant from the Freedom and Justice Party (FJP), the Brotherhood’s political wing. This interlocutor urged me to view the Muslim Brotherhoods not only as a mother organisation, a transnational movement, or a school of thought, but as something closer to a corporation, ‘a multinational, like Coca-Cola, that has been there for a hundred years and suddenly decided to spin off into smaller entrepreneurial projects’.0
I took on board all the participants’ input, particularly this insight, which inspired the distinctive perspective of this book. In response, I developed an integrated institutional framework that engages with organisation studies through the application of the Institutional Logics Perspective (ILP) and Institutional Work. This framework seeks to counter both the dominance of SMT and its variants and the externally oriented approaches that have characterised the study of change in Islamist and Islamist-inspired groupsactors.
Accordingly, this book treats Islamist movements as organisations and institutions, adopting an approach that places organisational culture and intra-party politics at the centre of the analysis.0 Although political parties in the Middle East and North Africa have remained under-studied both before and after the Arab Uprisings,0 this approach conceptualises the processes of party formation and derivation undertaken by the movements examined here as a ‘critical case of organising’.0 This enables a closer examination of organisational dynamics, reconstructed through the views and critiques of first-hand witnesses within the organisations, including dissenting voices, former members and supporters, and current affiliates. This participant recruitment strategy mitigates the risk of producing a leadership-centred analysis marked by elitist bias. Thus, despite an organisational focus, the micro-level experiences of members are not treated as peripheral; rather, they inform the central chapters insofar as they shape organisational dynamics.0 By contrast, the Uprisings themselves and subsequent political developments, including the violent ousting of President Mohamed Morsi (d. 2019), remain in the background, serving primarily as context for the organisational dynamics under examination.
The contribution of this book is both conceptual and empirical. Conceptually, it advances the study of contemporary Islamism by adopting a less epistemically ladenoaded framework (Chapter 1) that offers an alternative approach to analysing change within the Islamist landscape. The institutional perspective underpinning the central chapters advances an unconventional understanding of ‘change’ through a multi-explicative lens encompassing meanings, directions, and intentionality. Based on these three interdependent levels of analysis, the book argues that ‘change’ within Islamist and Islamist-born organisations corresponds either to a controlled and therefore intentional mechanism of replication or to an incomplete and contested process of variation.
Moreover, the application of the ILP to Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers brings together the ideational and material components of institutions within a single conceptual and analytical framework.0 This enables the attribution of meanings to organisational structures and dynamics. The book, therefore, contends that organisational dynamics are neither incidental nor merely reactive phenomena. Rather, they carry specific meanings that tend to remain consistent with pre-existing identity markers and group ideas. The contrasting models of party derivation and transformation adopted by Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers, on the one hand a gradual non-isomorphic change and on the other a coercive modelling on the likeness of an exemplary movement, reveal fundamentally different conceptions of change: ‘variation’ versus ‘replication’, and a ‘possibility’ versus a ‘threat’ to a long-standing group idea.
The organisational dynamics experienced by Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers in the post-Uprisings period indicate that change capacity can be constrained by institutional agents’ fixation on preserving the group idea intact and by an inadequate theorisation of the need for change.0 Ennahda’s longer experience in power, analysed in Chapter 5, highlights the limitations of pursuing substantive organisational change in the absence of a homogeneous identification with a new organisational identity. This, in turn, underscores the agentic role of identification and change receivers in organisational transformation, within a field where change has often been portrayed as a maturation process guided by an enlightened leadership.
Empirically, the central chapters update existing knowledge on the organisational condition of the Egyptian Muslim Brothers and Ennahda. They demonstrate how the cumulative effect of internal dynamics since the Uprisings has produced low levels of consensus and damaged unity in both organisations. In Ennahda’s case, a shaken value system and the coexistence of distinct group identities have affected the party’s overall ‘system-ness’, understood as the combination of coherence and cohesion, projecting the image of a political organisation in search of meaning.0 For the Muslim Brothers, the most visible imprint left by a decade of internal developments has been structural atrophy and inactivity, which have contributed to maintaining the organisational status quo following leadership struggles and sustained criticism of the Brotherhood’s historical leadership.0
Without anticipating the detailed arguments of the chapters that follow, this book may be summarised asseeks an attempt to narrow the distance between organisation studies and Islamism studies. Further research along these lines, however, remains necessary to bring the two fields into closer dialogue.
Conceptual note on Islamists and Islamism
This book conceives the Islamist groups at the core of its analysis as Organised Islamiyyun: ‘socially conservative, politically active’ organisations and institutions in which references to the Islamic tradition permeate organisational structures and inform practices.0 This definition partially echoes Ahmed Khanani’s use of Islamiyyun, which has the advantage of being less empirically and semantically burdened while reproducing the patterns of use of Arab speakers.0 To emphasise the organisational dimension, the term ‘organised’ is juxtaposed with Islamiyyun, highlighting the structured nature of these actors0 in contrast to the widespread presence of independent or ‘informal Islamists’ that proliferatedemerged across the Islamist landscape after the Arab Uprisings.0
Given its focus on Islamist groups involved in institutional politics, this book equates Islamism with political Islam.0 Islamism is understood more broadly as a political culture in which national politics and Islamic expressions are intertwined, and Islamic references function as drivers or inspiration for policies.0 This definition is sufficiently inclusive to encompass both Ennahda and Egypt’s Muslim Brothers, even though the former officially exited the Islamist landscape in 2016.0
The reference points that Islamist organisations draw upon vary considerably. Each movement constructs and continually renews its own frame of reference.0 Accordingly, this book refers to Organised Islamiyyun as socio-political actors who uphold Islamic reference points selectively and flexibly within institutional politics and the nation-state framework, whether the political arena serves as a means to achieve socio-religious reformist objectives, as in the case of the Muslim Brothers,0 or constitutes the principal focus, as in the case of with Ennahda after 2016.0
Furthermore, the book recognises that Islamist groups today are more context-specific than in the past. It therefore refers to the Organised Islamiyyun under scrutiny by their own names – (the Egyptian Muslim Brothers and Ennahda –), acknowledging the distinctivenessuniqueness of the historiesy and contexts in which they operate and challenging tendencies toward sweeping generalisations about Muslim Brotherhoods-like movements.0 Despite this focus on context specificity, the broader definition of Organised Islamiyyun presented in the concluding chapter provides a useful abstraction, allowing the organisational dynamics of the Muslim Brothers and Ennahda to be meaningfully compared. It conceptually captures the interrelation between their material and cultural-symbolic components, illustrating both the complexity of these institutions and the meanings they attach to change.
On research design and methods
This book employs a case study approach, which is most suitable for investigating organisations and institutions.0 It consists of two ‘within-case analyses’,0 resembling quasi-independent assessments. In the central chapters, the case studies of the Muslim Brotherhood’s and Ennahda’s organisational dynamics serve bothsimultaneously as both the object of analysis and the product of inquiry. This conflation reflects Robert K. Yin’s observation that a ‘case is not a sample’, and therefore findings are not assumed to be directly transferablecannot be generalised to other organisations or individuals. The book’s concluding remarks, thus, summarise conceptual ‘lessons learned’ regarding change and the enablers and constraints relevant to the Organised Islamiyyun under scrutiny.0
To build tThe comparison, is built﻿ onthe research identifies a set of ‘embedded units’ of analysis that inform the book’s core arguments:0
  1. Dynamics of party formation
  2. Types of organisational change
  3. Agency
  4. Organisational legitimacy
Although ‘maximum contrasts’ predominated over similarities in structuring the comparison,0 ‘common points of reference’ guided the initial selection of the subjects, ensuring conceptual comparability.0 These common points include:
  1. Party foundation with roots in social movements
  2. Transition from an illegal or semiclandestine state to a leading political party
  3. Selective references to Islam
The two case studies are situated within their spatial contexts (Tunisia and Egypt) and bounded temporally. Time is a critical factor, as it shapes the research questions posed in this book and the understanding of organisational change.0 The focus on ‘dynamics’ encourages the reader to consider time as part of a set of contextual conditions, intertwined with space.0
The book’s core arguments derive from a thematic analysis of primary and secondary sources, including:
  1. Interviews with 3542 current and former members across the organisational spectrum of Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers;
  2. ‘Digital’ observational notes on organisational developments gathered through ongoing interactions with participants and by following the movements’ social media channels;0
  3. Publicly released audiovisual and written interviews of influential but inaccessible leaders;
  4. Historical official documents, communiqués, manifestos, and programmes;
  5. Existing literature on both movements.
The interview excerpts presented in the central chapters illustrate recurring themes that emergeding from data collected online between early 2020 and late 2021. The aAnalysis relied onrelied on a ‘hybrid coding scheme’,0 comprising a preliminary cycle of descriptive coding followed by a second cycle of both ‘focused’ and ‘pattern coding’.0
Book outline
This book comprises five chapters, in addition to an Introduction and Conclusion . After providing an overview of previous approaches to examining Islamist movements’ capacity for change, Chapter 1 introduces the institutional approach and the multilevel perspective on ‘change’ adopted throughout the study.
Chapter 2 analyses the formation of the FJP, the political wing of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, as a major organisational development following the Arab Uprisings. Chapter 3 examines the Brotherhood’s organisational restructuring after the military coup of 2013 and concludes with an assessment of the effects of these dynamics, coupled with the group’s violent expulsion from state institutions, on the organisation ten10 years later. A briefer version of the group’s internal developments was published in 2024 in the co-authored article ‘A movement in exile: The Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood’s survival action frames in the post-coup era (2013–2023).’
The second half of the book opens with Chapter 4, which investigates Ennahda’s incomplete and partial transformation into a modern political organisation. Chapter 5 examines the impact of Ennahda’s internal transition from an Islamist movement to a civil party of Muslim Democrats on the movement’s system-ness in the post-specialisation period. This case study draws on an adapted version of the co-authored article ‘An organizational perspective on fading system-ness: Insights from Ennahda’s post-specialization period (2016–2021).’
The book concludes with a comparative analysis of the organisational dynamics of Ennahda and the Muslim Brotherhood, applying the multilevel perspective on change introduced in Chapter 1 to fully address the central research question that inspired this study.

Institutional framework for understanding change in the Egyptian Muslim Brothers and Ennahda
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Institutional framework for understanding change
Debating ‘change’: Quest for an alternative to epistemic stagnation
Within the field of Islamism studies, scholarly perspectives on ‘change’ have often conceptualised it as a mechanistic, progressive, and linear process, assumed to result from the inclusion of Islamist movements in institutional politics.0 Consequently, over the past decade since the Arab Uprisings, scholarship on contemporary Islamist movements has descended into a state of ‘epistemic stagnation’, driven by an excessive reliance on Social Movement Theory (SMT) and its variants as analytical frameworks for understanding their trajectories and capacity for change.0
However, this dominant understanding of ‘change’ has increasingly proved inadequate for capturing the complexity of Islamist movements’ pathways. The ‘inclusion-moderation’ thesis (and its inverse) reduces change to ideological or behavioural moderation, often overlooking temporary, partial, or contradictory shifts that are critical tofor understanding the enablers and constraints of change. It also prioritises outcomes over the processes of transformation, culminating in Asef Bayat’s ‘post-Islamist turn’, which conceives change as both a ‘condition and a project’ involving transformed ideas, approaches, and practices that transcend classical Islamism.0
Framing moderation as a pragmatic, unilateral ‘push towards the political centre’ to broaden appeal0 obscures the extent to which Islamists’ political participation is frequently constrained, manipulated, or conditionedcontingent upon conditions imposed by dominant political actors.0 Moreover, the elusive nature of ‘moderation’ has often prompted scholars to introduce additional points of comparison and external categories to relate Islamist parties and their leaders to; thus examining ‘change’ in relational terms.0 In the context of the 2011 Uprisings, the debate on the inclusion-moderation thesis concluded that, during unsettled periods such as political transitions, the logic underpinning this thesis becomes less applicable due to the instability of emerging political institutions, highlighting the need for conceptual tools better suited to capturing change.0
Its inverse hypothesis, the exclusion-radicalisation nexus, presents similar limitations and has been further challenged by scholars who argue that both low and moderate levels of repression, combined with the fear of further oppressivesuppressive measures, can induce moderation.0 Similarly, long-term societal rejection, harsh political exclusion, or conditions of exile can produce a moderating effect on social movements seeking acceptance, popularity, or mere survival.0
While revisiting the debate on Islamist movements’ exclusion, Mohammad Affan draws on rational choice and political opportunity theories to argue that exclusion may trigger ambivalent reactions at both the meso and micro levels. At the meso level, a group may moderate its positions to secure future integration, whereas individual members may perceive exclusion as an existential threat, prompting the opposite response.0 Analysing exclusion in these terms, however, reduces behavioural changes to almost predictable outcomes, offering limited explanatory insight focused primarily on structural incentives while treating change as a reactive mechanism.0
Contributors to the debate on how to conceptualise change in Islamist movements have urged scholars to move beyond the ‘linear and mechanistic hypotheses of inclusion-moderation and its inverse principle’0 by incorporating mediating and intangible factors, such as memories, personal experiences, and emotions.0 Among them, Khalil al-Anani, drawing on disaggregated reactions to repression, argues that opposition movements respond unevenly to new domestic environments marked by increasing state violence.0 These interventions call forto contextualise the interplay of individual experiences and human reactions to be contextualised within the rapidly shifting local, regional, and international landscapes of the post-Uprisings period, persuadinghas often led scholars to reconceptualise change as a process of adaptation.0
Adaptive change functions ‘as a [strategic] or tactical response’ to a rapidly evolving external environment and emerges as a ‘result of either persuasion or coercion’.0 Adaptation entails a gradual acquisition of compromised positions, combined with ‘a pragmatic self-restraint in rhetoric and practice’0 and organisational reconfiguration to cope with new conditions.0 Framed in this way, change is understood simultaneously as a response to and a product of external dynamics. However, tThis perspectiveadaptation turn shifts the analytical focus towards macro-level influences as primary drivers of transformation, thereby downplaying the roles of individual agents and potential inherited organisational constraints.0
Recently, a new focus has emerged in the study of Islamist movements’ trajectories. Scholars have increasingly turned to the micro level of analysis, treating individual experiences as ‘micro-studies’ that illustrate broader dynamics of change.0 This perspective reconstructs mechanisms of transformation on the basis of personal experiences and accounts, while theorising ‘impact’ as a generalisable outcome that these micro-level changes may reflect at the organisational level. From this standpoint, lived experiences, including imprisonment, torture,0 geography, and displacement,0 are understood as key drivers and indicators of a group’s ideological and behavioural moderation0 or radicalisation.0 While reconstructing individual trajectories can help explainilluminate factionalism across ideological lines0 and leadership divides,0 this approach often focuses narrowly on one or two small, competingnflicting groups and risks projecting these limited experiences onto the broader organisation. Consequently, the emphasis on ‘subjectivities’0 and personal experiences0 may yield a partial understanding of complex internal developments, potentially producing a distorted picture of a movement’s organisational state.
Beyond individual or factional trajectories, onea strand of scholarship has frequently conceptualised change as ‘an evolutionary process of maturation’.0 This approach implies a continuum of development from origins to a later condition, often driven by an enlightened, pragmatic, or self-interested elitete.0 Within this framework, the personal development of prominent Islamist leaders is employed to trace and explain the transformation of movements over time, generating leadership-centred analyses.0
Building on this evolutionary premise,e same premise of an ‘evolutionary process’, scholars have developed macro-comparative studiesanalyses to systematically assesslly the trajectories of specific categories of political actorsgroups and to reconsider the broader phenomenon of political Islam.0 Examples include studies of the Muslim Brotherhood as a transnational movement, with attention toexamining its ‘evolving nature’ and the impact of the late President Mohamed Morsi’s violent removal from powerousting on Brotherhood-inspired and aligned movements, including Ennahda.0 Viewed through this lens, change in Islamist movements entails an evolutionary learning curve, often triggered by shocking events that reshape behaviour and strategic choices in light of the experiences of more successful, ideologically proximaterelated groups.
A decade after the Arab Uprisings, only a small number of scholars have examined change in institutional and organisational terms. Moving beyond dominant frameworks, Jérôme Drevon and Pietro Marzo conceptualise changes in strategies within Islamist groups as the constrained institutionalisation of choices made at critical junctures, whose effectsich continue to shape subsequent behaviour, drawing on historical institutionalism.0  To explain why some Islamist parties undergo significant transformation and how such change affects organisational structure and identity, Sebnem Gumuscu and Rory McCarthy focus on the role of factional and intraparty politics.0
In a similar vein, Nora Medhat Abdelkader and Barbara Zollner employ New Institutionalism to explore the relationship between social movements and political parties in the cases of Ennahda and the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood.0 Using the cases of Ennahda and the Brotherhood's political wing, the Freedom and Justice Party (FJP) (the Brotherhood’s political wing), Zollner frames change as the successful or failed emancipation of a party from its parent movement, with the success or failure of this process creating conditions more or less favourable to national democratisation.0 Marie Vannetzel echoes this perspective, arguing that the Muslim Brotherhood’s failure in the post-Uprisings period stemmed from the FJP’s constrained party development, highlighting the organisational nature of such an outcome.0
Aside from this small group of scholars, change is often approached as a mechanistic, linear process of ideological and behavioural variation or ‘approximation’,0 or  as a reactive adaptation driven by external pressures or strategic cost–benefit calculations on the part of theby leadership. In seeking to move beyond this state of epistemic impasse, this book challenges linear conceptions of change, whether framed as progress or regression toward a predetermined outcome. It instead advances an understanding of change as a non-linear, contested process that may remain partial, reversible, or too organisationally costly to complete.0
This approach avoids interpreting the divergent paths of Ennahda and the Muslim Brotherhood since the Uprisings through a quasi-deterministic lens. In lineAligning with Gumuscu and  McCarthy’s view that intraparty politics offers fresh ‘explanatory leverage’ for understanding change in Islamist movements,0 this book foregrounds organisational dynamics and recognises their potential to de-ideologise the literature on Islamist and Islamist-derived parties. As the remainder of this chapter shows, this approach enriches scholarship that values intra-organisational developments. It offers an alternative to the epistemic stagnation characterising the field by ‘transcending the emphasis on ideological and behavioural moderation and freeing Islamist actors from the constraints of the “post-Islamist turn”’,0 which often denies them agency by associating ‘change’ with the unrestrained depletion of the Islamist project.0
Towards an iIntegrated institutional framework
Introduction to the Institutional Logics Perspective
As outlined in the introduction, this book treats Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers as comparable institutions and organisations. Drawing on the Institutional Logics Perspective (ILP), it conceptualises them as institutions in the sense of enduring systems of beliefs and organised practices,0 and as organisations,  understood as goal-oriented groups with defined structures.0
Emerging from sociological institutionalism in the early 1990s and largely applied inwithin organisation studies,0 the ILP is valuable for bridging the gap between external ‘macro-level influences’, emphasised by neo-institutionalists, and the role of internal values and vested interests in shaping organisational behaviour, foregrounded by earliertraditional institutionalist approaches.0 Unlike historical institutionalism, the ILP does not confine institutions to the ‘inertial tendency’ of choices made at ‘critical junctures’, thereby moving beyond path dependency.0
The ILP situates individuals and institutions within their societal context, reaffirming the significance of macro-level influences for institutional analysis. It also contributes to a ‘structural theory of culture’ based on the patterned relations and interactions between symbols, beliefs, norms, and practices within an organisation or organisational field.0 Following Patricia H. Thornton, William Ocasio and Michael Lounsbury, institutional logics are defined as:
socially-constructed, historical patterns of cultural symbols and material practices, including assumptions, values, and beliefs, by which individuals and organisations provide meaning to their daily activity, organize time and space and reproduce their lives and experiences.0
By definition, institutional logics are accessible to individuals and organisations through long-term memory and can be ‘invoked for social sense-making, problem-solving, decision-making and coordination’ during periods of disorientation or crisis.0 As belief systems and vocabularies of meaning guiding group behaviour, institutional logics are key constructs for understanding the interplay of cultural symbols and material practices that generates ‘a sense of common purpose and unity’ within institutions and organisations.0
In Islamist movements operating across differentverse institutional orders, multiple institutional logics tend toinevitably coexist. These logicsy  may cohabit, hybridise over time, or compete with one another. Among themse plural logics, however, the prevailing or (also described as embedded or dominant) logic shapes organisational behaviour and official narratives.0 For example, throughout their organisational histories, the Muslim Brothers and Ennahda have operated according to institutional logics derived from the ‘culture’ of the institutional orders under which they formed and evolved.0 The aAuthoritarian Egyptian and Tunisian states constituted the institutional orders shaping the secretive and clandestine groups, whereas their respective Muslim-conservative societies, perceived as under threatened by corrupt social habits and un-Islamic leaderships, moulded their logics as socio-reformist religious Islamist movements tasked with correcting society and the political orders. Thus, institutional logics are historically contingent and context-dependent.0
As indicated above, the ILP emphasises the coexistence of material and cultural-symbolic components of institutions rather than framing them in terms of a rational-irrational dichotomy.0 It encapsulates a duality in which these components are ‘mutually constitutive’ and ‘ontologically complicit’.0 Moreover, ILP theorists argue that the ideas and meanings constituting the cultural-symbolic components of institutions are not fixed.0 This attribute renders the ILP particularly suited to examining change within Islamist movements. As Chapter 3 demonstrates in the case of the Muslim Brothers, a dialectic tensions between competing institutional logics can also explain in-group partitioning and low system-ness within movements and parties.
Although not formally included among the micro-foundations of institutional logics, collective emotions, including historically rooted traumas, also function as additional ‘embodied understandings’ of institutions’ material practices and ideational components.0 Accordingly, Roger Friedlanda leading ILP theorist observes that ‘emotion not only mediates the formation and the reproduction of institutions but can itself be institutional’,0 meaning that social emotions constitute a crucial ‘link between what we are and what we do’.0 In the cases of Ennahda and Egypt’s Muslim Brothers, state repression and existential fear representute social emotions capable of shaping conduct over the long term.0 Beyond fostering a sense of belonging within a group, ‘ontological insecurity’, historical traumas, and suspicion of the ‘other’ also contribute to the emergence of autocratic tendencies in long-banned organisations, influencing both their organisational culture and their material structures and practices.0
Institutional agents, identity work, and institutional maintenance
The ILP accords a significant the role to individual agency, on the premisegiven that ‘social actors are key to understanding institutional continuity and change’.0 Although institutional orders reflect macro-level influences that regularise the behaviour of institutions, individuals can also act as powerful agents, reconciling and exploiting multiple, often contradictory, logics through mechanisms that both enable and constrain change.0 Despite organisational behaviour being shaped by prevailing institutional logics, the application of thean ILP still ‘implies individual agency, albeit subject to constraints’,0 as actors are considered ‘partially autonomous’.0 The so-called ‘paradox of embedded agency’ therefore becomes less problematic, though not fully resolved, since social actors are not whollyexclusively enabled or constrained by the institutions they seek to change.0 Rather,  ‘they can be enabled and constrained through them’.0
Drawing on W. Richard Scott’s definition, this book conceptualises agency as an ‘actor’s ability to affect the social world by altering the rules, relational ties, or distribution of resources’.0 To operationalise this concept, the following chapters distinguish between three categories of agents.
The first are ‘institutional agents’,0 an elite group of actors capable of initiating coercive organisational change, applied here to the Brotherhood’s historical leadership (Chapters 2 and 3).0 These actors form a small clique engaged in ‘change  resistance activities’ to protect the institutional logic of the secretive socio-reformist movement and its group ideas.0 Their actions constitute what is termed ‘institutional maintenance work’, a concept derived from ‘institutional work’ and often contrasted with the ILP,0 referring﻿ to the ‘creative act’ of repairing and maintaining institutions in accordance with certain preferences and interestsself-interested considerations.0
The next category is the ‘institutional entrepreneur’.0 Exemplified by Ennahda’s founder and Islamic thinker, Rached Ghannouchi, the local entrepreneur theorises the need for organisational change (Chapter 4).0 In this role, the entrepreneur acts not only as a charismatic promoter of change0 but also as a ‘broker’ mediating between plural logics.0 Entrepreneurs contribute to the de-institutionalisation of outdated values and practices while fostering the integration of new organisational norms and ideas (Chapter 4).0
Alongside institutional agents and entrepreneurs, this framework emphasises identity and identification as crucial in enabling and constraining change.0 Identity occupies an intermediate position between institutional logics, individuals, individuals, and group behaviour.0 Reflecting the organisational focus of this book, the concept of ‘organisational identity’ addresses the question ‘who are we as an organisation?’ by referring to the party rank-and-file members’ internalisation of the group’s ‘central, distinctive and enduring characteristics’.0
Building on ‘institutional work’, ‘identity work’ denotes the purposive reconstruction and recrafting of organisational identities and group ideas through everyday actions, discourses, and practices.0 Correspondingly, ‘identification’ functions as an agentic process through which individuals, acting alone or in small groups, accept, resist, or reject new institutional logics and organisational ideas.0 This process positions the recipients of change (‘identity targets’) as active agents rather than passive subjectsrecipients of transformation (see Chapter 5).0 Attention to identity work counteractsaddresses the long-standing tendency in institutional analysis to prioritise the effects of that macro-level influences on institutions over the agency of social actorsthe role of social actors.0
Theorising change and change capacity
This book adopts a multilevel perspective on change. The first analytical level concerns the ‘meanings’ associated with change. Change is bivalent: it may be non-isomorphic, involving variation in organisational practices, goals, or norms following transformative or destabilising events (Chapter 4),0 or isomorphic, equating to organisational modelling and mimicry, whereby established norms and practices are reproduced rather than varied (Chapter 2).0
In contexts where organisations operate under similar unsettled conditions, they may tend towards or be forced into convergence in organisational form and thinking.0 Although institutional theorists identify normative, mimetic, and coercive pressures driving isomorphism,0 this book focuses exclusively on ‘coercive modelling’, defined as a constraining process by which one organisation comes to resemble a more powerful one in form, thinking, and goals one.0 Despite its constraining character, cCoercive  modelling, or isomorphic change, still allows for some degree of agency.0 This first analytical dimension thus unpacks the significance of change in terms of both alteration and reproduction of institutions.0
The second analytical level concerns ‘change direction’. For Ennahda and the Muslim Brotherhood, organisational change may involve a transition from clandestine, underground movements to public actors at the forefront of institutional politics. Change direction could also entail the partial or complete transformation from a comprehensive organisation into a political party focused solely on institutional politics, and vice versa. Both scenarios generate institutional contradictions, manifesting as tensions between distinct logics and creating opportunities for social actors (individual and collective) to act as change agents.0 In this context, change may be temporary, partial, or stalled if it reflects limited adjustment rather than the formation of a new, enduring organisational arrangement.
Finally, change dynamics can be assessed by reference to the degree of ‘conscious intentionality’.0 Change may be deliberate, aiming to reproduce, restore, or diversify institutional meanings and practices, or it may occur spontaneously through less centrally -directed processes.
Beyond these three analytical dimensions, this book draws on Richard Soparnot’s concept of ‘change capacity’ to examine the ability of long-standing organisations to initiate and implement change. Change capacity is conceived as the ability ‘to produce solutions (content) that respond to environmental evolution (external context) and/or organisational evolution (internal context) and to implement these change processes successfully (process)’.0
Institutional logics at work in the pre-2011 Muslim Brothers and Ennahda
The Muslim Brothers’ prevailing logic: A gGradual reformist movement or an oppositional political group?
Since its establishment in 1928, Hasan al-Banna envisioned the Muslim Brotherhood as a distinctive and ‘virtuous society’ of true Muslims,0 bound together by the shared idea of being a ‘Brotherhood in faith’ (al-uUkhuwwa fi-l-imanImaniyya).0 Conceived as a unique spiritual and exemplary community, the Brotherhood has always prioritised reforming the social order over the pursuingt of political power,0 in line with its mission to gradually restore authentic Islamic morality within Egyptian society.0
As a comprehensive socio-reformist movement upholding a gradual, ‘multidimensional program of belief and action’, the Brotherhood accords primacy to the daʿwa (religious and moral outreach) above all other activities.0 This educational mission begins with reforming those who have deviated from the right path by re-instilling a ‘deep commitment to the role of religion’ as a corrective to moral decay and as a prerequisite for establishing a pure Islamic society.0 It then extends to the reform of the nation and the broader Islamic communityr ummah.0
As Hasan al-Banna explained in his treatise Daʿwatuna (Our Mission), ‘the mission of the Muslim Brotherhood is the preaching of a principle’.0 Through continuous cultivation of the Brothers’ ethos and religious upbringing (tarbiya), which moves beyond correctly executed worship, the grouporganisation ﻿ steadily pursues the ‘dynamic goal of monitoring social changes and takes what is necessary to deal with them from an Islamic perspective […]’.0
The value system underlying the ideal Society of Muslim Brothers reflects the core tenets of any puritanical movement. It embraces a patriarchal conception of the family, opposes the liberalisation of divorce laws and marriage, advocates state protection for daily acts of Islamic worship, and supports the enforcement of bans on behaviours deemed indecent or immoral.0 The foundational principles of the Brotherhood’s fikr (thought) and organisational culture are encapsulated in the Arkan al-Bayʿa (Pillars of Allegiance)0 and explained by al-Banna in his Risalat al-Taʿlim (Epistle of the Teachings). The first and most fundamental pillar is fahm (the understanding of Islam), conceived as:
as a comprehensive belief system addressing all aspects of life. It is a state and a homeland (or government and ummah). It is morality and power (or mercy and justice). It is a culture and a law (or knowledge and jurisprudence). It is material and wealth (or gain and prosperity). It is jihad and daʿwa (or an army and a missioncause). And ultimately, it is true belief and perfected worship.0
The Muslim Brotherhood’s organisational structure embodies a holistic and self-sufficient vision of a virtuous society, bound by a shared understanding of Islam.0 The organisation functions as the vehicle for the gradual Islamisation of broader society, aiming to create a new generation of true Muslim men and women while presenting itself as a model for like-minded movements.0
Before turning into a movement in exile in the post-2013 period, the Brotherhood operated in Egypt through a ‘tight-knit and compartmentalised’ structure that stretched along vertical and horizontal axes.0 Vertically, the structure encompassed leadership and the administrative apparatus across seven administrative levels, while operational sections, committees, and units were positioned horizontally. The vertical axis ensured centralised decision-making, whereas the horizontal axis allowed for transversal execution of tasks0 in support of the group’s proselytising mission. This double structure also proved vital to its resilience and survival (Chapter  3).0
Following three major crackdowns in 1948, 1954, and 1965, the Brotherhood’s second founding (1968–1982) produced a markedly different organisation from al-Banna’s public  Society.0 Over time, the Brotherhood evolved into a mass-based organisation that expanded in both membership and activities. Upon the reconstitution of its ranks-and-files and the refutation of takfiri ideas under Hasan al-Hudaybi’s guide (1949–1973) – the General Guide who succeeded al-Banna – the group also adopted increased secrecy and a more closed, highly disciplined and elitist outlook.0 Notoriously, al-Hudaybi established a tradition of monopolistic leadership while attempting to preserve the organisation in the dark years of persecution under Gamal Abdel Nasser’s rule.0 Over time, the Brotherhood evolved into a mass-based organisation that expanded in both membership and activities.
For the Brotherhood, political participation has always been instrumental, serving ‘as a means to extend its daʿwa to another domain’, an objective achievable without forming a legally recognised political party or provoking social upheaval.0 This approach reflects al-Banna’s teachings, which regarded governance as an ‘important cornerstone’ of the religious reformist project and ‘a means’ rather than an end, without which the reformist cCall would remain ‘a cry in the wilderness’.0 After its second founding, the Brotherhood has’s engagedment in politics according tohas followed the logic of a non-violent, reformist Islamist movement, aiming to work ‘within the framework of existing laws and institutions in order to transform them’0 throughby commanding the good and the practice ofimplementing religious and ethical upbringingcultivation.0
In pursuit of this objective, some Brotherhood figures engaged in politics as early as 1976 to petition the Egyptian Parliament to enact laws in accordance with Sharia and repeal those incompatible with Islamic teachings. At this stage, the Brotherhood focused on lobbying parliamentarians to designate Sharia as ‘the primary source of legislation’ in the constitution,0 a change that President Anwar Sadat later introduced to appease Islamic activists and conservative sectors of Egyptian society after extending women’s legal rights in marriage and divorce.0
In 1984, motivated by the same rationale, the Muslim Brotherhood entered the Egyptian Parliament by fielding candidates under the list of the Wafd Party’s list, a nationalist liberal party. In 1987, under the banner ‘Islam is the solution’, some Brotherhood figures formed the Islamic Alliance with the Labour Party and the Liberal Party. As Mustafa Mashhour, who later became the group’s fifth General Guide, explained to the readers of Liwaʾ al-Islam, the Muslim Brothers’ engagement in institutional politics aimed to ‘educate the state, the institution and the people […], and complete the transformation in the way of thinking of all towards God and Sharia’.0
The Brotherhood’s participation in national elections was guided by a strategy of incremental legal reform, primarily targeting laws deemed inconsistent with its interpretation of Islamic teachings. Its main focus was Sadat’s revised Personal Status Code, which the group sought to amend as un-Islamic.0 To achieve this, the Brotherhood functioned as a pressure group rather than forming a political party or seeking a parliamentary majority, strategies that would have exposed its leadership and members to heightened repression.0 As Sumita Pahwa notes in Politics as Worship, the Muslim Brothers’ leadership framed political activity in terms of ‘active piety’, positioning themselves in Egypt’s political arena as ‘actors committed to public righteousness without partisanship’.0
The advent of Hosni Mubarak’s presidency coincided with the Brotherhood’s  outreach to civil society and its growing appeal among Egyptians, compelling the regime to acknowledge the movement as a responsible socio-religious rather than political actor.0 Amid the dismantling of Nasser’s statist model, the Brotherhood sought to fill the vacuum left by the Egyptian state in providing social welfare to the impoverished, making ‘a pious road inside the state’ through the ‘politics of goodness’.0 While consistent with Islamic precepts, the Brotherhood's social initiatives alsoboosted expanded itthe Brotherhood’s popularity among, particularly among Egypt’s lower socio-economic groups.0
Mubarak deliberately allowed the group to operate and expand its social welfare activities to mitigate the effects of rapid economic liberalisation. Consequently, the Muslim Brothers became unofficially part of an ‘authoritarian coalition’0 that , de facto, contributed to sustaininged the former regime until its fall in 2011, enabling the group to consolidate popular support and surviveensure its survival.0 Remaining a tolerated yet far-reaching socio-reformist movement, capable of shaping individuals, society, and state institutions, constituted the operational logic guiding the Brotherhood. Through this subtle alignment with Mubarak’s regime, the Brotherhood embodied a non-systemic and non-revolutionary form of opposition under the former  rais.0
From 1984 onwards, the group gradually extended its influence within Egypt’s major professional syndicates, securing positions on executive boards and thereby consolidating its presence among Egypt’s educated middle class.0 Yet, iIts control over the five most politically active syndicates functioned more as low-level pressure than a direct challenge to state authority. The Brotherhood refrained from contesting syndicate presidencies, which were typically held by government-backed candidates.0 Nevertheless, this period produced a generation of politicised Brotherhood-affiliated figures active within unions and professional associations, sensitive to workers’ issues and later identified as the group's reformist trend (al-tayyar al-islahi).0
During Mubarak’s era, a self-preserving institutional logic emerged within the Brotherhood’s senior leadership. A clique of long-term leaders prioritised safeguarding the tanzim (the organisation’s inner apparatus) and maintaining the group’s organisational culture as prerequisites for fulfilling its reformist mission.0 They sought to protect the purity of the ‘Brotherhood in faith’ (its underlying group idea) from corrupting tendencies, viewing this as essential to influencing society and state institutions according to Islamic principles. In their view, without the ‘Brotherhood  in God’ there could be neither a return to an authenticpure Islamic order nor compliance with Sharia provisions in government.0 Thus, preserving the organisation and its group idea became integral to the prevailing logic of the reformist movement embedded in the historical leadership’s vision of what came to be labelled as the ‘historical leadership’ (al-qiyada al-tarikhiyya).0 For this small group of long-term leaders, this logic translated into operating in Egypt cautiously, without ever crossing the lines drawn by the Mubarak’s regime.
The death of Mamun al-Hudaybi (sixth General Guide, 2000–2004) reinforced this ‘self-limiting’ and accommodationist approach.0 During the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, the Brotherhood did not take a leading role in anti-war mobilisations, some of which evolved into anti-goverment protests led by leftist and secular groups and were violently repressed by Mubarak’s regime.0 Instead, it coordinated an anti-war rally in close collaboration with the government.0
In 2005, under the new General Guide, Mohammed Mahdi Akef (General Guide 2004–2010), the Muslim Brothers participated in what Mubarak presented as a ‘free and open elections’.0 Following the Brotherhood﻿’sir initial electoral gains, Mubarak’s National Democratic Party (NDP) intervened to intimidate opposition forces before the subsequent round. While the Kefaya Movement (a grassroots, cross-partisan coalition opposing Mubarak) and the reformist Muslim Brother Abdul Munim Abul Futuh called for an election boycott, the Brotherhood’s historical leadership refrained from joining the Kefaya-led demonstrations, which openly challenged Mubarak’s presidency.0 Similarly, the group remained aloof from the waves of workers’ protests that emerged from 2006 onwards, projecting the image of a cautious and timid opposition.0
In the second round of the 2005 parliamentary elections, the Brotherhood deliberately avoided contesting more than a third of the available seats, in line with its motto ‘participation not domination’, due to concerns that a broader victory might provoke confrontation with the security eforcestablishment.0 This decision, still regretted by some former members as a lost opportunity to delegitimise Mubarak’s NDP and to begin purifying state institutions of ‘deep-state’ elements, intensified the generational and ideological rift within the movement.0 On one side stood the Brotherhood’s old guard and their loyalists; on the other, its youth (al-shabab al-ikhwan) and a small group of reformists.0
Meanwhile, the senior leadership consolidated its control by restructuring the chain of command to increase reliance on its approval.0 Their endorsement became essential for promotion within the Guidance Bureau, the Shura Council, and the leadership of its political office.0 Internal elections held between 2009 and 2010 culminated in the appointment of Mohamed Badie as General Guide, reinforcing the dominance of the established elite over reformist figures.0 These elections drew criticism from younger and reformist members, who alleged that procedural irregularities had been engineered by the historical leadership to secure its hold on power.0
At the onset of the Arab Uprisings of 2011, pre-existing ties between young Brothers and the Kefaya Movement’s activists became a key driver behind the broad participation of young Brotherhood members in the protests.0 However, the old guard perceived this proximitycloseness as a potential secular threat to the Brotherhood’s group identity.0 Reflecting its cautious, gradualist approach to societal and instand political reform, the leadership issued a programmatic statement on the eve of the Uprisings, outlining strategies to avoid a full-scale revolution in Egypt.0 On 25 January, ordinary members joined marches and demonstrations individually, in accordance with directives from the historical leadership, which opposed the Brotherhood’s collective and visible participation, particularly at a time when protesters were vocally demanding the resignation of the Minister of Interior and denouncing police abuses.0
The Brotherhood’s non-revolutionarysystemic opposition to Mubarak’s regime,0 rooted in al-Banna’s gradual reformist approach and the belief that ‘success could only follow patience and planning’,0 reinforced its posture as an ‘accommodationist actor’ rather than a revolutionary counter-elite.0 The group'sis cautious stance is critically labelled as intizar, a term that, in this context, denotes its ‘wait-and-see’ strategy. The term is frequently invoked to criticise the old guard’s response to the post-2013 military coup that ousted the late President Morsi (see Chapter 3), a response that reflecteding the enduring logic of the Brotherhood as a gradualist, reform-oriented movement.
Ennahda and the prevalence of the ‘political’ logic
Established as a religious proselytising group,0 Ennahda’s founders initially convened within the circles of the Association pour la Sauvegarde du Coran, a state-sponsored organisation founded in 1967 under the Tunisian Ministry of Culture, without establishing formal organisational ties.0 The movement’s early mission was to promote religious practice and Quranic teachings in halaqat (small study circles), with the aimas a means of reviving Tunisia’s Arab-Islamic heritage and identity in response to the perceived threat posed by President Habib Bourguiba’s modernisation project.0
As a child of the Enlightenment, a Sorbonne graduate, and the leader of a modernist, Francophile intellectual elite,0 Bourguiba aimed to effect systemic social change through legal, educational, and land reforms. These policies marginalised the ulama,208  (Muslim legal scholars), abrogated certain Maliki practices, and reorganised religious life under the strict control of the Neo-Destour Party, renamed the Socialist DestourianSocialist Destourian Party (PSD) in 1964.0 Against this backdrop, those who joined Ennahda quickly embraced a mission to defend the country’s Islamic identity.0
In 1979, Ennahda’s leaders sought to formalise their early preaching and educational activities in mosques and university faculties by applying for registration as a religious association. Their request, however, was denied by the authorities.0 Later that year, they secretly convened their founding congress in Manouba, adopting theformalising the organisation as nameal-Jamaʿa al-Islamiyya bi-fi Tunis (the Islamic Group in Tunisia) and formalising thethrough the adoption of a  organisationalformal structure  and internal regulations.0 The Congress (al-muʾtamar), composed of 70 delegates representing regional branches, was established as the movement’s highest authority.0 It was tasked with reviewing leadership performance, appointing or dismissing the amir (head of the movement), and revising the group’s strategies, ideology, and operations. The amir had the authority to appoint both the leaders of the regional Shura Ccouncils and the members of the Central Executive Bureau.0
Ennahda’s organisational evolution departed early on from its initial phase of preaching and proselytising mission, setting the movement on a distinct trajectory. By the early 1980s, it had evolved into an underground political opposition group, the Islamic Tendency Movement (MTI), before rebranding as the Ennahda Movement ahead of the 1989 national elections.0 Throughout its history, Ennahda remained clandestine. Despite four separate attempts to obtain legal recognition,0 it achieved official status only in the aftermath of the Arab Uprisings.0
By the mid-1980s, young Tunisian students found in Ennahda’s preachers an innovative discourse imbued with an emotional tone which spoke directly to their quotidian problems and contemporary political issues.0 As an Ennahda’s senior member who joined the movement as a high school student in the  1980s recalls:
They told me, ‘we have this halaqa, why don’t you join us? We’ll be studying Quran, fiqh, hadith and [will] discuss the situation in Palestine and the Islamic ummah…’ These topics sounded so interesting to me because they were some sort of extra-curricular activities that you could not find at school or anywhere else!0
Within Ennahda, the traditional concept of daʿwa evolved rapidly, conferring on religion a practical social dimension and freeing it from an unattractive, static message. By linking Islamic teachings to pressing social and political issues, such as economic injustice, Arab unity, and the Palestinian cause, the MTI foregrounded the social dimension of religious engagement and merged it with broader political activism.0
Throughout the 1980s, Ennahda’s trajectory closely mirrored that of student activism in Tunisia, expanding its focus beyond socio-religious reform to include labour struggles, feminism, human rights, and democratisation.0 This broadened its ideological framework, making it highly adaptable.0 Confrontations with the more established and politically experienced Tunisian Lleft on university campuses accelerated the movement’s politicisation, as Ennahda militants adopted many of the leftists’ methods of mobilisation and communication.0
Internally, despite the predominant role of the amir and the Congress at the top of Ennahda’s organisational hierarchy, repeated arrests and the need for secrecyconstraints of clandestine operation compelled the leadership to adopt flexibility and decentralisation,0 le aving a lasting imprint on its structures. In the wake of the 1984 bread riots and the subsequent crackdown, the movement restructured its higher education sector into autonomous units to preserve student activism,0 mirroringechoing the self-reliant regional structures.0 Given the regime’s limited ability to control youth politics on university campuses and the autonomy granted by Ennahda’s leadership to student activists, Islamist students were ‘free to function as [members of] a political group’, agitating for political change.0
The movement’s internal composition further explains why preaching and educational activities diminished early in favour of the ‘worldly reward’ associated with political activism.0 Many student activists, including known as﻿the sons and daughters of the so-called ‘ IIslamo-destouriaen’ group within the PSD members), later joined Ennahda, bringing with them politicised perspectives shaped by their family backgrounds.0 Moreover, the top leadership’s increasingly politicised stance reinforced this trend.
At the 1986 Congress, Ennahda’s leadership formally acknowledged the primacy of the political dimension, even as the prevailing view among members continued to favour a broader socio-reformist mission.0 Throughout the 1980s, the group adopted a more oppositional stance within Tunisia’s tightly controlled political system, where the lack of pluralism hastened the leadership’s embrace of democratic principles as a means to challenge the authoritarian political order.one-party state. One might argue that Ghannouchi was, to some extent, compelled to drink ‘the cup of democracy in one gulp back in the 1980s’, a far swifter change than that of many other Islamist movements.0 In 1989, longing to become a political party, Ennahda applied for legal recognition, but the; authorities rejected the application, citing the criminal records of some members.0
In May 1991, Ennahda faced severe repression after the regime accused it of plotting to overthrow the state, assassinate President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, and establish an Iranian-style Islamic Republic. As a result, the imprisonment of members and leaders increased sharply, alongside a wave of Nahdawis fleeing the country. Thereafter, Ennahda shifted its activities towards social assistance, mobilising support for detainees and their families.0
At the 1992 Congress, Ennahda’s leadership reassessed and renewed the movement’s strategies, providing the members in exile with a formal ‘institutional framework’. This included the election of a new Shura Council to operate from abroad. Following Ghannouchi’s voluntary exile, the Executive Bureau relocated to London.0 As leaders and members were dispersed across France, Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Canada, Italy, and parts of the Gulf, the Congress authorised the establishment of parallel structures abroad to mitigate the travel, visa and financial constraints that restricted coordination and movement among members.0 Even prior to the 1992 Congress, Ennahda had established a Political Bureau and a Communication Office in France in 1987, tasked with informing the international community about state abuses against Tunisians and mobilising support for detained Nahdawis.0
From the mid-1990s onwards, Ennahda became deeply involved in human rights advocacy,0 framing its mission around the defence of civil liberties, political prisoners, and fundamental rights. This shift reshaped its public image and aligned its discourse with the language and priorities of transnational advocacy networks.0 In response, the Ben Ali regime intensified repression by implementing an extensive system of surveillance and harassment aimed at deterring anti-regime activism at home and abroad. Measures included passport confiscation, denial of employment and university access to relatives of detainees, compulsory daily reporting to police stations, house raids, street intimidation, and arbitrary detention.0
From abroad, Ennahda sought to expose state abuses and attract international attention.0 In 1995, in addition to officially adopting non-violence as a means of political change in Tunisia, the leadership voted to collaborate with a broad range of political and social actors and political groups, signalling the movement’s commitment to advocating ‘political rights for all’.0
In 1999, Ennahda launched an internal re-evaluation of its practices and methods. A document accessed from the movement’s online archive emphasised the need to adopt the principle of tamyiz (differentiation, or distinction) between politics and daʿwa, based on the differentstinct methods, training, and requirements of each field. It anticipated the sensitivity of a debate that would continue over time (Chapter 5).0 The document not only reflected the political maturity of Ennahda’s leadership but also revealed the predominance of a political party logic shaping its conduct.
In the early 2000s, Ennahda consolidated its decision to participate in cross-ideological forums and alliances with opposition parties that had not been co-opted by the regime.0 Paris hosted not only Ennahda’s Political Office but also other Tunisian opposition figures and human rights activists,0 and it soon became a key meeting place for the formation of an anti-Ben Ali fronts. Nevertheless, not all secular forces were willing to bridge the ideological divide with the Islamists.0
Since the official establishment of the MTI in 1981, Ennahda prioritised political action aimed at challenging the Tunisian hegemonic state. This political orientation did not only reconfigure the﻿ traditional conception s and practices of daʿwa; it also shaped organisational practices, including recruitment and training processes. Throughout the 1980s, for the generation of university students active within the Tunisian student movement, recruitment and training involved a specialised socialisation process designed to cultivate political skills and fostershape an activist identity oriented towards political and societal wengagement.0 However, due to sustained repression and the impossibility of realising its political ambitions prior to 2011, before 2011 Ennahda was compelled to operate clandestinely across multiple domains and according to a plurality of institutional logics. Its simultaneous engagement in pressure politics, human rights advocacy, and social assistance thus constituted a ‘methodological necessity’ for confronting a totalitarian and despotic regime from multiple angles.0
Since its inception, Ennahda has been an ideologically and organisationally evolving force, responsive to shifting socio-political dynamicscontexts.0 Throughout its history, the movement repeatedly reassessed and revised its strategies and internal structures, demonstrating a sustained capacity for self-reflexivity and critique.0 From the founding of al-Jamaʿa al-Islamiyya onwards, Ennahda’s organisational apparatusstructure evolved in tandem with political developments.
Despite persistent repression and marginalisation, Ennahda’s leadership never abandoned its ambition to become a recognised political actor capable of challenging the Ben Ali regime. However, as McCarthy observed, although the leadership progressively downplayed the pursuit of a correctional Islamic agenda in favour of political objectives, a ‘subculture’ of faith and morality, alongside an ‘individual understanding of the Islamist project’, remained a substratum upon which rank-and-file members built and sustained their sense of belonging for decades.0 For many long-time Nahdawis, this religious and ethical foundation continued to constitute a key identity marker and a core source of loyalty to the movement’s Islamistc origins (Chapter 5).0
