The fFormation of the Freedom and Justice Party as a case of coercive modelling
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Formation of the Freedom and Justice Party
The mMaking of the Freedom and Justice Party: A case of coercive modelling
The ousting of Mubarak after three decades in power ushered in a brief yet tumultuous transitional period. This phase was characterised by the absence of established modern political organisations, the ambiguous agendas of newly formed parties, and their struggle for political legitimacy. In such an uncertain environment, organisations tend to gravitate towards increasing similarity. This tendency often produces processes of modelling and emulation, whereby emerging actors replicate the structures, visions, and strategies of an perceived successful organisation perceived as successful.0 In organisation studies, modelling, whether subtle or explicit, can function both as a response to external uncertainty and as a coercive mechanism driven by the urgency to secure legitimacy for new entities.0
Although the idea of establishing a political party did not command unanimous support within the Brotherhood,0 its Shura Council approved the decision to establish the Freedom and Justice Party (FJP) in April 2011.0 The Muslim Brothers’ leadership opted to engage in party politics through a ‘hybrid formula’:0 the creation of a political wing emerging from a parent movement. This model mirrored that adopted by the Jordanian Muslim Brotherhoods in founding the Islamic Action Front pParty in 1992.0 In June 2011, the FJP was announced as a civil party with an Islamic frame of reference, open to all citizens.0
First-hand testimonies from the FJP’s formative phase identified three conditions that favoured the homogenisation and convergence of organisational forms, practices, and modes of thinking between the FJP and its sponsor organisation, the Muslim Brothers:
  1. the sponsor organisation’s role in selecting the party’s leadership;
  2. the party’s financial dependence on the Brotherhood;
  3. the party’s lack of an independent vision.
The presence of these conditions suggested that the FJP was destined to resemble its promoter organisation as:
the greater the dependence of an organisation on another organisation, the more similar it will become to that organisation in structure, climate and behavioural focus.0
Handpicked from within: The Brotherhood’s control over Freedom and Justice Party leadership
Some people say that the party [while in power] used to go to Maktab al-Irshad [the Guidance Bureau] or to the Supreme Guide of the Brotherhood to take orders, and you’d be surprised if instead, I tell you that this did not really happen because it did not have to. The same guys [the FJP’s leaders] with that same mentality were already there managing things in the old-fashioned manner.
A FJP minister in Qandil’s cabinet (2012–2013), author’s interview (2020)
Before the party gained legal recognition, the Muslim Brotherhood’s General Shura Council delegated Mohamed Saad al-Katatni, an influential member of the Guidance Bureau and former head of the group’s parliamentary bloc, to oversee the party’s establishment and the selection of its leadership.0 A series of internal consultations within the Brotherhood’s upper structures culminated in the nomination of pragmatic conservative figures favoured by both Khairat al-Shater and Mahmoud Ezzat, two long-standing powerbrokers within the organisation.0 Mohamed Morsi (d. 2019) and Issam al-Aryan (d. 2020) were appointed Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the party, respectively, while Katatni assumed the post of Secretary-General.0 Although these figures formally resigned from their leadership positions within the Brotherhood as a symbolic gesture of the FJP’s autonomy,0 they contributed to shaping the new party’s vision in close alignment with that of its parent movement.0
The FJP’s internal structure comprised a Higher Council and an Executive Bureau, both elected by the a General Assembly (GA) made up of representatives from each governorate.0 However, the initial GA members were appointed rather than elected, not by the party founders but by the Brotherhood’s Shura Council. This arrangement undermined the party’s claim to organisational independence from the outset. The sole exception occurred in Giza governorate, where the election of Amr Darrag and the inclusion of non-Brotherhood members generated internal tensions.0 Given that up to 70% of the FJP founders were active Brotherhood members, the party’s GA effectively reproduced the movement’s leadership on a smaller scale.0
Following the FJP’s establishment, approximately 80% of its ranks were immediately filled by Brotherhood affiliates, producing a quasi-replication of the movement’s internal composition.0 Political cadres from the Brotherhood’s Political Committee were redeployed almost en bloc to the FJP, while a significant number of members of the Student Section were channelled into the party’s Youth Secretariat. Theseis transfers explains the rapid growth in party membership achieved in fewer than four months.0
While it may initially have appeared reasonable for the Brotherhood to guide the party’s formation, its this involvement quickly extended beyond short-term coordination.0 What emerged was a comprehensive transfer of leadership, structures, and organisational culture. As the remainder of this chapter showsdemonstrates, the Brotherhood’s ambitions and institutional dominance effectively curtailed any prospect for the FJP to develop into a distinct political entity with an independent strategic vision.
‘Who funds, rules’: Organisational overlap and resource dependency
In March 2011, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (SCAF) announced a new electoral law requiring political parties to secure a minimum of 5,000 members, with at least 300 members drawn from ten10 Egyptian governorates.0 It also established a commission to review party applications within 30 days, thereby easing the conditions for party formation compared to the Mubarak era.0
An official FJP statement claimed that party finances relied solely on annual membership fees of E£150, asserting financial independence from the parent movement.0 Nonetheless, during the 2011 legislative elections, the Brotherhood’s extensive social networks, assets, and resources were visibly deployed, blurring the distinction between the movement and the party.
Former and current Brotherhood members acknowledged that the movement’s material and human resources were mobilised during the 2011–12 parliamentary elections, contradicting claims of administrative and financial separation between the party and the movement:
Initially, they [the Muslim Brothers’ leadership] decided that the party would only engage in politics while other activities, like social or cultural work, would remain with the Brotherhood. But when the party entered the parliamentary elections, there was no party there […] Indeed, the Muslim [Brotherhood] was on the ground with its machinery—resources, structures, leading members and communication lines. Since then, it became the one running the show, and when the party tried to gain some power and autonomy in certain governorates, it entered into conflict with the movement’s leadership.0
To the detriment of the FJP, the Muslim Brotherhoods, as the financially stronger organisation, occupied an advantageous position from which to coerce the weaker, newly established party to ‘adopt its practices in order to accommodate the stronger party’s needs’, namely those of the Brotherhood’s historical leadership.0
‘No model but the movement’: Lacking vision, mimicking the parent
When the Muslim Brothers established the FJP, there were no clear views about the relationship between the new entity and the movement; there was no knowledge on how to build a party or determine who should lead it […]. Initially, the Brotherhood itself, with its organs and hierarchy, tried out certain individuals to officially become FJP leaders while preventing other Brotherhood’s members from joining the party […].
A FJP co-founder, author’s interview (2021)
This testimony highlights the lack of specialised knowledge in creating effective political organisations. Combined with a lack of financial autonomy, interviewees repeatedly cited the absence of alternative organisational models as a key reason for the FJP’s reproduction of Brotherhood-like structures and norms.0
The Brotherhood’s influence extended beyond logistics and personnel selection. Another former minister in the Heisham Qandil-led government (2012–13) described theis coercive emulation of the party as stemming from the shared perception that the Brotherhood was an ‘original brand’, a long-standing movement that had attempted to impact politics for decades, ‘combining religious outreach and political activism even before the removal of the King’.0
After the Uprisings, the Muslim Brotherhood carried both the prestige and the burden of acting as an entrepreneur for the political parties that rapidly crowded the Egyptian political scene as:
most of the small parties who emerged after the political opening [brought about by the Arab Uprisings] originated from the Muslim Brothers. Think about them as an 80-year-old big brand or factory; actually, think about them as a multinational company like Coca-Cola that has been around for almost 100 years and decided to spin off and start smaller entrepreneurial projects. You cannot say that this willould be a success, but it is not a coincidence that most of the [parties’ founders] used to belong to the Brotherhood’s political committee.0
According to the theory of isomorphic change, the absence of clearly articulated political goals and alternative organisational models often results in the reproduction of what is perceived as ‘exemplary’.0 In the eyes of its leaders, the Brotherhood was not only a successful social movement but also a fully functioning organisational archetype.0
Theis modelling of the FJP on the Brotherhood is evident in the FJP’s founding statement in Arabic, which echoes the Brotherhood’s social mission of individual reform, including the ‘construction of a sound human being’ as an objective:0
The first aspect of our party’s programme is based on purifying souls, refining hearts, the elevation of feelings, and the re-shaping of characters by preaching, adherence to worship, honourable morals, good companionship and treatment, and the reminding [tadhkir] of Allah and the hereafter until the conscience awakes, self-control is practised and the values of good are settled in the souls, and evil and its intentions are repelled; in addition, [it aims to] create a good atmosphere that encourages integrity and righteousness and provide positive examples while employing the school, the house, the mosque, the church and the media in achieving that.0
The emphasis on moral purification and the reformation of the individual reflects the legacy of Hasan al-Banna’s original vision for the Brotherhood: a virtuous, exemplary society capable of addressing societal ills and ‘keeping the nation healthy’.0 The convergence of mission and discourse between the FJP and the Brotherhood was further reinforced through the adoption of symbols and programmes.
During its brief political experience, the party revived the slogan ‘al-Islam huwa al-hall’ (Islam is the solution), frequently displayed on flyers and in marches during the post-Mubarak period, alongside ‘Nahmil al-khayr li-Misr’ (We bring goodness to Egypt), a slogan previously popularised by Muslim Brotherhood members of parliament between 2005 and 2010, later incorporated into the FJP’s logo.0 In addition to closely modelling the FJP party programme on the pre-existing 2007 electoral draft circulated by the Brotherhood to gauge reception,0 the FJP officially adopted the Brotherhood’s ‘Nahda Project’, an idealistic document setting outpresenting a comprehensive vision for socio-political and economic reform, presentedintroduced by Khairat al-Shater in April 2011 during a public lecture at Alexandria University.0
Shater described it as a ‘comprehensive’ project encompassing economics, society, and politics, aiming to ‘develop the Renaissance of the Islamic community on the basis of the Islamic reference’, a vision that allowed the Brotherhoods to ‘open up to society to a great extent’.0 The document was distributed on leaflets during Morsi’s presidential campaign and was intended to establish the ‘movement’s political and economic credentials’ during its governmental tenure.0 However, its reliance on vague and morally prescriptive ideas of piety and salvation, and the emphasis on the Egyptian individual and family undermined the credibility of its political and economic objectives.0 The lack of implementation details, coupled with an emphasis on the private sector and foreign investment to restore Egypt’s lost prosperity,0 attracted criticism for betraying the revolution’s social aspirations and replicating the economic and development model of Mubarak’s National Democratic Party.0 Rather than signalling programmatic independence, the ‘Nahda Project’ demonstrated the FJP’s inability to articulate distinct positions from its sponsor organisation.
The FJP’s dependence on the Brotherhood was reinforced by internal rules that mirrored the Brotherhood’s membership requirements. Only those deemed ‘regular and active’ members could participate fully in the party’s political life and decision-making.0 This exclusionary and elitist practice, particularly resented by younger members, reinforced the perception that the FJP was not a truly independent political entity but a bureaucratic extension of its promoter organisation.
The FJP’s formation illustrates how the absence of political preparedness and viable alternative models enabled the Brotherhood to exert coercive organisational influence, shaping the party in its own image. The outcome was a political party-movement hybrid rather than an independent civic actor, deeply﻿ rooted in an the Muslim Brotherhood’s inherited vision and constrained by structural mimicry.
Purely mimetic or coercive modelling? Role of agency in isomorphic change
The problem has always been one: the complete agency of the Brotherhood lies in its historical leadership […]. They firmly believe that without their guidance and control the movement would be annihilated. How do they see lay members including youth and women? Nothing more than tools!
A Fformer member of Shabab al-Ikhwan, author’s interview (2021)
In institutional theory, modelling an organisation like the FJP after a promoter organisation can result either from mimetic pressures in unsettled environments characterised by a lack ofing viableclear organisational models and, normative imperatives to enhance professionalisation, or from direct coercive mechanisms.0 In the case of the FJP’s formation, this process was not merely a mechanistic reaction to uncertainty or the lack of political archetypes. It was primarily ‘a constraining process’0 activated by the Brotherhood’s historical leadership, who acted as exclusive ‘institutional agents’ and exploited the absence of alternative organisational models.0 As a young member of the Istanbul-based Administrative Office explained to the author:
Since the onset, there was not enough acceptance of the idea of the party inside the organisation […]. Also, in the Brotherhood’s top brass, some people did not accept the possibility of losing their monopoly on some associational activities inside the Egyptian society which would have empowered other organisations.0
Ten years after the Arab Uprisings that toppled Mubarak, interviewees across the Brotherhood’s organisational spectrum described the isomorphic change (Chapter 1) initiated by its historical leadership during the FJP’s formation as a ‘very strategic move’. The coercive modelling of the FJP on the likeness of the Brotherhood aimed to prevent the emergence of a distinct institutional logic for the new party, which might have weakened the movement’s broader reformist mission by prioritising politics and, consequently, altered its almost century-old conception of being ‘Brothers in faith’ invested in a cross-sectoral educational mission (Chapter 1).
Institutional agents within the Brotherhood’s top leadership intentionally employed coercive modelling to preserve the movement’s group identity, organisational culture, and reformist mission against potential distortions, as ‘the idea of an independent political party was creeping them’.0 The leadership imposed its organisational vision on the FJP not only by transferring loyal, handpicked leaders from the Brotherhood’s upper echelons to the party’s leadership but also by transplanting aspects of the Brotherhood’s organisational culture, group identity, and mission into the ‘civil party with an Islamic frame of reference’.0 These features include an authoritarian organisational imprint, a gradual-reformist approach, elitism, and a combination of fear and suspicion, social-emotions that sustained the secretive culture embedded within the Brotherhood’s vanguard elite, inherited from the structural conditions of the group’s second founding (1968–1982).0
‘Listen and obey’: Sacred obedience and the militarisation of belief
In the wake of the Arab Uprisings, the Brotherhood’s historical leadership initiated an organisational purge of those ‘who did not listen and obey’, including outspoken senior members of its upper ranks. Abd al-Munim Abul Futuh, who later founded the Strong Egypt Party, offers the clearest example of this practice. As a reformist member of the Brotherhood’s GuidanceExecutive Bureau, Abul Futuh opposed the hardline conservatism within the organisation and openly criticised the executive leadership for remaining trapped in the culture of secrecy and clandestinity.0 After announcing his independent candidacy in the Egyptian presidential elections (2012), he found himself no longer welcome within the movement.0 Prior to him, Mohammed Habib had departed after publicly challenging the ideological rigidity of the Muslim Brotherhood and the control exerted by Mahmoud Ezzat and Khairat al-Shater over the movement.0
In addition to these senior figures, younger members faced exclusion for expressing divergent political views regarding post-transition Egypt and for advocating a more open and inclusive vision for the FJP. These positions clashed with the top-down, hierarchical spirit embedded in the Brotherhood’s vanguard elite.0 As one recalls:
During the initial stage of the revolution, they [the Brotherhood’s historical leadership] were more receptive to youth-led initiatives. But after Mubarak’s fall, the tone changed and the message became the following: ‘you are not in the leadership, you are not part of the decision making, don’t overestimate your role in the movement!’. I recall Morsi saying: ‘how did this group [of senior reformists and youth] came to know each other without having the same share within the organisation? The implicit message was clear: within the Brotherhood, one cannot move across hierarchical lines freely—even in the midst of a revolution!.0
In June 2011, Islam Lotfy, Mohamed al-Qassas and other few young Brotherhood activists announced the formation of the Egyptian Current Party, which also included members of the 6 April Movement and Kefaya.0 Significant tensions quickly emerged between the new party and the Brotherhood’s leadership, which issued warnings that any member joining a party other than the FJP would face expulsion.0 To maintain the ranks of the FJP, even apolitical members were reportedly coerced into joining.0 These authoritarian practices were not new but deeply rooted in the Brotherhood’s organisational culture.
Since its foundation, the Society of Muslim Brothers has been guided by the teachings codified in al-Banna’s Epistle of Teachings, which sets out the movement’s key principles. Within its organisational culture, the motto ‘listen and obey’ constitutes an essential pillar, underpinning internal consensus (ijmaʿ) and unity (wihda).0 This principle encapsulates the triad of bayʿa (allegiance), taʿa (obedience), and thiqa (trust), which constitute someare part of al-Banna’s ‘Pillars of Allegiance’ (Chapter 1 ).0
Within the Brotherhood, the oath of allegiance,  a traditional Islamic precept, was initially understood in the Brotherhood not as allegiance to a person but as a commitment to the ideology and cause of the group. Full members pledge allegiance to the General Guide or his representative, marking the commencement of their obligations. Following the Brotherhood’s second founding, this practicee bayʿa acquired a broader meaning, which scholars have interpreted as a mutual contract linking members, the General Guide, and the Islamic mission.0 As Khalil al-Anani observes, the submissive and devotional character of this modern bayʿa functions as a mechanism granting ‘a blank check to the leadership’.0
Taʿa, or obedience, complements allegiance. A commentary published on IkhwanWiki amid post-2011 internal tensions, reflecting on the significance of obedience and shura (consultation) within the Brotherhood, published on IkhwanWiki against the backdrop of post-2011 internal tensions, explainsclarifies that:
Obedience to the Muslim Brotherhood is neither an innovation nor a Brotherhood invention, but rather a hallmark of institutional and collective work, as long as it is tied to shura [consultation] and decision-making procedures, there is nothing objectionable nor harmful about it. Obedience is rather an obligation from this angle.0
The same text explains that ‘the difference between obedience in Islam—and thus in the Brotherhood—and obedience in modern positivistic philosophies is that obedience in Islam is a devotional matter, whereas in positivistic philosophies it is a worldly matter concerned merely with the management of mundane affairs’.0
The excerpt presents obedience within the Brotherhood as an extension of obedience in Islam. This close relationship, and the near-conflation of obedience to Islam with obedience to the Muslim Brotherhood, serve to foster a form of uncritical submission among those who have internalised obedience in these terms. Such obedience not only stifles dissent but also encourages a process of de-intellectualisation within the organisation.0 The idea of submitting to orders and decisions that no one dares to question evokes both a military and a sufi-like sense of discipline,0 captured in al-Banna’s imperative, ‘be practical, not argumentative’.0 Strategically, the cultivation of comprehensive obedience to the leadership, the group’s cause, and Islam strengthensed the movement’s cohesion, ensuring the unquestioned execution of decisions made at the upper levels.0 As Mustafa Menshawy observed in his study on individual experiences of disengagement from the movement, obedience functionsserves as a trait d’union linking the Brotherhood’s organisational culture to the practices of military institutions.0 This authoritarian organisational vision, later transplanted into the short-lived FJP, derives from:
the old guard’s dogmatic ideology that they want to protect and preserve; thus, they justify a highly centralised decision-making process and the systematic repression of ideas deemed unorthodox because they want to preserve [the organisation] the way it is.0
For the Brotherhood’s historical leadership, the organisation constitutes a virtuous society of committed Muslims and the indispensable medium through which the Islamic mission is fulfilled.0 In their view, without the ‘Brotherhood in God’ as an organisation, there can be no return to Islamically reformedinfluenced state institutions and society. Maintaining the Brotherhoodorganisation’s authenticitypurity, which al-Banna himself also conceptualised as a ‘social idea’, requires insulating it from ideologically divergent currents and internal pluralism.0
The post-Uprising organisational purge targeting reformists and youth aimed to shield the integrity of the Brotherhood’s group idea and values from dilution, both within the parent movement and its political offshoot. The presence of diverse factions with alternative political visions was perceived as a threat to organisational unity, prompting the leadership to reinforce institutional mechanisms of exclusion.0
The Brotherhood’s complex organisational machinery was carefully designed to embody al-Banna’s ideal society and pursue the gradual Islamisation of the broader societal order, thereby creating a new generation of virtuous men and women (Chapter 1).0 Its sophistication and efficiency underpin the Muslim Brothers’ reputation as an exemplary organisation, providing a strong incentive for its leadership to resist change.0
In the post-Uprising period, after a brief phase of political opening and cross-ideological encounters in Tahrir Square, the Brotherhood’s historical leadership continued to prioritise the pre-2011 movement’s logic of maintaining the organisational status quo rather than reforming it (Chapter 1). Reasserting the ‘listen and obey’ principle within both the FJP and the Muslim Brothers functioned as an institutional mechanism to silence demands for a more open, less elitist organisational culture and for an independent civil party capable of challengingthat could potentially challenge the Brotherhood’s core mission and group idea.
Freedom and Justice Party in power: Gradual approach to formal politics, informal and elitist practices
On 28 January 2011, the Muslim Brothers officially declared their participation and support for the mass protests in central Cairo. On the same day, the army was deployed in Cairo and other major cities.0 On 29 January, Mubarak dismissed Prime Minister Ahmed Nazif’s cabinet and appointed his intelligence chief and loyalist Omar Sulayman as vice-president and Ahmed Shafik as prime minister. A few days later, Sulayman met with senior Brotherhood’s representatives and other opposition figures.0
After both the army chief and the air force commander refused Mubarak’s request to deployuse force against civilians, public sentiment quickly rallied behind the military. Crowds chanted, ‘el-geysh we-l-shaʿb iyd wahda’ (the army and the people are one hand).0 Following Mubarak’s resignation, the SCAF assumed full control of the political transition, pledging to hand power to an elected civilian government. The Brotherhood did not publicly question SCAF’s role; indeed, they welcomed the inclusion of a Brotherhood-affiliated lawyer in the exclusive eight-member committee tasked with drafting provisional constitutional amendments in February 2011.0
By spring and summer 2011, however, a second wave of protests erupted, demanding transitional justice and the prosecution of Mubarak and senior regime figures for corruption and abuse of power. The Brotherhood largely remained aloof from this new revolutionary wave. During the SCAF-led transition (February 2011–June 2012), the Muslim Brothers’ absence from the ‘second wave of revolution’ and the leadership’s initial decision to appease SCAF in order to secure itsa role within the transition, reflected the movement’s accommodationist attitude and the logic of a non-radical reformist movement that preferreding to work within state institutions.0 In August 2012, following the FJP’s victory in the 2011–2012 parliamentary elections, the Brotherhood’s non-confrontational approach towards SCAF and remnants of the old regime led to the formation of what Alison Pargeter called the ‘cabinet of appeasement’.0
In this cabinet, the FJP held only five portfolios, all related to services, while the remaining ministries were allocated to independent technocrats and ‘formidable figures from the former regime’, some of the latter allegedly with and to independents and technocrats, some allegedly with  Islamist inclinations.0 This distribution was not merely a response to the FJP’s lack of members with specialised expertise, who were often criticised as ‘daʿwa figures’.0 Rather, it reflected a cautious choices aimed at maintaining a delicate balance of power between SCAF and  the  Brotherhood.0
As an originally exclusive ‘society of true Muslims’, the Brotherhood’s historical leadership transferred its elitism and exclusivism to the FJP. Strategically, the FJP appointed an Egyptian Christian, Rafiq Habib, as vice-president0 and, during the 2011–12 parliamentary elections it nominated a woman in each district, 46 in total, in compliance with the 2011 Parliamentary Election Law, which required all political parties to include at least one woman on each electoral list.0 Nonetheless, the scant number of women and the absence of youth in leadership roles closely mirrored the composition of the Brotherhood’s upper echelons. This led to criticism of the FJP as overwhelmingly male-dominated, exclusivist, and aligned with the conservative culture of its parent organisation. It also further accentuated the party’s inability toof projecting an identity and modus operandi distinct from the Brotherhood.0
The Muslim Brothers’ habit of operating in informal politics as a semi-clandestine group also characterised President Morsi’s tenure (June 2012–July 2013).0 Bargaining and ‘striking deals’ through a tight-knit presidential advisory team of ‘faithful allies’ reflected practices embedded in the semi-clandestine movement, which operated with caution and suspicion of ‘others’.0
Appointed in late August 2012, Morsi’s Advisory Committee drew criticism for reflected its the same exclusivist compositiontendencies. Although some Egyptian liberals were included, the 17-member team was dominated by Muslim Brothers and FJP figures, some criticised for lacking political experience and effectively shadowing government officials. These members could be trusted by Brotherhood standards, as they were selected for loyalty rather than competence.0 The advisory team lacked representatives from outside the Brotherhood or its like-minded sympathisers, further insulating conservative thinking and organisational behaviour within the newly established party.
‘Still sitting in the dark:’ Tracing fear in the legacy of underground survival
Sometimes, when people remain underground for decades, it is very hard for them to liberate themselves from that underground mindset. I think many of the Brotherhood’s leaders never managed to move beyond that mindset, which had a very negative impact on the behaviour of the party’s leadership. You see, it is like when you sit in a dark room for too long and then you suddenly open the curtains […], that light does not allow you to see yet. Well, I think that something similar happened in Egypt. We only needed more time to identify and resolve those problems. We would have found more avenues to learn how to agree to disagree and how to be more inclusive, […] without being subjected to the pressure of multiple fears. If only we had managed to free ourselves from this fear, we would have done a better job.0
An FJP parliamentarian from Upper Egypt, author’s interview (2021)
This reflection encapsulates a recurring theme in interviews with both current and former members of the Brotherhood and its political armarm: the movement’s entrapment in a mindset of fear and suspicion, inherited from decades of clandestine activity.
The lingering fear of the ‘other’— (non-Ikhwan actors such as liberals, Salafists, the military, and the judiciary—) remained deeply embedded in the Brotherhood’s political psyche. It stemmed from an organisational culture shaped by authoritarian repression and survivalist strategies of survival.0 Following Mubarak’s fall, the ensuing political uncertainty revived this deep-seated insecurity and suspicion, a historically contingent emotion rooted in the authoritarian conditions under which the Muslim Brothers had been established and  had learned to survive.0 This fear hampered the Brotherhood’s capacity to engage openly, reform internally, or build sustainable alliances.
Fear, however, was not only directed outward. It also turned inward, with some Brotherhood members describing the organisation as ‘a group that fears changes and alterations’ that could destabilise the organisational status quo of the nearly century-old reformist movement:
They are afraid that if they change anything within the organisation, this may collapse, and they [the historical leadership] will be responsible for having destroyed the Brotherhood. The best achievement that they can leave to history is keeping the movement alive as it is.0
This suggests that the Brotherhood tolerates only minimal change, primarily to preserve the organisation.The tanzim, the inner core of the Muslim Brotherhood’s organisational apparatus, functions as an impregnable iron cage designed to protect the group’s idea from perceived threats. Its historical leadership, referred to as ‘tanzimiyyun’ (organisational leadership) for their focus on maintaining organisational integrity,0 is morally tasked with ensuring continuity against any change that could alienate the idea of the ‘Brotherhood in faith’.
Another interviewee offered a similar reflectioned similarly on missed opportunities for reform during the 2011 Uprisings:
After the revolution, we had every reason and opportunity to implement some changes at an organisational level. We had an open environment, a public office, and all members, including the Shura Council, could have met anytime. We should have scheduled fair elections and listened to all members across the districts. But this did not happen. The same dogmatic mindset, the organisational vision of the highly centralised movement, and the same fear of change were still there. […] It could not be stopped at that time. I spoke to some high-ranking members, and they said they could not introduce organisational changes so rapidly because otherwise, we could have lost ijmaʿ (internal consensus).0
This aversion to change is deeply rooted in the conditions surrounding the Brotherhood’s second founding. The movement’s rigid and exclusivist organisational culture traces back to the vision of the former leaders of the Society of Muslim Brothers’ paramilitary wing, the Special Apparatus (SA), established between 1938 and 1940, and the Organisation 1965.0 The appellative ‘Qutbist trend,’ used in the Brotherhood’s own jargon to denote the historical leadership,0 links this organisational culture to the secrecy and elitism that characterised Organisation 1965. This underground group was an attempt in the mid-1960s to revive the Muslim Brotherhood under the leadership of influential SA figures and Sayyid Qutb, the group’s ideologue and spiritual guide.0
The legacy of the SA and Organisation  1965 lies in the vanguard leadership they produced and the imprint they left on the reconstituted Brotherhood’s organisational culture.0 Leaders emerging from the SA acquired prestige within the organisation’s upper echelons, maintaining influence until recent times. Some became members of the Guidance Bureau, while others, such as Mustafa Mashhour (1996–2002) and Mohammed Mahdi Akef (2004–2010), were appointed General Guides.0 Morest recently, one of Mashhour’s associates, Ezzat, a follower of Qutb’s elitist and secretive organisational vision and a founder of Organisation 1965, became deputy to the General Guide during the group’s 2010 internalgeneral elections, in which Mohammed Badie (another Qutbist) was appointed General Guide.0
Framed as an intellectual development of al-Banna’s thought, their organisational vision presupposes a strong attachment to hierarchy, unquestioning obedience, and secrecy. This vision persisted among influential personalities who, from the mid-1990s, included younger affiliates such as the Egyptian businessman Khairat al-Shater.0 Repeated crackdowns in 1948, 1954, and 1965 inevitably entrenched a habit of secrecy. Combined with the trauma of persecution inherited by this vanguard elite, these ordeals rendered the Brotherhood’s historical leadership averseresistant to altering its organisational practices, group ideology, or reformist mission.
The vision they cultivated conceives Islam ‘as a living organisation’, emphasising the Islamic project of reforming the individual and preserving the purity of the Brotherhood’s ideal society. In their view, centralised decision-making, the ‘listen and obey formula’, and those ‘clear lines of hierarchy’ that must not be transgressed constitute prerequisites for maintaining the organisation, conceived as the ‘incubator’ of a vast Islamic reformist project.0 In line with the clandestine logic shaped by inherited from their suffering under Nasser’s repressive regime, this vanguard elite prioritises the preservation of the organisational apparatus, its wihda (unity), ijma’ (cohesion), and exclusivism. Consequently, they closely supervise recruitment, socialisation curricula, and promotion mechanisms to ensure that members adopt the same organisational vision.0
Structurally, since its second founding (1968–1982), the Brotherhood remained largely intact until 1992,0 when a number of specialised committees were introduced and a limit was placed on the General Guide’s term of office.0 Later, General Guide Mohamed Mahdi Akef’s aspiration sought to ‘renew the blood of the movement’ and delegate responsibilities on the basis of merit. Yet his initiative did not effectfailed to produce  substantive organisational change, resulting only in the promotion of a few younger members, a change deemed largely cosmetic.0
Nonetheless, a subtle transformation in the Brotherhood’s internal composition emerged in the 2009 internal elections, which led to the establishment of a new Guidance Bureau dominated by tanzimiyyun. This Bureau reflected what Hossam Tammam described as the ‘ruralisation of the Brotherhood’, a gradual shift in the social composition of itsthe leadership that enabled loyalist tanzimiyyun to occupy senior positions.0 In the early 2000s, Brotherhood membership increased notably in Egypt’s provincial universities. In response, the organisation’s bylaws were amended in the 1990s and 2000s to reflect the growing presence of Muslim Brothers in rural Egypt.0
The amendments revoked the clause requiring 9 of the 16 members of the Guidance Bureau to be from Cairo. Consequently, the 2009 Guidance Bureau includedcomprised a larger number of conservative members fromand from rural backgrounds, including Morsi and Katatni.0 The ruralisation of the Brotherhood thus functioned as an ad hoc strategy to promote individuals loyal to iststhe historical leadership to the upper tiers of the organisation,0 privileging those ‘who listen and obey more’ over those with skills or competence .0
Throughout its history of cyclical crises, the Brotherhood’s survival has depended on the leadership’s ability to transform communal fear into a ‘source of solidarity’, reinforcing vertical cohesion and securing exclusive control over decision-making.0 This rigid organisational culture did more than preserve cohesion; it insulated the Brotherhood from internal dissent and external engagement, framing change as a vulnerability. The emphasis on wihda (unity), ijmaʿ (consensus), and strict hierarchies became sacrosanct principles, with recruitment, training, and promotion mechanisms designed to sustain this closed organisational system.0
During Morsi’s presidency, the Brotherhood influenced the FJP through tightly controlled advisory circles and loyalist networks, wary of outsiders or those without the proper share in the organisation’s al decision-making. Historically, this mindset shaped the leadership’s response to internal reformist currents championed by some of , such as the islahiyyun, politicised Brothers active in Egypt’s unionism who joined the group in the 1970s and 1980s without prior ties to al-Banna’s Society. Their demands for leadership accountability, greater transparency, and a more flexible organisational culture were consistently met with suspicion and resistance.0 Following the Uprisings, this fear of change transferred directly into the FJP, manifesting as coercive organisational modelling.
For the Brotherhood’s historical leadership, fear was both a psychological response and a strategic resource—, a means to consolidate control, suppress dissent, and preserve the sanctity of the group idea. As the opening interview excerpt poignantly captures, this is a movement that had operated in darkness for so long that, when the curtain was finally drawn aside, it remained blinded by the light.
Side -effects of a coercive isomorphic change
In the aftermath of the Arab Uprisings, one could argue that it was ‘logical and natural’ for the FJP to benefit from the movement’s long-standing presence and support,0 as ‘in most situations, reliance on established, legitimated procedures enhance organisational legitimacy and survival characteristics’.0 Yet, the formation of the FJP as the end product of a broader process of isomorphic change revealed significant side -effects.
The party’s accountability was almost nullified by the ongoing interference of the movement’s leadership in its internal decision-making processes, which had undermined the FJP’s autonomy since its inception. As an interviewee noted, ‘sometimes, decisions were taken without even gathering the party’s leadership Council’.0 Attempts by certain FJP leaders to establish even modest decision-making independence from the Brotherhood’s historical leadership ultimately proved futile.
Although the FJP possessed defined internal structures, including its own bylaws, a Higher Council, an Executive Bureau, and a GA, it failed to develop a coherent and cohesive independent organisation due to the lack of clear decisional boundaries and a division of labour between the party and its parent movement.0 Nevertheless, despite the FJP’s lack of decisional autonomy, accountability for its performance during its brief tenure in government could not easily be transferred to the Brotherhood, which remained formally illegal.0
To the detriment of the Muslim Brothers, establishing a political arm while remaining a semi-clandestine group with links to numerous satellite associations and business entities, generated heightened animosity among political competitors.0 In the aftermath of the 2011 Uprisings, the Muslim Brothers’ extensive economic assets and social capital led electoral rivals to perceive both independent Brotherhood candidates and those running with the FJP as almost unassailable in the legislative elections.0 This sense of unfair political competition amplified opposition to the Brotherhood.
Despite the FJP’s positive electoral performance, its derivation from an illegal and secret movement generated additional collateral effects. The Brotherhood retained its illegal status even after the authorities called on it to legalise, including after March 2013, when the Supreme Constitutional Court exerted significant pressure on its leadership to comply with the registration requirements.0 On that occasion, they opted to register a parallel organisation engaged in only some of the Brotherhood’s activities, licensed under the name of the former General Guide, Akef, who had resigned in 2009.0 According to one interviewee, security concerns were the primary motivation behind this choice, which was also informed by the Brotherhood’s practical and strategic inability to obtain recognition under any of the legal association categories existing at the time.0 Its organisational comprehensiveness precluded both formal categorisation and legalisation under the then-existing association framework.
A further side -effect of this model of party formation concerned the FJP’s credibility. While the ‘party-movement hybrid’ facilitated the FJP’s initial quest for legitimacy and popular support, it soon aroused public suspicion regarding the party’s political objectives, which led to its immediate labelling as the ‘party for the Muslim Brothers’.0
Hybrid formula and coercive modelling: Top-down organisational strategy
In the process of the FJP’s formation, adopting a party-movement hybrid model did not reduce the organisational comprehensiveness of the Brotherhood—a defining feature of Islamist organisations—by  transforming it into a purely political entity. Rather, Within the historical leadership mindset of the Muslim Brotherhood perceived, this model of party formation was perceived as consistent with the logic of the all-encompassing reformist institution envisioned by al-Banna (Chapter 1).0
The coercive modelling of the FJP on the Brotherhood’s organisational practices, vision, and mission arose from an agentic response to the urgent need to preserve the cross-sectoral reformist missionfunction and the associated group idea of the ‘Brotherhoods in faith’ (Chapter 1). Choosing the party-movement hybrid as a model for party derivation facilitated the constraining process of organisational emulation, enabling the Brotherhood to conduct political activities.0 However, upon closer look, this model of party derivation did not only align with the movement’s prevailing logic of being a comprehensive, socio-reformist institution (Chapter 1 ). It also followed increasingly vocal demands for internal reform voicedadvanced since 2009 by young, urban and tech-savvy Muslim Brothers.0
Between 2009 and 2010, a group of these young Muslim Brothers (or Shabab al-Ikhwan) drafted a proposal titled Daʿwaʿtuna… La budda an tadkhula tawran jadidan (Our call… We must enter a new phase) and submitted it to the Brotherhood’s leadership.0 In this proposal, theyShabab al-Ikhwan called for professionalism, transparency, and clear membership criteria. They advocated for the specialisation of activities, roles, and profiles within the organisation, particularly regarding daʿwa, tarbiya, and politics. Crucially, the proposal emphasised that activity differentiation would not contradict the organisation’s all-encompassing nature or the foundational pillar of fahm: understanding Islam as a system that deals with all aspects of life (Chapte r 1). It alsoT clarified that this approach would have protected the movement from political competition and possible failures.
The initiative also requested that the old guard redefine the organisation’s identity and ultimate objective, specifically clarifying whether it aimed to be a socio-reformist movement or a political organisation. These  young Brothers sought to end secrecy and challenge the notion of trust as ‘a key criterionelement for holding office’, urging the old guard to conduct open, transparent, and official elections for the Guidance Bureau, directly confronting the organisation’s secretive culture and the outcome of the 2009––2010 internal elections.
In the final document, the young Brothers behind the initiative anticipated the scenario in which the movement would adopt a hybrid formula, establishing a political party while remaining a socio-reformist movement, and stressed the need for a clear separation between the two.0 Such a separation would have compelled the leadership to address the issue of specialisation in political activities and the division of labour between the political party and the socio-reformist movement, thus challenging the logic of the all-encompassing reformist movement.
These issues were priorities not only for the young Brothers who authored the proposal but also for senior reformists within the Brotherhood’s upper echelons. Yet, as a former activist involved in the initiative recounted, ‘the proposal was not only rejected; it was completely ignored by the movement’s leadership, which did not even discuss it within the Shura Council’.0 Nonetheless, the ideas it containedn the proposal continued to circulate and becamewere increasingly perceived as a challenge to the almost century-old organisational culture that the old guard sought to preserve. 
About a year after year after the proposal was drafted, the Brotherhood’s historical leadership established the FJP in the mould of its parent organisation, adopting a formula that maintained the close party-movement (hizb-haraka) relationship. In doing so, it reasserted the logic and identity of the comprehensive reformist movement, neutralising any potential threat arisingraised from within.
