Repairing and maintaining the Bbrotherhood
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Repairing and maintaining the brotherhood
Breaking with tradition?
In the aftermath of the military coup, for the first time in their history, the Muslim Brothers stood firm against the regime, calling for change rather than surrendering to the state’s brutality—an anomaly for a non-radical reformist movement!
Former member of the CFFJP co-founderrisis Management Committee Abroad, author’s interview
On 3 July 2013, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, was ousted in a military coup. coup.0  Following his removal, the military installed Adly Mansour, Chief Justice of the Supreme Constitutional Court, as interim president (in office July 2013–June 2014), although effective power remained concentrated in the hands of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces.0 One month later, Morsi’s ouster and the mass killing of his supporters at the sit-ins in Rabaa al-Adawiya and Nahda Square in Cairo triggered a chain of events that culminated in the banning of the Muslim Brothers’ activities in Egypt, the dissolution of its political party, and a sweeping crackdown on its leadership.0
The ensuing campaign of arrests that followed shook the organisation’s vertical structures.0 In response, the Brotherhood launched an ambitious effort to revive anti-coup mobilisation, with the aim of challenging the newly imposed political order and restoring Morsi as Egypt’s legitimate president. For the first time since its second founding, the Muslim Brothers temporarily embraced resistance as a group strategy, marking a clear departure from their traditionally non-confrontational approach.0
In June 2013, the movementBrotherhood spearheaded the formation of the National Coalition to Support Legitimacy (NCSL), a bloc of ideologically aligned parties that included the Muslim Brothers’ Freedom and Justice Party (FJP), the political wing of al-Jamaa al-Islamiyya, and the Salafi al-Watan Party.0 The NCSL sought to counter the growing momentum of Egypt’s Rebel (Tamarrod, a grassroots campaign mobilising Egyptians to demand Morsi’s removal. Yet the NCSL quickly unravelled due to a shared sense of political failure and the perception among some of its members that they wielded limited bargaining power within the coalition.0
MeanwhileAt the same time, younger Muslim Brothers focused on organising pro-Morsi demonstrations and public actions under the anti-coup student movement Tullab Didd al-Inqilab (Students Against the Coup).0 The frequency and scale of these protests steadily declined as the security apparatus intensified its violent repression and the state formally banned all Brotherhood-associated activities in September 2013.0 Three months later, the group was officially designated a terrorist organisation.0
Under the military-appointed interim government led by Mansour, the authorities froze the Brotherhood’s financial assets, confiscated its medical and recreational facilities, dissolved a wide range of affiliated associations and sub-organisations, and arrested key figures across the movement.0 For the first time since 1981, the regime targeted the group’s vertical command, including the General Guide Mohamed Badie, who was imprisoned in August 2013 along with other influential members of the Guidance Bureau and the Shura Council.0
Facing persecution, prominent FJP and Muslim Brotherhoods figures either went underground or fled the country. Among them were former Secretary-General Mahmoud Hussayn, who had left Egypt on the eve of the coup, and former acting General Guide Mahmoud Ezzat, who remained in hiding until his arrest in August 2020.0 Between August 2013 and February 2014, the Brotherhood’s headquarters experienced acute organisational disarray. In response, its leadershipe movement introduced a series of structural and strategic adjustments to survive in the post-coup environment. In the immediate aftermath of Morsi’s ouster, a small group of lesser-known Guidance Bureau members took the initiative to re-establish leadership structures and reactivate internal lines of communication.0
Restructuring under repression: New leadership and specialised committees
Once the crackdown struck the Brotherhood’s vertical command, partial decentralisation of executive authority and decision-making became necessary to coordinate anti-coup activities across Egypt, particularly in key governorates such as Cairo and Alexandria. In an unprecedented move, the Brotherhood’s leadership merged its three main membership tiers (associateregular, organiser, and active, and affiliated),0 thereby allowing even low-rankingregular members to assume senior administrative roles.0
In early 2014, a series of meetings involving Guidance Bureau members still at large in Egypt and younger second-rank leaders from administrative offices led to the establishment of the Higher Administrative Committee (HAC), soon dubbed the ‘new leadership on the ground’. This body, which received the endorsement of both the Shura Council and Ezzat in his capacity as acting General Guide, comprised middle-aged leaders0 and was headed by Mohamed Kamal, a less publicly exposed member of the Guidance Bureau and former head of the Asyut administrative office.0
Although not a bureau per se, the HAC functioned as an executive body overseeing the movement’s operations inside Egypt. Under its directives, each governorate-level administrative office appointed a young deputy responsible for managing local mobilisation.0 This arrangement fostered a new organisational culture characterised by broader consultation, inclusiveness, and attentiveness to diverse different segments of the membership.0 In the view of the new leadership, the Kamal-led HAC derived its legitimacy from its capacity to restore internal communication and organisational effectiveness, and ‘for having been granted full powers by the historical leadership in all portfolios except for the foreign relations, financial resources, vision and strategy’.0
Among the new wave of tech-savvy leaders empowered during this period were young members of the Central Youth and Media Committees, who assumed leading administrative roles in various governorates.0 These two committees reported directly to the HAC. Meanwhile, demonstrations were organised locally across the country, with these young deputies overseeing anti-coup protests, supervising social media platforms, and managing grassroots mobilisation.0 In practice, they ran the Brotherhood’s anti-coup activities within their respective governorates with little centralised oversight.0
As operating conditions continued to evolve, further structural adjustments followed. Some committees were newly created, while others were repurposed to meet emerging priorities. Even before the coup, ‘Deterrence Committees’ had been established to protect Brotherhood premises and supporters from anti-Morsi demonstrators.0 In the aftermath of the coup, two Guidance Bureau members created a Committee for Activities to coordinate organisational efforts around marches and demonstrations.0
Subsequently, the committee devoted to daʿwa (the Proselytising Committee) was reconstituted as the ‘Awareness Committee’, tasked with mobilising support for the restoration of Morsi’s presidency. The Charity Committee, which oversaw social welfare activities, was renamed the ‘Committee for Those Affected’.0 Largely managed by the Muslim Sisters, a section of the Muslim Brothers, this committee focused on alleviating the severe material hardships faced by members and their families following the death or imprisonment of primary breadwinners.
During this phase of organisational adjustment and increasing specialisation, the influence of the Muslim Sisters and the Central Youth Committee grew significantly. Their organisational and logistical roles in coordinating rallies became particularly crucial after successive waves of arrests between 2016 and 2017 decimated the male senior leadership, under directives issued by Interior Minister Magdy Abdel Ghaffar (in office 2015–2018).0
Additional changes included the establishment of the ‘Sharia Committee of the Muslim Brotherhood Scholars’,0 which issued a document endorsing the legitimacy of the revolutionary approach proposed by the Kamal-led HAC to overturn the post-coup order.0 Further restructuring led to the creation of the Qualitative Action Committees (QACs). The QACs wereas reportedlyallegedly composed of mid-ranking officials and members drawn from the Brotherhood’s Youth and Media Committees0 a nd from across its Student Section. TheirIts initial mandate wasas to protect demonstrators from sabotage by baltagiyya (regime-mobilisedplainclothes thugs) mobilised by the regime. The QACs wereas later divided into two branches: one focused on public qualitative operations aimed primarily at defending demonstrators againstfrom state-sponsored violence, and another dedicated to ‘special qualitative operations’, which targeted selected police officers and public figures on the basis of the Islamic principle of retributive justice (qisas).0
In January 2015Outside Egypt, the HAC sanctioned the creation of the Crisis Management Committee Abroad (CMCA) in January 2015. Led by younger mid-ranking figures who had relocated abroad after the coup,0 the CMCA soughtaimed to delegitimise the coup internationally, document human rights violations, and coordinate diaspora activities outside Egypt.0 It managed multiple portfolios including political engagement, legal and human rights advocacy, foreign affairs, media, and training, and recruitment, each overseen by a small specialised teams.0 Its membership was drawn from Brotherhood’s major exile communities in Qatar, Sudan, Malaysia, and Turkey.0
The rise of both the CMCA and the HAC generated a sense of marginalisation among long-standing senior figures within the Brotherhood in Egypt and abroad. These included former Secretary-General Mahmoud Hussayn, a divisive figure who previously managed the organisation’s affairs in Istanbul through a non-institutional body known as the ‘Liaison Office of the Brotherhood Abroad’, and Ibrahim Munir, head of the Rabita, the London-based liaison office and headquarters of the ‘International Network of the Muslim Brothers’.0 In January 2015, the HAC’s appointment of the young spokesman Mohamed Muntassir as spokesman fuelled resentment within the old guard and its supporters, who perceived the move as a hostile takeover of the organisation. This perception and growing tension sowed the seeds of a year-long organisational crisis (mid-2015–mid-2016) and set the stage for the subsequent reassertion of the old guard.0
Innovative non-violence
Between August and September 2014, under mounting pressure from the Brotherhood’s youth cadres, the Kamal-led HAC proposed a three-phase plan known as ‘Confusion and Exhaustion–Weakening–Termination’.0 Presented as the group’s new strategy against the post-coup order, the plan was approved by 26 heads of administrative offices and the secretaries-general of Egypt’s seven geographical sectors.0 The strategy centred on the concepts of al-silmiyya al-mubdiʿa (innovative non-violence) and al-ʿamaliyyat al-nawʿiyya (qualitative operations). Although these terms carried connotations of non-violent resistance, they increasingly served to justify unconventional and targeted low-level violence.0
The first phase sought to ‘confuse and exhaust’ the new political order by creating a pervasive sense of instability and disruption. This entailed coordinated acts of civil disobedience and vandalism targeting public infrastructure, including roads, electricity generators and power stations, telephone repeaters, selected businesses, and ATMs, alongside the mass mobilisation of protesters in major urban centres.0 As initially conceived by the Kamal-led HAC, the plan confined actions to the use of light weapons (primarily fireworks and cartouche shotguns) for the defence of peaceful protesters. It neither authorised the formation of armed groups nor the use of heavy weaponry.0
Tactically, these operations aimed to generate chaos. Large crowds blocked roads, disrupted traffic, and set fire todamaged police convoys in deliberate attempts to obstruct security forces’ access to protest sites and provide demonstrators with a degree of protection. The broader objective was to expose state vulnerabilities and undermine regime legitimacy while also inflicting economic damage and causing public embarrassment.0 A notable example of this strategy of publicly embarrassing the post-coup regime was the  attack attributed to the QAC attributed to QACs on several electrical transformers in April 2015, which disrupted Media Production City and temporarily took state television broadcasts off the air.0
Within this framework, QAC operatives were authorised to exercise self-defence and protect demonstrators, particularly women, through non-random violence. The permissiveness of violence reportedly extended to targeted retaliation against police and army officers, as well as organised groups of regime-backed thugs, especially in cases involving murder, torture, or sexual violence.0 In some instances, QAC operatives issued direct threats to officers implicated in detainee abuse or gender-based violence.0
Despite this shift towards targeted violence, the HAC-led Brotherhood continued to frame these tactics within a discourse of non-violence, frequently invoking the slogan ‘what is less than killing is non-violence’ to signal a sustained commitment to avoiding lethal actions.0 Although the three-phase plan was approved by a narrow majority, it received broad support from young local leaders and mid-ranking figures in a number of several administrative offices.0 Nevertheless, the prospect of a transition to full armed struggle remained deeply contentious and generated significant concerns among the Brotherhood’s historical leadership, both inside and outside Egypt and ., as subsequent internal disputes indicate.
The combination of escalating state brutality, the decentralised structure of the QACs, and weak oversight of street mobilisation across governorates often resulted in violent clashes with security forces.0 As anger intensified over the growing number of young Brotherhood activists﻿ killed by the security apparatus, calls for vengeance became increasingly widespreadproliferated among youth activists. This environment of grief and rage facilitated defections from the QACs and contributed to the emergence of splinter groups with explicit militant agendas.0
New rebranding effort: Muslim Brothers’ anti-coup narrative
The Brotherhood’s temporary strategic shift coincided with the development and dissemination of an ad hoc anti-coup narrative. This narrative combined revolutionary rhetoric adopted by young Brothers and some senior figures with the more uncompromising discourse of some ‘revolutionary Salafis’, who no longer categorically rejected violence after the Rabaa massacre.0
In May 2015, a Brotherhood-affiliated digital media outlet publicly endorsed a fatwa entitled Nidaʾ al-Kinana (Egypt’s Call), issued by a collective of Islamic scholars, many of whom were affiliated with or sympathetic to the group, alongside Salafi preachers from 20 Muslim-majority countries.0 This statement followed the publication of a doctrinal text, The Jurisprudence of Popular Resistance Against the Coup, issued by the Muslim Brothers’ Sharia Committee. Theat earlier document sought to provide religious legitimacy for the Brotherhood’s efforts to overturn the post-coup order while reinforcing support for the three-phase resistance plan discussed above.0
Presented in a dialogic format, the text advances a series of legal arguments declaring post-coup institutions illegitimate from an Islamic jurisprudential perspective. Its primary aim was to emphasise President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s political, religious, and moral illegitimacy, argue for the restoration of Morsi’s mandate, and promote a collective obligation to secure his release from detention.0 SIn signalling a clear break from Hasan al-Banna’s non-confrontational reformist approach, the document aligned fully with the new Brotherhood’s revolutionary operational logic and sought to mobilise anti-coup supporters beyond the organisation’s formal ranks. It opens with a forceful denunciation of the post-coup regime’s legitimacy, stating:
Sisi prevailed over someone who was sworn in, but he did not triumph over someone like him [Morsi]. Morsi’s pledge of allegiance still hangs on the necks of the Egyptian people because he did not withdraw from what is legitimate [to be replaced] with a coup. It is, therefore, [the Egyptian people’s] duty to liberate him from captivity.0
The text further argues that allocating resources to anti-coup efforts will be religiously rewarded. Such efforts include ‘the support for the families of detainees whose households have lost their breadwinners, the treatment of those injured and the efforts to rebuild homes that were destroyed’. It also specifies that ‘supporting the prisoners is among the greatest obligations’,0 before concluding:
Whoever equips a fighter in the causepath of Allah has [also] fought; and whoever looks after a fighter’st family in his absence of a fighter in the path of Allah has [also] fought.0 IThf toppling the coup-regime, —which is backed by Zionists and Americans, —is a duty, then whatever is necessary to fulfill that duty also becomes obligatory.0
Building on this narrative, Nidaʾ al-Kinana explicitly labels the ruling regime a ‘criminal and murderous system’ and stresses the urgency of resisting and dismantling post-coup institutions by all legitimate means:
It is imperative for the ummah, its rulers and peoples, to resist the regime, and work towards breaking it and dismantling it by all legitimate means to safeguard the fundamentals of the ummah and preserve the higher objectives of Islam.0
The fatwa further declares that ‘coup’s supporters, including rulers, judges, officers, soldiers, muftis, media professionals, and politicians, should all be considered murderers… They must receive retributiveon punishment (qisas) within the limits of the Islamic law’.0
Central to Nidaʾ al-Kinana is a call to support and liberate anti-coup detainees, a responsibility assigned to the Islamic community as a whole rather than exclusively to Muslim Brotherhoods activists:
Everyone who has been arrested by this criminal regime for rejecting the coup and for demanding that the will and freedom of the ummah be respected—especially women—must be fully supported by the ummah. It is an obligation upon the uUmmah to strive and spare no precious resource or effort to secure their release and free them from imprisonment, using all means that are legitimate in the religion of GodAllah.0
As part of its rebranding strategy, the Brotherhood promoted a ‘de-territorialised’ narrative rooted in a transnational Islamic identity. This rearticulation positioned the ummah as the primary political subject and challenged the military’s nationalist discourse centred on territorial sovereignty and patriotic loyalty. In doing so, the movement’s new leadership sought to counter state-promoted narratives valorising attachment to the homeland with appeals to cross-border Islamic solidarity.0
This emerging narrative did not remain confined to Nidaʾ al Kinana or  The Jurisprudence of Ppopular Rresistance Against theto the Ccoup. Both old and new media, particularly satellite television channels, were deployed to reach audiences inside and outside Egypt. By mid-2014, the Brotherhood reportedly had access to nearly six Turkey-based satellite television networks broadcasting its anti–post-coup narrative opposing the coup. These platforms not only mobilised supporters but also displayed the organisation’s financial and logistical capacity to sustain a ‘multi-million long-term media opposition campaign against the Egyptian government’.0
Within this media ecosystem, the discourse of revolutionary Salafi networks conflated with the confrontational tone of the new operational leadership. This convergence produced more extreme and polarising content, at times portraying Morsi’s opponents ‘as either nonbelievers or traitors’.0 Following the Rabaa massacre, a new Salafi space, described as ‘an Islamist commune’, emerged among, in which segments of urban Salafi youth, who interpreted framed Morsi’s violent ouster as evidence of the futility of that Islamist participation in institutional politics as a means of reforming the state from within. to reform the state from within was futile. Instead, they advocated dismantling the existing state apparatus as the only viable route to establishing an Islamic order.0 This revolutionary Salafi discourse widened the dividegap between the anti-coup camp and those who had initially coup supported the coup by recasting the conflict in stark ideological terms, as one between believers and nonbelievers. As Mohammad Yaghi notes, this new Salafi discourse also exerted a ‘radicalising effect’ on young Muslim Brothers and the new leadership.0
By May 2015, however, the Brotherhood’s branded anti-coup rhetoric had already collided with thea more conciliatory position articulated by its historical leadership. Alarmed by the growing detachment of young members from the QACs and the emergence of radical factions,0 senior figures reaffirmed that the Muslim Brothers adhere:
to absolute peacefulness and non-violence in all its forms and that it will accept any harm it faces as a result of abuse, arrest, killing, torture, and persecution, for the sake of its commitment to these principles.0
The fact that both discordant positions claimed to represent the organisation’s official stance points to the presence of a competing institutional logic to the traditional logic of peaceful reformism. This alternative logic rested on thea rejection of the long-standing organisational strategy advanced by the Brotherhood’s historical leadership, namely gradual reformism and the preservation of the organisational status quo. Supporters of this new﻿ revolutionary logic rejected al-Banna’s non-radical approach, and instead favoured direct confrontation with what they regarded as an illegitimate post-coup order.
The absence of a unified narrative at a moment of deepening crisis also underscores the internal division between two camps: those who supported Kamal’s strategy of escalating confrontation with security forces and those who opposed or remained sceptical of it. As Noha Mellor observes, during the ensuing intra-movement struggle between mid-2015 and 2016, media outlets became a critical arena of contestation. They served not only as instruments of (re)branding or as platforms for amplifying each camp’s position, but also as strategic assets in a broader struggle for control over the Brotherhood’s media ecology, through which both the old guard and the younger operational leadership sought to assert their authority and influence.0
Rising challenge to the power vertical
The revolution became a spirit opposed to every status quo, even inside the Brotherhood, […], and to al-Banna’s gradual reforming method, which proved to be no longer valid. It became clear that they could not continue moving in circles.0
Former CMCA member, author’s interview (2021)
These words encapsulate a widely shared sentiment of disillusionment among current and former members, especially younger Brothers﻿ th, regarding the old guard’s hierarchical vision and al-Banna’s gradual method of reform.
The emerging revolutionary logic crystallised in individual members’ rejection of the Brotherhood’s foundational principle of ‘listen and obey’ (Chapter 2 ). This refusal of blind obedience stemmed from the erosion of trust in the historical leadership, particularly following the Muslim Brotherhood’s violent ousting from power and the brutal repression that ensued. Many members held the old guard responsible for strategic failures that culminated in the 2013 coup and its aftermath.
Reflecting the personal transformations experienced by rank-and-file members after the revolution and subsequent repression, a Muslim Sister recounted:
I don’t listen and obey. The revolution changed me, and what happened to me afterwards changed me even more. I won’t listen and obey […], I’m a journalist by training and an activist; of course, I won’t shut up either about them [the group’s historical leadership].0
Even members who remained within the organisation began to question the Muslim Brothers’ organisational norms and conduct. A young, newly elected  leader of the Istanbul-based administrative office asked angrily:
Who is responsible for our fate? The people [talking about the Brotherhood’s old guard] who decided everything before the military coup? If this is the case, how can we trust them again? How and why can we obey them again if we don’t become part of the organisation’s decision-making process?0
Following the coup, the breakdown of trust and the rejection of blind obedience led to the emergence of individual initiatives beyond the Brotherhood’s formal structures. A growing number of members, including second-tier leaders, established their own media and television channels, think tanks, and research centres. Disillusioned youth independently pursued academic studies in fields such as political science, international relations, and sociology to make sense of the organisation’s failures and the broader political crisis they witnessed in post-revolutionary Egypt.0 Previously, such pursuits had required approval from senior leaders, indicating a significant rupture with internal norms and a critique of the old guard’s wariness ofresistance to specialised roles.
Interview data also reveal widespread frustration with the organisation’s reliance on unelected and unaccountable leadership, produced through internal lobbying and sustained by blind loyalty. Many viewed this leadership style as a barrier to reform. Proponents of the new revolutionary logic criticised the absence of deliberative mechanisms, transparency, and professionalism, organisational deficiencies that had long characterised the Brotherhood’s internal functioning.
The experience of governing, the subsequent violent repression, and the prison experience, led some young members inside Egyptian prisonscells to embark on a prolonged process of re-evaluation (murajaʿa) of the Brotherhood’s organisational culture, methods, and behaviour.0 Initiated in early 2017, this revisionist exercise extended beyond prison walls to include members in exile, who articulated a comprehensive critique of the group’s ideological immobility.
Despite the intellectual weight of these efforts, the revisionist turn failed to produce a unified alternative within the organisation. It proved insufficient to reverse the deepening membership crisis and ongoing disengagement that the Brotherhood experienced in the decade following the Uprisings.0 As a result of these individual revisionist exercises, some dissenting voices went so far as to question the supposedly unalterable Islamist nature of the organisation, namely the idea of the group as an all-encompassing and exemplary movement:0
the dominant argument within the group’s old guard is that Islam is all-encompassing—arts, economics, politics, law, etc.—which is true […]. To them, the organisation should reflect that too. But I disagree. To me, this does not mean the organisation itself must be comprehensive and involved in all of the above […]. Who’s not fit to be in a football team shouldn’t be in the League.0
This vision decouples the comprehensiveness of Islam from that of the Muslim Brothers as an organisation,0 subtlydirectly challenging the old guardleadership’s self-ascribed role as guardians of the idea of being ‘Brothers in faith’, historically embodied in and safeguardedprotected by the movement’s all-encompassing organisational architecture . Yet tThis was not the only challenge they faced. Between May 2015 and May 2016, amid an acute organisational and leadership crisis, the old guard also feared the growing prominence of a younger cohort of second-tier leaders. These figures had gained considerable support through their coordination of mobilisation efforts, their temporary stewardship of the Brotherhood’s decentralised structures, and their influence over the anti-coup narrative and the group’s media ecology.0
Institutional maintenance work
At first glance, the leadership crisis between the new and historical leadership and their supporting factions, which unfolded from mid-2015 to mid-2016, appeared to be a ‘legalistic-organisational struggle’, centred on who possessed legitimate authority to represent the Brotherhood in Egypt and abroad and to lead its activities after an unprecedented disruption to its hierarchical lines.0 Closer examination, however, reveals that the conflict ran much deeper. It reflected a fundamental divergence in organisational philosophy and strategic direction, with the Kamal-led campfaction envisioning a horizontal, decentralised, and more inclusive movement responsive to the views and needs of younger members and local cadres.0
Faced with the growing risk of institutional disruption to the tanzim (the organisation’s inner apparatus) and their top positions, the historical leadership, supported by long-standing leaders abroad, including Mahmoud Hussayn and Ibrahim Munir, intervened as ‘institutional agents’ to resist proposed changes in vision and strategymethod.0 Acting in two stages, they engaged in institutional maintenance work, understood as an intentional, creative, and purposeful process through which powerful actors repair institutions, reverse change, and re-establish the status quo.0
They initially channelled their energies to restore the pre-coup institutional norm of obedience and peaceful strategy while reasserting control over the organisation. They subsequently sought to maintain the re-centralised structure and preserve the institutional logic of the socio-reformist movement as dominant.0 Contrary to approaches that treat ‘maintenance’ as an uncontested ‘reproduction of institutional scripts’,0 the Brotherhood’s case suggests that maintenance can be coercive, contentious, and ‘language-centred’.0
Repairing the Brotherhood
In July 2015, the Egyptian regime launched another severe crackdown on the Brotherhood’s leadership, reducing the Guidance Bureau to only three members.0 However, the survival mode forced upon the group provided the historical leadership with an opportunity to resolve the organisational crisis in their favour and reassert their traditional, entirely peaceful approach0 by rejecting ‘unapproved’ initiatives on the grounds of preserving group cohesion and internal consensus.0
Earlier in 2015, the Brotherhood’s old guard accused the new operational leadership of authorising violence as part of an unapproved strategy. They also questioned its legitimacy to assume a guiding role and to determine a new approach and vision for the group, since the HAC was an approved committee but not a bureau.0
Initially, the old guard conducted an internal investigation of the Kamal-led HAC for organisational irregularities and alleged promotion of violent activities.0 This was followed by the dismissal of the young media spokesman supportive of Kamal’s faction, Mohamed Muntassir, for administrative violations.0 Later, a number of leaders and members of the Youth and Media Committees and the QACs were officially removed on the grounds that their actions and initiatives had failed to comply with Guidance Bureau instructions.0
In April 2015, former Secretary-General and senior leader Mahmoud Hussayn had attempted to prevent Kamal’s supporters from holding executive posts in future elections, replacing certain Shura Council members with ‘pro-Guidance Bureau loyalists’.0 By mid-2015, following a severe critique of the conditional permissibility of violence, Ezzat, the acting General Guide, dissolved the HAC and placed the CMCA under the London-based Liaison Office of the Muslim Brothers, led by Ibrahim Munir, a senior figure aligneda﻿ close t﻿witho the Brotherhood’s historical leadership.0 This move aimed to formally sever the CMCA’s ties with Egypt-based HAC members, thereby shifting the internal power balance in favour of the Brotherhood’s old guard.0 When the CMCA’s leadership refused to operate under Munir’s supervision, financial restrictions were imposed on the committee to halt its activities. Its leading members were also accused of disregarding the official leadership’s instructions, abandoning the traditional notion of the ‘Brotherhood in faith’, and misrepresenting al-Banna’s teachings.0
The historical leadership’s fear of losing control over the organisation to a broadly supported new leadership, coupled with the mounting risk of distortingeforming the Muslim Brothers’ group identity and al-Banna’s peaceful, reformist method, prompted the use of drastic measures to repair the organisation and restore its full authority over the organisation.
In addition to imposing financial restrictions and withholding organisational and material support from  members aligned with Kamal’s faction who had fled Egypt,0 the leadership pursued a process of ‘demonisation’ against dissenting Muslim Brothers. This included fabricating facts, spreading falsehoods, and accusations of failing to understand the idea underlying the Muslim Brotherhood. In August 2015, Ibrahim Munir compared those defying the Brotherhood’s official commitment to ‘peacefulness’ to the ‘Society of Our Master Muhammad’s Youth’, a dissenting group that opposed to Hasan al-Banna’s leadership in 1939.0
Some Muslim Sisters, particularly daughters of prominent leaders, were accused of immoral and irresponsible conduct for participating alongside men in revolutionary activities against the regime within grassroots groups such as Women Against the Coup and Youth Against the Coup.0 A more severe measure involved purging members who refused to recant dissenting positions, either by freezing their memberships or pressuring outspoken individuals to exit the movement voluntarily.0
After weakening the CMCA-HAC connection, the old guard concentrated on regaining control over the group’s social media accounts and online platforms.0 The acting General Guide replaced the previously appointed young spokesman with Talaat Fahmi, a figure trusted by the historical leadership.0 In August 2015, following the dissolution of Kamal’s administrative committee, a second HAC was established under a leader loyal to the old guard.0 The leadership also began to closely monitor those Muslim Brothers affiliated with other opposition groups abroad, such as the Egyptian Revolutionary Council.0
As the leadership crisis within the Brotherhood’s upper ranks deepened, even Qatar-based Global Mufti Sheikh Yusuf al-Qaradawi attempted to mediate, urging both the old and new leaderships to hold general elections to form a new Shura Council and Guidance Bureau.0 Upon resigning, Mohamed Kamal, the former head of HAC, called for younger members to step into leadership roles, emphasising the urgent need for new general elections and generational renewal within the Brotherhood’s upper echelons.0 This proposal was also supported by the CMCA leadership (Yahya Hamed, Amr Darrag, and Ahmed Abd al-Rahman), but firmly rejected by the old guard.0 Afterwards, the historical leadership froze the memberships of all who endorsed the proposal of holding new elections, including CMCA leaders.0
Between late 2016 and 2017, a significant portion of members became disillusioned with the Brotherhood’s capacity to challenge the post-coup order. Some formally left the organisation, becoming ‘independent Islamists’, while others became inactive.0 Young members, discouraged both by state repression and the Brotherhood’s ideological immobility, experienced political apathy and despair.0 A smaller faction of former Kamal supporters declared the Society’s ‘third founding’ after holding general elections in whichvolving 65% of the membership partecipated.0
Initially named ‘The Current of Change’, this group sought internal reform. In December 2016, upon recognising that the old guard would not acknowledge their elections, they established their own body, knowns as the ‘General Bureau’.0 Unsurprisingly, members of the General Bureau found themselves no longer part of the Muslim Brothers.0 The widespread disillusionment regarding the prospects for internal reform demonstrates that the historical leadership remained the Brotherhood’s sole effective agents.0
In Egyptian maximum-security prisons, the old guard’s repair strategies prompted harsh organisational measures. Prison-based members conducted internal elections for the role of prison blocks coordinators and reinstated committees to manage activities behind bars. However, as the internal rift widened, supporters of the old guard cut off financial aid to detainees and families who supportedive or symphatiseding withof Kamal’s faction.0
Ultimately, the historical leadership and its loyalists resolved the internal conflict in their favour both inside and outside Egypt. This success, however, came at a considerable cost.: Tthe Brotherhood lost a significant support base, second-tier leaders, and reformist members. The old guard’s reversal of post-coup strategy contributed to the failure to preserve revolutionary momentum in post-coup Egypt, with the movement suffering heavy losses, including the deaths of Kamal and numerous young activists.0
Supporters of a more revolutionary approach could not supplant the entrenched logic of the Brotherhood’s non-radical reformist tradition, as ‘energy and revolution are not academic words present in the dictionary of the Muslim Brotherhood’.0
Maintaining the organisational status quo
By late 2016, Following the reassertion of having reasserted their authority, the group’s old guard and its loyalists focused on recentralising the movement’s operations and decision-making.0 To prevent the re-emergence of a leadership with a competing organisational vision and to safeguard their positions, they deliberately induced a state of ‘organisational atrophy’ through a top-down phase of inactivity and ‘leadership inertia’.0
Between early 2017 and 2021, Tthe Muslim Brotherhood’s historical leadership significantly restricted the organisation of anti-coup demonstrations in Egypt and abroad.0 They categorically rejected proposals for organisational change or unapproved initiatives emerging from within the movement.0 A notable example is the old guard’s effort to demobilise those Muslim Sisters who continued to engage in protests against the post-coup order. This was already attemptedchieved by co-opting the umbrella group Women Against the Coup through the creation of the Revolutionary Coalition of Egyptian Women, a body which, despite its name, discouraged women from participating in street protests.0
Between late 2016 and 2021, ﻿enforced demobilisation, while serving to maintain the organisational status quo, also responded to an increasingly hostile regional and international climate, alongside the old guard’s perception that the post-coup order represented a stable reality as confirmed by the 2019 referendum that consolidated al-Sisi’s power until 2030. This belief is also reflected in one of Badie’s letters from prison (2018), which allegedly called on Brotherhood leaders to compromise with the regime.0
In both 2017 and 2019, the White House considered designating the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organisation.0 In 2017, the UK Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committeegovernment, responding to the findings of the Muslim Brotherhood Review (2015), asked the Foreign and Commonwealth Office to explain the omission of post-2013 developments and reaffirmed its intention to ‘keep under review whether the views and activities of the Muslim Brotherhood meet the legal test for proscription’.0 Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Egypt imposed a blockade on Qatar, accusing it of supporting Iran, Hamas, and the Muslim Brotherhood.0 In response, Qatar reaffirmed its stance of non-support for exiled Brotherhood leaders and ordinary members.0
In Turkey, where reconciliation with Egypt did not occur until 2021,0 Hussayn’s monopolistic leadership for nearly seven consecutive years contributed to the Brotherhood’s retreat from political activism.0 Although some anti-regime initiatives emerged in 2021, including the Union of Egyptian National Forces led by the liberal figure Ayman Nour, the establishment of the International Commission on the Death Penalty, and an unsuccessful attempt to revive the FJP abroad, these efforts remained largely symbolic. Brotherhood-sponsored political activism was deliberately put on hold, pushing many members in Egypt and abroad into a state of political disengagement.0
Organisational atrophy also manifested in leadership inertia. The historical leadership habitually recycled administrative committees led by the ‘usual faces’ within the elite, rather than establishing new organs, holding internal elections, or proposing amendments to the group’s bylaws.0
Following the arrest of Ezzat in August 2020, the then acting General Guide, Munir, assumed leadership after being appointed by his predecessor. Munir, aligned with the old guard, declared that he could not lead the organisation alone.0 Consequently, he abolished the secretariat-general previously headed by Hussayn and established a new HAC to co-lead the movement.0
The formation of this HAC, in which leaders were appointed rather than elected, appears to have been a deliberate mechanism to avoid general elections within the upper ranks.0 Although the Brotherhood’s electoral tradition has always been inconsistentrregular, former and current members interpret this leadership inertia as a form of ‘change resistance’resistance to change, a strategy employed by the old guard to preserve their organisational vision and retain power while deferring meaningful reform.0 However, this approach proved untenable when a new internal rift emerged.
During the 2011 administrative elections held in Istanbul in 2021, Hussayn’s faction suffered a setback. Hussayn then attempted to remove Munir, arguing that, under the group’s internal bylaws, he lacked authority to lead the organisation through yet another HAC. Munir responded by opening an investigation into six of Hussayn’s associates for administrative violations. The dispute escalated through public exchanges on the Brotherhood’s social media platforms, culminating in the dismissal of Hussayn and his close associates from their positions on grounds of administrative misconduct.0
Although Munir’s brief tenure (d. 2022) was noted for re-establishing a political committee in Istanbul and renewing focus on political detainees and prisoners of conscience in Egypt, restoring broader political relevance did not appear to be a priority.0 Instead, his strategy sought to reinforce organisational cohesion by re-engaging former and inactive members, healing internal divisions, and countering the organisation’s shrinking membership. Political activism abroad was again deferred,0 prolonging the movement’s inactivity and diminishing its influence.
Amid mass defections, leadership disputes, and the challenges of operating in exile, the Brotherhood increasingly turned inward, using internal retrenchment as another mechanism for maintaining the organisational status quo.0 This reflects the old guard’s conviction that organisationalgroup survival is paramount. Striving to preserve a nearly century-old institution under internal and external threats has become a mechanism for deliberate stagnation. As a former member connected to Istanbul Brotherhood circles in Istanbul observed:
They [the Brotherhood’s old guard] still thinks that they managed to preserve the organisation despite the massive crackdown thanks to their closed and disciplined structure [as an achievement]. After the revolution, many of my friends from the Brotherhood [who decided to stay] said that [it was] no time for division because ‘wethey are in a state of crisis and the secular traits were attacking the movement  […]’. But here is the point: during a crisis, the Muslim Brothers always said that after the crisis there will be some changes, but as soon as the ordeal is over, they are grateful that they managed to survive through the crisis thanks to the previous and unchanged strategies […] this means that they will never change!0
More than a decade after the Arab Uprisings that toppled Hosni Mubarak, Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood has become a smaller, inward-looking, and increasingly elitist organisation. Despite retreating into the shadows and experiencing forced disconnection from its base,0 the group paradoxically became more ‘publicly visible and accessible’,0 with leaders openly condemning one another via social media and current and former members circulating memes that mock what had once been revered as a ‘sanctified leadership’.0
Despite deep internal disagreements over strategy and declining trust and obedience among members, the historical leadership has thus far preserved the nearly century-old notion of the group as a ‘Brotherhood in faith’. By focusing on institutional maintenance,  organisation by reaffirming they have reaffirmed the logic of thea peaceful, reformist movement, even after repeated challenges. Once again, the organisation appears to be waiting for the storm to pass. While the leadership has temporarily reasserted the organisational status quo to its advantage, it remains subject to public scrutiny and internal contestation.0
Propensity not to change?
[…] giving up or compromising the Brotherhood’s fikra [idea] would constitute the real defeat for the organisation.
Ibrahim Munir, interview with Aal Jazeera Mubashir (2020)﻿ (2020)
Munir’s words, in one of his last interviews as acting General Guide, suggests the source of the Brotherhood’s irreconcilability with prospects of substantial change.0 This resistance stems from the vanguard elite’s fear that any deviation from the group’s founding idea would compromise its identity and mission, resulting in the end of the movement. Such persistent anxiety underpins the organisation’s fundamental reluctance to undertake deep transformation. For the leadership, the organisation constitutes both the guarantor of the group’s authenticity and the vessel through which its reformist mission is sustained.
The temporary and partial organisational adjustments following the Arab Uprisings primarily served to ensure the group’s survival in the face of an imminent existential threat posed by the post-coup regime. Beyond this, the Brotherhood’s institutional maintenance appears to function as a defensive mechanism, readily available to leaders seeking to preserve the organisation’s established configuration, together with its method and mission.
More than ten﻿ 10 years after the military coup that removed Egypt’s first democratically elected president, the historical leadership continues to frames the ‘fourth ordeal’ the group is experiencing as a phase within a recurring cycle imbued with specific meaning. The old guard perceives this cycle of tribulation as an opportunity to reaffirm the original sense of ukhuwwa (Brotherhood in God in faith’) and to rebuild the organisational cohesion disrupted by geographical displacement and the emergence of dissenting factions.0 This context provides the backdrop for the ‘institutional maintenance work’ described above, allowing leaders to preserve the organisational apparatus and culture in its traditional form while maintaining their positions of authority. Furthermore, the state crackdown on the organisation and its base enabled the old guard to further re-centralise decision-making processes and organisational structures.
As early as 2009, Essam al-Aryan, a former member of the Guidance Bureau (d. 2020), had critically assessed the collateral damage that prolonged state repression had inflicted on the movement throughout its organisational history. While he identified ‘positive patience, sacrifice and steadfastness’ as the Brotherhood’s customary response to the Egyptian regime’s repressive machinery, he also highlighted a ‘tendency to conservatism and attitudinal stagnation’, accompanied by an ‘incapacity to renew methods’ in the group’s social and political project. This incapacity, he argued, hindered the organisation’s ability to confront the state of siege and escape the clandestine mentality imposed by the regime.0
Following the brief political opening of the Arab Uprisings and the historical leadership’s response to post-coup restructuring, the ‘incapacity’ that Aryan had attributed to external pressures, particularly state repression, proved to have becomebecame internalised as an organisational propensity not to change. This tendency is evident in the prolonged inactivity and stagnation characterising the group in exile.0 It derives from the historical leadership’s secretive culture and their firm belief that ‘standing still without making a move’ constitutes the most effective strategy during an ordeal, given that it has allowed the movement to survive multiple crises.0
Although the Muslim Brotherhood’s engagement in post-revolutionary politics and its traumatic removal from power presented opportunities for deep organisational transformation, the historical leadership consistently acted as a barrier to any long-term change that might have distorted the group’s founding idea or departed from al-Banna’s gradualist approach to reforming the political and social order. The ‘institutional maintenance work’ performed by the old guard stems from the same aversion to change that underpins the institutional logic of the exemplary reformist movement, one that views the Brotherhood as an already perfected ‘Society of tTrue Muslims’ that must be preserved as it is.
