Ennahda’s process of party transformation
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Ennahda’s process of party transformation
Ennahda a decade before the Arab Uprisings: A ‘dormant’ movement?
Before the Arab Uprisings, wherever you go across Tunisia, you’d always find a small, long-standing historic group of Nahdawis capable of mobilising resources and led by a de facto charismatic leader. But the Tunisian society couldn’t see them.… The regime used to say ‘they no longer exist among Tunisians.…’ Indeed, they were right there but invisible to many.
Tunisia-based researcherscholar of Islamism, author’s interview, 2020 
In the early 2000s, Ennahda’s organisational capacity continued to erode following a prolonged phase of systematic repression (1992–1997).0 According to Vincent Geisser and Éric ﻿Gobe, by the mid-2000s, intense repression and widespread defections had reduced Ennahda’s active membership to no more than one thousand individuals, with the movement relying increasingly on the influence of its long-time leader, Rached Ghannouchi.0
Inside Tunisia, under constant surveillance, and the persistent threat of repression, Ennahda no longer functioned as a comprehensive movement. ‘There was neither daʿwa nor cultural activities linked to Ennahda’, remarked a former female member of the movement’s exile community.0 Ennahda’s organisational and ideological life was severely erodedessence vanquished  as a result of the ‘social death’ that it had been condemned to.0 Abroad, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali’s repressive apparatus further constrained the movement by restricting communication among members and limiting their mobility.0 Its reach extended beyond Tunisia’s borders, with security services closely monitoring prominent exiles and, in some cases, even inspecting their household waste in an attempt to trace political activity.0
The period between the early 2000s and 2007 is often described as Ennahda’s ‘dormant phase’.0 This characterisation, however, obscures a form of discreet dynamism centred on the mobilisation of human and material resources in support of detainees and their families.  Far from being a period ofRather than inactivity, this phase proved foundational. It ensured the movement’s organisational survival under repression and laid the groundwork for its later reconstitution and transformation into a political party.
Within Tunisia Dduring the early 2000s, a well-organised and extensive networks developed in Tunisia around pro-human rights associations dedicated to defending political detainees—, many of whom were affiliated with Ennahda—, and to providing social assistance to their families.0 One such organisation was the Association Against Torture in Tunisia, led by Radhia Nasrawi, a prominent human rights lawyer who defended numerous Nahdawis in court.0 Another example was the Association Internationale de Soutien aux Prisonniers Politiques, founded in 2002 and headed by Saida Akrami, the wife of senior Ennahda member and lawyer Noureddine Bhiri., a senior Bhiri later served as Minister of Justice in the Hamadi Jebali government (December 2011–March 2013).0 Throughout the 1990s a nd 2000s, the wives of Ennahda activists played a crucial role in sustaining this organisational dynamism. With their support, these networks reinforced solidarity among members and their families by preserving their commitment to a ‘shared moral and ethical project’ that endured despite social marginalisation and life under police surveillance.0
Nevertheless, maintaining cohesion and relevance as a movement in exile posed significant challenges. Ennahda’s political and communication offices were based in Paris, while its leadership operated from London, where Ghannouchi resided. With members dispersed across numerous countries, organisational fragmentation intensified.0 Amid In this context of weakening structures and different exile experiences, cross-ideological cooperation with other Tunisian opposition forces emerged as a pragmatic strategy for survival and political relevance.
As early as 2001, Ennahda established contact with Moncef Marzouki’s opposition party, the Congrès pour la République (CPR). This dialogue culminated in the signing of 2003 when Ghannouchi signed the the Call of Tunis Agreement by Ghannouchi in 2013, an initiative aimed at forging a united front against Ben Ali’s regime across ideological lines.0 During this period, Ennahda’s leadership reassessed its priorities and intensified efforts to improve relations with both international actors and domestic opposition groups.
In 2005, Ennahda joined the October 18 Collectif, a cross-ideological coalition demanding an end to state-sponsored human rights violations, restrictions on freedom of expression, association and information, and the release of political prisoners. The Collectif brought together prominent opposition figures, including Ahmed Najib Chebbi, Moncef Marzouki, Hamma Hammami and Samir Dilou.0 Despite its endurance, the initiative eventually dissolved due to personal rivalries, ideological disagreements and persistent doubts regarding Ennahda’s democratic credentials.0
Frustration over the failure of cross-party efforts to weaken Ben Ali’s grip on power led some Nahdawis abroad to pursue gradual normalisation with the regime. This shift produced the Right of Return initiative, through which individuals petitioned the Tunisian authorities for permission to return.0  While welcomed by sections of the exile community in France, the initiative was criticised by Ghannouchi as excessively individualistic.0 During this period, secret meetings and what participants described as ‘pseudo-negotiations’ took place between Tunisian officials and Ennahda membersleaders abroad.0
At the same time, internal disagreements within the exile community generated sharp criticism of the London-based leadership, accused of being excessively uncompromising towards the regime and of prolonging the hardships faced by exiles. Responding to mounting pressure, Ghannouchi stated the need for rapprochement with Ben Ali’s Tunisia and called for national reconciliation during Ennahda’s Eighth Congress in 2007.0
Inside Tunisia, following their release from prison in 2006 and 2007, Hamadi Jebali and Abdelhamid Jlassi, two senior Ennahda leaders, began discreet efforts to reorganise the movement’s internal structures and revive some of its activities.0 This process led to the creation of a Tunisia-based leadership organised around two senior figures: Jebali in Sousse and Ali Laarayedh in Tunis, another Ennahda senior figure who had recently been released from prison.0 According to some interview accounts, they sought to rebuild Ennahda’s grassroots presence by reviving socio-cultural engagement through the youth forum al-Jahaz, a legally recognised umbrella organisation led by former Ennahda figure and human rights activist Salaheddine Jourchi.0
During this phase, one particularly effective strategy was the informal reconstitution of youth sections on university campuses. Beginning in Sfax and later extending to al-Manar University in Tunis, the sons and daughters of Nahdawis independently formed small student groups. From 2005 onwards, these groups coalesced under the neutral label ‘Independent Students’. Although covertly linked to Ennahda, the network adopted a form of religiously oriented activism that explicitly excluded overt political engagement.0
On the eve of the Arab Uprisings, Ennahda was far from resembling a homogenous movement. Distinct exile trajectories and personal experiences produced varied ideological perspectives on democracy and religion.0 Tensions between Ghannouchi’s wing in the United Kingdom and the France-based exile community were frequent and undermined consensus within the diaspora. Criticism of Ghannouchi’s leadership also became more was also pronounced.0 Moreover, differences in priorities emerged between the leadership abroad and the grassroots base in Tunisia. According to an internal inquiry launched on the eve of the Uprisingsconducted during the clandestine reconstruction phase, Ennahda’s domestic base, particularly its youth, favoured re-establishing the movement as a socio-cultural actor rather than as a n underground political organisation, in contrast to the preferences of its leadership.0
Abroad, attempts at rapprochement with Ben Ali’s regime reflected Ennahda’s organisational fragility and concerns about survival amid declining membership and internal divisions. This weakening was confirmed by a former member with family ties to the movement, who revealed that in the late 2000s the leadership had even considered dissolving the organisation.0
According to Anne Wolf, Ennahda’s organisational weakness was a key factor in Ben Ali’s decision to release many of its members from prison, as the movement no longer appeared to pose a serious threat to the regime. This development coincided with a broader ‘Islamic revival’ in Tunisia in the decade leading up to the Uprisings.0 What Ben Ali failed to anticipate was the quiet reconstitution of Ennahda’s support base and leadership structures within the country, as well as the resonance of religious revival among more traditional segments of Tunisian society. Ironically, the organisational weakness that convinced the regime that the Islamist threatchallenge had been neutralised ultimately enabled Ennahda to rebuild. It created space for underground reorganisation and eased the movement’s formal transformation in the post-Uprisings period.
Ennahda’s early phase of party formation
When I return home today, I am returning to the Arab world as a whole […]. I am still the leader of my party. I want to organise a conference.
Rached Ghannouchi, co-founder and President of Ennahda (2011)
After 22 years in exile, Ghannouchi returned to Tunisia to a hero’s welcome, with thousands waiting for him at the airport, some shouting ‘God is great!’.0 As a weakened opposition movement, Ennahda had faced the risk of dissolution. The wave of social unrest that toppled Ben Ali ‘saved Ennahda’ by enabling almost 70 exiled leaders to return to Tunisia, legalise the group and gain public recognition.0
On the eve of the Jasmine Revolution, Ennahda’s organisational apparatus consisted of three main entities: the official Executive Bureau Abroad, based in London; an underground executive office in Tunisia, led by two prominent figures based in Tunis and Sousse; and the ‘Independent Students’, Ennahda’s reconstituted student wing, which by 2009 had formed a steering committee that met regularly while maintaining secrecy regarding its links to Ennahda.0
Following the ousting of Ben Ali, the first formal step towards Ennahda’sin party formation was the creation of a founding body (hayʾa asisiyya). This body elected Rached Ghannouchi as party president and formed a new Executive Bureau.0 From mid-January to March 2011, Ennahda’s leadership focused on establishing local offices. Within only six weeks, it succeeded in opening more than 2,000 offices nationwide.0
Although Ennahda obtained its party licence as early as March 2011, it only formalised its organisational structures a year later, at the Ninth Congress held in 2012, following its strong performance in the 2011 National Constituent Assembly election.0 The ‘Statute Revised Following the Ninth Congress’ (2012), published on Ennahda’s official website, describes the party as organised into central, regional and local structures.0 According to the Statute, the central structures comprise the General Congress, the Presidency and the Consultative Body (or Shura Council), alongside an authority board and a financial supervision and auditing committee.0
During this early phase, prospective members were required to submit internal references provided by members of local offices.0 They were also expected to ‘respect and defend the Arab-Islamic identity’, to follow the ‘programme of cultivation, education and training’, and to adopt ‘good behaviour’.0 Membership remained largely confined to individuals who shared Ennahda’s Islamist vision and values, and religious training continued to be formally required.
According to the Statute of Ennahda (2012), full membership required at least three years of engagement in party activities, regular participation in training programmes and a clean disciplinary record.0 Until the Tenth Congress (2016), the usar (cells or families) of the former Islamist movement were reactivated as units tasked with educating a new generation of Nahdawis about Ennahda’s history and instilling a sense of belonging similar to that fosteredcultivated amongby their parents.0
At the Ninth Congress, decisions concerning the movement’s identity and the relationship between daʿwa and politics were deliberately postponed.0 Rather than abruptly abandoning socio-religious activities, the Congress concluded with the establishment of Daʿwa wa Islah (Preaching and Reform). This organisation aimed to provide the party with a mobilisable activist base and to curb Salafist influence.0 Despite this initiative, a member of Ennahda’s Executive Bureau and a former member of parliament explained that the organisation failed to establish a meaningful presence in Tunisian society. Its creation, therefore, remained largely symbolic, reflecting Ennahda’s prioritisation of internal cohesion over addressing a sensitive intra-party ideological debate that might have led to splintering.0
Ennahda’s transformation from a clandestine Islamist movement into a modern political organisation was facilitated by its limited prior presence as a public associational movement, a condition produced by Ben Ali’s systematic repression.0 Despite its official name, the ‘Party of the Ennahda Movement’, the process of party formation did not fully resemble that of a party emerging from a broader social movement.0 Unlike movement-parties, the weakened pre-2011 movement could not serve as a successful or exemplary promoter organisation capable of triggering the coercive modelling of the newly formed party after its parent movement, as seen in the case of Egypt’s Freedom and Justice Party (Chapter 2). Instead, the weakened status of the pre-2011 movement encouraged a process closer to party formation than derivation, thereby facilitating the emergence of a distinct and autonomous political organisation.
Nonetheless, before the Arab Uprisings, the London-based leadership already functioned as a defined entity within Ennahda that for years assumed limited party-like functions and responsibilities. The Executive Bureau Abroad effectively acted as the movement’s officialpublic and international face, ‘from where we used to pick up phone calls, answering “Ennahda Party speaking”’.0 While Barbara Zollner characterises the pre-2011 Ennahda Movement in its entirety as﻿ a proto-party seeking ‘legal recognition and [using] civil society platforms as its main stage, while building structures that supported its religious, social and political work’,0 interviewees specifically identified the Executive Bureau of the Ennahda Movement as the ‘embryo-party’ that laid the groundwork for formal party formation after the revolution.0
Ennahda’s ability to establish numerous local offices nationwide in such a short period cannot be explained without recognising the effectiveness of the invisible networks and familial ties connectingamong Nahdawis acrosswithin Tunisia. The discreet yet enduring presence of  informal local leaders (ʿummal, plural of ʿamil), who retained their social legitimacy and possessed strong mobilisation skills, proved central to the rapid reconstruction of Ennahda’s territorial presence.0
In Ennahda’s original organisational structure (1979–1987), the ʿamil headed regional Executive Bureauscouncils and served as the principal liaison with the Central Executive Bureau.0 Each ʿamil supervised a network of usar grouped under 18 regional Shura Councils.0 Crucially, the ʿummal were responsible for recruitment, political and religious training, and the welfare of members, particularly during periods of imprisonment.0 Their longstanding practice of covert mobilisation of human and material resources, especially after the 1992 military trial, combined with strong intra-group solidarity among detainees’ families, kept Ennahda’s clandestine networks alive throughout decades of repression.0 Consequently, the post-2011 establishment of formal regional offices appeared as a natural extension of pre-existing informal structures.
Diluting the old movement’s Islamist flavour?
Following its public re-emergence after the Arab Uprisingsrevolution, Ennahda re-entered Tunisia’s political arena amid a society that viewed Nahdawis simultaneously as the ‘pariahs’ and victims of Ben Ali’s authoritarian regime. Against this backdrop of conflicting perceptions, during the 2011 electoral campaign the movement portrayed itself as a principled oppositional force returning to fulfil its long-standing mission of upholding liberty and justice in Tunisia, presented as tas the higher objectivessocial aims of IslamIslam.0
At this stage, Ennahda’s 2011 party programme described Islam as ‘a fundamental reference that is balanced and in interaction with any human experience of proven benefit, through the application of ijtihad (independent human reasoning)’.0 Similarly, in 2012, a senior Ennahda leader defined Ennahdaleadershipstated in an interview with Egypt Independent (August 2012) asthat ‘Ennahda is a modern party in terms of its structure, mode of operation and discourse, but also something bigger than just a politicalthe party. It is also a cultural, proselytizingproselytizing and social movement’.0 
After obtaining legal status in March 20111, the leadership viewed the preservation of the movement’s value system as beneficialadvantageous. In the initial phase of transformation into a modern political party, reaffirming these values allowed Ennahda to reposition itself as a historic defender of Tunisia’s Islamic character during a period of profound social and political change. At this point, the party was still perceived as ‘a tool to realise certain ends’ and thus ‘a consumable organisation’.0 Accordingly, in its ‘‘Closing Statement after the Ninth Congress’ (2012)’, Ennahda situated itself within a longstanding Arab-Islamic and Tunisian reformist tradition associated with figures such as Khayr al-Din al-Tunisi, Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Abd al-Rahman al-Kawakibi.0
Ennahda’s re-emergence coincided with a rise in Salafism that had already ended the ‘religious desert’ left by Habib Bourguiba and Ben Ali since the early 2000s.0 This revival generated confusion in public consciousness and initially distorted the image Ennahda sought to project. The absence of established political concepts in post-revolutionary Tunisia led many young Salafis to believe that Ennahda spoke their same language.0 This ambiguity, combined with pressure from regulatory bodies overseeing the democratic transition and from the international community expectingawaiting Ennahda to prove its democratic credentials, placed the party in an embattled position.
On the one hand, the leadership felt compelled to recalibrate its discourse to meet both domestic demands surrounding the democratic transition and the expectations of international observers. On the other hand, the unfoldingongoing Islamic revival encouraged it to retain its ‘clear religious foundation’ and its organisational role as a promoter of Tunisia’s Islamic character.0 As a result, Ennahda remained anchored to its traditional religious references until it became too deeply involved in a long and intense constitutional debate and in prolonged ‘pacted politics’ with political figures from the former regime.0
Ultimately, the normative pressures of consensusal politics, combined with fears of exclusion from the post-Uprisings political landscape, especiallyparticularly after the the ill-fated end of the Muslim Brotherhood’s experimentence in government in Egypt, prompted Ennahda’s leadership to distance itself from its Islamist past and organisational identity. In 2016, the party formally declared its departure from political Islam and accelerated far-reaching internalorganisational reforms.0
Ennahda’s non-isomorphic change
Ben Ali’s departure on 14 January 2011 marked a critical juncture for Ennahda, which at the time was then a weakened movement with little incentive to retain its previousthe organisational structures and practices developed under authoritarian rule. following its legal entry into Tunisia’s political arena. This formative conditioncontext, combined with a series of post-Uprisings developments, including intensified ideological polarisation along the secular–Islamist divide and the concomitant rise of the jihadi threat from the summer of 2013 onwards, prompted Ennahda’s leadership to initiate a far-reaching process of transformation, or non-isomorphic change (Chapter 1).0
In contrast to the theory of isomorphism, which holds that organisations tend to become increasingly similar under normative, mimetic, or coercive pressures (Chapter 2),0 organisations may respond to unsettling conditions by diversifying their repertoire of organisational ideas, symbols, and practices and by hybridising different institutional logics.0 Under these conditions, Nnon-isomorphic change entails the deinstitutionalisation of long-established practices and the introduction of ‘functionally superior’ organisational values.0 In the case of Ennahda, Sheikh Rached Ghannouchi took on the taskrole of theorising the need for organisational change, acting as Ennahda’s ‘institutional entrepreneur’.0
Ennahda’s specialisation in politics: A weak theorisation of organisational change
At the outset of any change process, the theorisation of the need for change focuses on diagnosing perceived organisational inadequacies and framing innovative ideas as legitimate and necessary remedies.0 This stage begins with the development of abstract categories and culminates in making these concepts accessible to organisational members, supporters, and the wider public.0 In Ennahda’s case, this process culminated in the Tenth Congress (2016), during which the leadership announced the party’s official departure from political Islam as an organisational innovation0, after voting in favour of its specialisation (takhassus) in politics as an organisational innovation.0 This shift was justified in light of the 2014 Constitution, which enshrined Islam as Tunisia’s official religion and Arabic as its language (Article 1), and designated the state as the guardian of religion and the guarantor of freedom of conscience, belief, and the political neutrality of places of worship (Article 6).0
Ghannouchi presented the rupture with political Islam to the public as both necessary and pragmatic. Following Ben Ali’s departure and the approval of the 2014 Constitution, Ennahda’s founder and leader declared that ‘there was no longer any need for political Islam’, as the Islamic character of Tunisian society was no longer under threat.0 In his speeches, he framed changing circumstances as requiring Ennahda to normalise its position in accordance with the new constitutional order. He further justified the party’s change on pragmatic grounds by asserting that ‘Tunisian society is already Muslim and has recovered its Arabic-Islamic heritage’.0
At the Tenth Congress, Ennahda formally announced its exclusive existence as ‘a civil party of Muslim Democrats’, in line with the nature of the Tunisian state and the liberties guaranteed by the post-Uprisings constitutional framework.0 For most senior leaders interviewed in late 2020, this shift towards political specialisation and the transition to a modern and professional party merely ‘reaffirmed the political nature of Ennahda’,0 while simultaneously defusing criticism directed at the leadership for its prolonged cross-ideological collaboration with secular parties in post-Uprisings Tunisia.0
Internally, the specialisation also served to further homogenise the party by marginalising more religiously oriented figures, who had been among the most vocal critics of Ennahda’s increasingly conciliatory stances towards secular coalition partners and its departure from political Islam and its increasingly conciliatory stances towards secular coalition partners.0 Meanwhile, both within and beyond Tunisia, the officialisation of thea division of labour between politics and daʿwa acquired urgency, as it allowed Ennahda to dissociate itself from the regionally banned Muslim Brotherhood.0 It also paved the way for enhanced professionalism and improved performance by enabling the party to focus exclusively on politics.0
During the theorisation phase of any organisational innovation, existing scholarship underscores the importance of framing new ideas as extensions of, rather than breaks with, an organisation’s established value system. This strategyDoing so enhances the intelligibility and legitimacy of emergent organisational values among affiliates, rank-and-file members, and sympathisers.0 In this vein, Ennahda did not initially present the specialisation in politics as a radical departure from its Islamic frame of references. Instead, the leadership embedded the 2016 specialisation motion within a longstanding internal debate, dating back to the 1980s, over whether and how to delineate the boundaries between daʿwa and siyasa (politics).0 As a senior Ennahda leader explained to the author, referring toon the occasion of the Tenth Congress:
We [Ennahda] decided to get out of the rigid categorisation between the ideological and political. We said NO, a political party can have an ideological foundation regardless of its type, but we can specify our work.0
These remarks suggest that incorporating the specialisation in political activities as an additional new organisational value functioned as a means of retaining ideological attachment to Islam, rather than weakeningabandoning it, by specifying the party’s roles, activities, and scope of action.0
However, fFor a new organisational idea to become fully institutionalised, however,  it must be theorised and embraced not only as a necessary response to a specific context, but also as inherently superior and valuable in its own right.0 Only under such conditions can an organisational innovation achieve ‘cognitive legitimacy’ and evolve into a stable and unquestioned arrangement.0 Ennahda’s leadership failed to meet this threshold, as it did not successfully present or endorse the specialisation in politics as a meaningful and valuable option independently of regional dynamics and domestic political contingencies.0
Although the weak theorisation of the need for change stalled Ennahda’s transformation into a modern civil party of Muslim Democrats and triggered an ambivalent re-theorisation of what change should entail (Chapter 5), the specialisation motion nonetheless secured broad approval within the party. A substantial proportion of members continues to regard it as a necessary development.0 Although Ennahda’s specialisation in politics achieved only pragmatic legitimacy, it nonetheless pushed the party to adopt several organisational practices typical of modern political organisations and to fully embrace the logic of the neoliberal economy while in government.
Revealing Ennahda’s organisational transformation
Following its legalisation, and more visibly after the Tenth Congress, Ennahda gradually replaced its selective recruitment rules to broaden its reach and appeal to wider segments of Tunisian society. This transformation sought to establish Ennahda as a civic and modern political organisation by phasing out practices incompatible with the organisational model of an inclusive political party. A central element of this shift was the party’s exclusive focus on political activities, which, from 2016 onwards, required members to choose between holding roles within the party or engaging in the associative field.0
After 2016, the party’s specialisation in politics led to the introduction of modern membership criteria that replaced earlier entry requirements, including mandatory religious training and a three-year probation period. Religious and spiritual formation gave way to an introductory course centred on communication, diplomacy, and political skills.0 However, as a senior member of the Executive Bureau clarified, adherence to ‘a code of morality’ and integrity continues to be expected of members. Whereas smokers or unveiled women were previously excluded from the movement, this is no longer the case:
Nnow you can actually see people smoking within the party. We used to have only women wearing the veil, but now you can see some ladies without hijabs in our parliamentary group. In fact, some even wear jeans […]. However, some social strata still do not see themselves as potential members of Ennahda Party. This will take time, but I believe it will happen in the future.0
Furthermore, the requirement for prospective members to obtain internal endorsement from a local office was formally removed from the ‘Statute Revised Following the Tenth Congress’,0 although some interviewees reportednoted the informal persistence of this practice.0
One of the most significant reforms adopted at the Tenth Congress was the introduction of the leadership rotation principle (tadawul). Article 31  of the revised Statute limited the party presidency to two consecutive terms.0 This reform marked a clear departure from the practices of the former clandestine movement, in which leadership changes occurred secretly and only under exceptional circumstances, such as heightened repression or incarceration.0
Although many party cadres supported reforming the procedure for electing members of the Executive Bureau in order to curb the president’s authority, the Tenth Congress reaffirmed that this prerogative remained with the party president, who would then submit the list of recommended members to the Shura Council for ratification. This decision generated widespread discontent within the party.0
Despite its formal specialisation as a political party, the Statute of Ennahda (2016) did not designate the parliamentary bloc as the party’s central driving force.0 As a former Ennahda MP observed, this ‘is an urgent matter to discuss in the next congress’, underscoring the importance of such a reform in consolidating the specialisation in politics and completing the party’s transformation into a modern political organisation.0 Similarly, the absence of a professional think tank dedicated to policy planning, an essential component ‘for any professional and modern political party’, further illustrates the incomplete nature of Ennahda’s organisational shift towards modernisation and professionalism.0
Evidence from the 2018 municipal elections suggests that the party’s internal transition towards greater openness and inclusion produced new profiles of representatives selected on an ad hoc basis to broaden its electoral appeal by opening up to independent candidates.0 A notable example is Souad Abderrahim, the former mayor of Tunis, an unveiled woman often seen in Western-style casual attire.0 On the same occasion, Ennahda’s leading candidate in Sidi Bou Said in 2018 similarly reflected the diversification of profiles emerging at the local level.0 While this opening increased internal diversity, a former head of Ennahda’s electoral office (2012–2018) acknowledged that this outcome was driven less by a deliberate leadership strategy than by thethe electoral law governing the 2018 municipal elections, which required﻿, rather than the leadership’s deliberate strategy, accounted for this outcome, as 50% of candidates on local lists were required  to be non-party members.0 Ahead of the 2019 legislative elections, Ennahda reversed this approach and returned to selecting candidates through internal elections.0
Ennahda’s evolution into a more open and modern political organisation remained partial, as youth and women continued to express frustration over their underrepresentation in leadership positions and decision-making bodies.0 Nonetheless, this transformation might have reached fuller realisation had the party not been forcibly excluded from the political arena following President Kais Saied’s power grab in July 2021.0
Ennahda in a neoliberal establishment: A new Democratic Constitutional Rally?
What began in post-revolutionary Tunisia as a promise of consensus politics became, under the polished veneer of technocratic governance, a decade-long consolidation of the neoliberal order, with Ennahda at its forefront.0 In October 2013, in response to the growing risk of Tunisia’s democratic transition being derailed, four civil society organisations brokered a landmark agreement: the Nobel Peace Prize-winning National Dialogue. This facilitated the approval of the 2014 Constitution, the establishment of a caretaker government led by Mahdi Jumaa (January 2014–February 2015), and the scheduling of the 2014 national elections. This agreement marked the beginning of a second phase of ‘pacted politics’ in the country, following the earlier coalition government led by Ennahda, known as the Troika (2011–2014).0 Mahdi Jumaa’s techn ocratic government reorganised the security apparatus to counter the terrorist threat undermining the tourism sector and sought to broaden political consensus on economic reforms through the establishment of a National Economic Dialogue.0
The 2014 elections resulted in the victory of the secular party Nidaa Tunis over Ennahda, which opted not to assume the role of opposition. Instead, Ennahda joined the Nidaa-led coalition alongside two of its secular allies.0 In addition to emphasising national security, the Nidaa-led coalition government reproposed a technocratic model of governance, drawing on a cadre of experts, some of whom had prospered under Ben Ali’s rule.0
Reliance on technocratic expertise was also central to Ennahda’s vision of governance. Prior to the 2014 elections, the governments led by Hamadi Jebali (December 2011–March 2013) and Ali Laarayedh (March 2013–January 2014) included independent technocratic ministers to compensate for the cabinet’s lack of technical administrative experience.0 In line with this approach, throughout the post-specialisation period (2016–2021), Ennahda actively sought to attract more careerists with professional expertise to its cadres.0
In 2016, nine political parties and various civil society organisations signed the Carthage Agreement, a pledge to produce governments of national unity to stabilise Tunisia politically and economically.0 Following the 2019 legislative elections, which confirmed Ennahda as the first parliamentary force, Tunisia was governed by two short-lived technocratic governmentscabinets, both facing the added challenge of managing the COVID-19 pandemic. Elyes Fakhfakh’s cabinet (February 2020–September 2020) was predominantly composed of independent technocrats with professional and academic credentials in key portfolios such as interior, industry, energy, and defence. He was succeeded by Hichem Mechichi, who led another technocratic government from September 2020 until July 2021, when President Saied invoked Article 80 of the 2014 Constitution, assuminggranting him exceptional powers amidfollowing nationwide protests over political gridlock and the precipitating socio-economic crisis.0
Despite the rapid turnover of governments and the rise and fall of numerous political parties, Ennahda remained the only political force to sustain a presence and position of power during the turbulent decade that followed the Arab Uprisings. Yet this longevity came at a cost. The experience of governing led political analysts, segments of the Tunisian public, and even Ennahda’s grassroots to draw striking parallelscomparisons between Ben Ali’s Democratic Constitutional Rally (RCD) and Ennahda. These perceptions arose from Ennahda’s embrace of neoliberal market logic, which some viewed as incompatibleat odds with its ideological origins, as well asnd from its growing reliance on a technocratic vision of governance.
Ennahda once championed strong socialist and anti-capitalist rhetoric. In its founding manifesto of 1981, when it was known as the Islamic Tendency Movement (MTI), the movement sided with the ‘mustadʿafin (the impoverished) masses of workers, labourers and all deprived people, in their struggle against the mustakbirin and the wealthy’, in pursuit of social justice, echoing the language of the Iranian Revolution.0 Eight years later, its anti-imperialist tone had softened. The 1988 manifesto emphasised building a self-sufficient national economy grounded in human principles, achieving a balance among the public, private, and cooperative sectors, and ‘eradicat[ing]e all social distinctions based on exploitation, the accumulation of wealth, monopolies and other their illegitimate means’.0
Over the decade following the Arab Uprisings, Ennahda gradually articulated its economic vision as a ‘social and solidarity economy with an Islamic tinge’, a synthesis of entrepreneurial culture, Islamic ethics, and principles of Islamic finance with the logic of the free -market logic.0 As early as 2011, in an effort to culturally and religiously appropriate capitalism, the economic section of Ennahda’s electoral programmecampaign emphasised individual effort, creativity, and initiative, values framed as intrinsic to ‘the cultural and civilisational heritage of Tunisian society and its Arab Muslim identity’.0 These values aligned with the entrepreneurial spirit of a market economy, where they could be rewarded within a capitalist framework.
Yet, as Giulia Cimini, Ibrahim Saif and Muhammad Abu Rumman have noted, Ennahda’s 2011 economic vision still positioned the state as the principalmajor actor in generating investment and employment, with Ghannouchi citing European Nordic countries as a source of inspiration while considering the potential entry of Islamic banks into Tunisia’s financial market.0
Notwithstanding its attempt to revive the Awqaf (endowments) institutions in 2013, the economic section of Ennahda’s 2014 electoral programme declared full commitment to the free market, accompanied by social compensation in line with the Islamic and moral principlesrequirement of social solidarity.0 By 2016, Ennahda’s economic vision further reduced the state’s central role in social and economic affairs, positioning it primarily as a strategic guide and forecaster, limiting its role to regulatory functions and interventions aimed at boosting sluggish private investment.0
Ennahda’s neoliberal orientation was also reflected in its voting behaviour and policy positions throughout the post-Uprising decade. In 2012, the party supported the reduction of corporate tax. In 2015, it endorsed a controversial bill lowering duties on imported alcoholic beverages, citing pragmatic justifications such as curbing the black market and accommodating European tourists.0 Moreover, in April 2016, Ennahda supported the Law on the Autonomy of the Central Bank, passed by Habib Essid’s cabinet (February 2015–August 2016) as part of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan conditions.0 Drafted with IMF support, the law insulated the Tunisian Central Bank from government directives and political interference in monetary policy by granting its executive board ‘absolute control over monetary policy, currency reserves and gold reserves’.0
In September 2016, under Youssef﻿ Chahed’s National Unity Government, and amid increased pressure from international lenders to address the fiscal deficit, Ennahda supported the New Investment Law. This legislation replaced the 1993 Investment Code to enhance investment freedom and ensure equal market access for domestic and foreign investors.0 Unlike the 1993 Investment Code, the new law explicitly sought to promote foreign investments by applying the principle of non-discrimination between Tunisian and foreign investors.0 It abolished prior-approval requirements for investment in Tunisia, except for certain activities specified in a subsequent decree. Notably, the code ‘sets out the principles of free acquisition, rental, and exploitation of non-agricultural lands by investors’.0
After proposing amendments to the original draft, Ennahda ultimately endorsed the controversial 2018 Finance Law. This legislation aimed to reduce the budget deficit to 5% of GDP by curbing civil servant salaries and lowering public debt. It also introduced a series of austerity measures, including a one-point increase in the VAT rate, higher taxes on various goods, and additional consumption-based levies on selected products, all of which were strongly criticised by Tunisian trade unions.0
To temper discontent within its traditional Islamist base, Ennahda framed its neoliberal economic vision with frequent references to the ‘social and solidarity economy’.0 A flagship initiative within this framework was the party’s support for a new national social assistance and protection systemprogramme. In 2019, Ennahda deputies backed the rollout of Amen Social, a World Bankn IMF-supported programme of targeted assistance to poor and low-income families, designed to offset the social costs of tax increases and subsidy cutsremovals mandated by IMF-driven austerity measures.0
Framed in the language of Islamic values of mutual aid (takaful) and dignity (karama), also enshrined in the 2014 Constitution, Amen Social served both as a tangible demonstration of Ennahda’s professed commitment to social justice within a free-market framework and as a strategic means to deflect criticism of its new economic orientation.0
As Maryam Ben Salem noted, from 2014 onwards, Ennahda ‘became the eulogist of reducing the role of the state as a social and economic actor without being anti-statist’.0 However, mMaintaining state intervention through social responsibility initiatives, while simultaneously supporting neoliberal policies, echoed a strategy previously employed by Ben Ali, who balanced rapid liberalisation under IMF loan conditions with social responsibility rhetoric and targeted assistance programmes.0 Such measures mitigated discontent while accelerating liberalisation, ultimately serving as a mechanism for regime survival.0
Instituted in 1992, Ben Ali’s National Solidarity Fund (FSN) ‘2626’ exemplifies this approach. Funded by ‘voluntary’ contributions from individuals and, firms, treasury allocationscredits, and domestic and international agencies, the FSN financed development projects across Tunisia, providing potable water, roads, housing, and health services, particularly in underdeveloped areas.0 This mechanism addressed inequality through social compensation without fully replacing state provision of services and welfare.
A decade after the Arab Uprisings that toppled Ben Ali and his ruling party, Ennahda increasingly resembled a technocratic party with a limited capacity to address Tunisia’s deepening socio-economic crisis, much of which stemmed from structural conditions0 and global economic forces beyond its control.0 In public perception, Ennahda replaced Ben Ali’s RCD, a party long associated with a neoliberal economic vision shaped by loan conditions and international economic recommendations, and lacking long-term, locally grounded solutions for Tunisia’s development.0
Ennahda’s integration into the political establishment, coupled with the post-revolution recession, led the party to adopt neoliberalism as dogma, aligning with broader global economic trends and crisis-driven policy imperatives.0 The uncritical adoption of the same economic orientation by Ennahda and other major political forces contributed to erasing distinctions in political and economic visions between the Islamist-born party, the secular Nidaa Tounes, and parties emerging from its fragmentation.0 Consequently, Tunisia’s post-revolutionary political elite fell short of articulating or implementing alternative economic solutions, leaving Tunisia increasingly subject to foreign lenders’ conditionalities.0
Politically, the absence of differentiated programmes or alternative solutions to social and economic challenges fuelled widespread voter disillusionment with Tunisia’s nascent democracy. This dissatisfaction was reflectedmanifested itself in low turnout on the occasion offor the 2018 municipal and 2019 national elections and culminated in the rise of aa distinctive form of﻿ anti-system populism embodied by President Kais Saied.0
