Organisational identity recrafting within the Pparty of the Ennahda Movement
The Muslim Brotherhood and Ennahda
Organisational identity recrafting
Rerouting Ennahda’s change process?
After securing a clear victory in the 2011 National Constituent Assembly election, Ennahda’s leadership pursued a strategy of sustained series of concessions that facilitated the adoption of the 2014 Constitution while and reflectinged a strong commitment to self-restraint0 and cross-sectoral consensus.0 AfterBy adopting an often criticised conciliatory approach towards secular coalition partners and figures associated with the former regime, the leadership articulated the need for major organisational change. This shift entailed introducing specialisation in political activities as a new organisational value and rebranding Ennahda’s identity as ‘a party of Muslim Democrats’. The﻿ The leadership  announced this reorientation at the Tenth Congress in 2016, when it formally declared Ennahda’sEnnahda’s departure from political Islam.0
Within the field of organisation studies, the diffusion of new organisational ideas follows successful theorisation. During this phase, new ideas and solutions become increasingly objectified, ‘gaining social consensus concerning their values’.0 However, institutionalisation occurs only when actors theorise and internalise new practices and norms as valuable and meaningful in themselves, rather than as temporary organisational remedies. In such cases, ideas are more likely to endure across generations because they are recognised as ‘cognitively legitimate’.0 As the previous chapter demonstrated, the ineffective theorisation of specialisation as an additional new organisational value prevented it from attaining cognitive legitimacy and from evolving into a durable, taken-for-granted organisational arrangement within Ennahda. When organisational change stalls at the level of pragmatic legitimacy, as in this case, the process becomes vulnerable to being rerouteding or recasting in divergent directions.0
At the micro level, once a major organisational change is formalised, members may accommodate, resist, or rework the innovation. Through processes of identification, they can reshape the organisation’s newly refashionedorganisational identity and, in turn, thereby influence dynamics at the meso level.0 Theseis processes empowers the recipients of change, or ‘identity targets’, which include senior leaders, rank-and-file members and support base alike, to act as change agents rather than as passive recipients of organisational transformation (Chapter 1).0
Non-homogeneous identification: The rRole of identity targets in affecting change direction
In the post-2016 period, Ennahda’s membership comprised three distinct generational cohorts.0 The first generation consisted of older members devoted to daʿwa-related activities and responsible for the religious education of new recruits. The second generation included individuals who rose through the student movement, trade unions, and human rights activism, many of whom joined Ennahda in the 1980s and later assumed leadership roles after 2011. A third cohort emerged in the wake of the Uprisings as a result of Ennahda’s increasing professionalisation and political focus. This younger generation included sons and daughters of, or individuals with familial ties to, members belonging to the two older generations. Unlike the previous generationsthe, they often expressed a less pronounced attachment to the party’s religious foundationIslam. This cohort also encompassed a small group of conservative members in their mid-thirties and forties who, while not religiously devout, joined the party in the post-2011 and post-2016 period.0
As Ennahda evolved into a specialised political actor, many functions traditionally carried out by the first two generations of Nahdawis were gradually outsourced to civil society. As the following sections show, since 2016, the rebranded identity of Ennahda as a civil party of ‘Muslim Democrats’ has come under strain, not only from political opponents but also across generational lines within the party. Theis process of identity redefinition encountered resistance from three distinct groups of identity targets, each articulating different positions on the party’s trajectory of change.
Ennahda’s Islamist base: Disidentification from a movement in denial
Among the most vocal opponents of Ennahda’s new identity are members of its Islamist grassroots and broader religious constituency. In an interview with the author, a female Ennahda mMember of pParliament described this group as a sizeable segment of supporters who reject the ‘Muslim Democrats’ label. ‘They want us to retain the religious label and identity’, she explained, ‘as though weif weree were abandoning the Islamic dimension in our platform or forsaking religious practices altogether’.0 For these supporters, Ennahda should remain anchored to the organisational identity of the pre-2011 Islamist movement: a political and social actor rooted in Islamic values and committed to preserving Tunisia’s Islamic identity.
Hager, a young university student and grassroots member, went further. She not only disassociated herself from the party’s new identity but also sharply criticised the leadership for aligning with political forces that, in her view, undermined the movement’s survival. She accused the leadership of betraying Ennahda’s ethos as an oppositional and morally superior Islamist movement. As she put it:
The transformation from an Islamist movement to a democratic party was of no use [...]. Tthe party seeks societal acceptability by denying itself, and this is a loss for the movement […]. Revisions are required, but this change has blown up the movement. Politically, this transformation opened the door for the party to communicate with all components of the political scene, but internally the value system that shaped Ennahda was deeply shaken.0
Similarly, a long-time Ennahda supporter from Sousse lamented the party’s departure from its original mission: ‘Ennahda has distanced itself from what it truly is. It is now only concerned with political survival, while some of us are still seeking continuity with the old social and ethical project it envisioned we once voted for’.0 Overriding the party’s former identity marker, rooted in a religious mission and a broader project of societal transformation, contributed to the perception that Ennahda had forfeited its core essence. Interview data repeatedly identify this perceived identity loss as a key factor in the party’s electoral decline.
Across generational lines, members of this group resist the ‘Muslim Democrats’ rebranding in two ways: by disidentifying from a party they view as having relinquished its religious commitments and by withdrawing electoral support, thereby sanctioning the leadership’s choices. Between the 2011 and 2019 elections, Ennahda’s voter base declined sharply, from approximately 1.5 million to around 500,000.0 While this decline must be contextualised within the wider fragmentation and disillusionment afflicting Tunisia’s party politics, it was also driven byreflected the disappointment of many early supporters who had initially turned to Ennahda after the Uprisings, viewing it as a principled oppositional force untainted by the former regime.0
In the post-2014 elections, tThe party’s post-2014 coalition with the secular Nidaa Tounis, together with the gradual dilution of religious references, further alienated its Islamist base.0 Although a core of historicalformer activists militants with deep emotional and familial ties to the pre-2011 movement might have continued to support Ennahda had it remained an active political player after 2021, the shift in identity and the loss of religious zeal proved alienating for many others.
This dynamic of disidentification and disillusionment has placed significant pressure on the party leadership, which, fearful of internal fragmentation and further erosion of its Islamist support base, has struggled to advance the organisational changestalled transformation towards a socially conservative political actor.0
Post-Uprisings’ newcomers: ‘Being part of a quasi-secular party’
I do not believe that our approach to governing—whether in the types of bills we propose, our tax policies, or parliamentary decisions—is driven by religion anymore. Frankly, I think we manage politics in a conservative way, but not a religious one. That’s why these changes must be enhanced, and the leadership should allow us to engage with a broader segment of Tunisians—most of whom are conservative, but not strictly in the religious sense.
A Mmember of Ennahda’s Pparliamentary Bbloc, author’s interview (2020)
These remarks were made by a mMember of pParliament who joined Ennahda after the Uprisings awithnd who has no pre-existing ties to the pre-2011 movement. In conversation with the author, he acknowledged that he does not resemble the ‘classic Nahdawi’. His difficulty in identifying himself as part ofwith the the﻿ party of ‘Muslim Democrats’ stems from the fact that, while he holds socially conservative views, he is not a practising Muslim. At the time of the interview (2020), hHe perceiveds Ennahda’s current political conduct as increasingly secularised and hopeds that the party wouldill continue to evolve in ways that accommodate more figures like himself, who remain a marginal presence within its ranks.0
This cohort of identity targets, which has also challenged Ennahda’s refashioned identity as a party of Muslim Democrats, includes younger Nahdawis who joined after the Uprisings and during itshe party’s turn towards political specialisation in politics. They describe Ennahda not as an Islamist movement but as a conservative political actor that has quietly embraced secular practices.
Within this group is a growing number of ambitious career-oriented newcomers who view the Islamist-born party as engaged in an ongoing process of secularisation, one that, in their words, ‘has put religion aside and shifted its full attention to political life’.0 They envisage a reformed party driven by a new generation of pragmatic actors committed to making Ennahda more inclusive and to pushing it further along a secular trajectory. One young Nahdawi, for example, described himself as part of ‘a national party rooted in coalition and dialogue, determined to unify – rather than divide – the diverse ideological strands of Tunisia’s youth’.0
This generation of change recipients thus portrays Ennahda as a party in transition that is redefining itself away from its Islamist roots. Their vision stands in sharp contrast to that of the movement’s Islamist base, which regards such a trajectory not as renewal but as betrayal.
In the shadows of the past: Conditional and subtle resistance to change
Ennahda will preserve its ideological reference to Islam until the time our civil society becomes fully independent from political agencies and state organs, and the rule of law is internalised as a custom and etiquette within our society, in a Khaldunian sense […].
Ennahda senior member of the Executive Bureau, author’s interview (2020)
These observations were offered by a senior Ennahda leader who joined the movement in the late 1980s as a university student. His position reflects a view widely shared among the party’s senior cohort. For this group, Ennahda’s historical role as a guardian of Tunisia’s Islamic identity remains relevant despite the formal protections enshrined in the 2014 Constitution. Their continued identification withattachment to the pre-2011 Islamist movement is conditional upon the full independence of civil society and the institutionalisation of the rule of law in post-revolutionary Tunisia. Accordingly, their stance constitutes a quiet resistance, rather than outright rejection, of Ennahda’s rebranding as a civil party of Muslim Democrats.0
For this group of identity targets, at the time of the interviews (2020), Tunisia hads not yet reached a final stage of state evolution in which the 2014 Constitution and the post-Uprisings constitutional framework enjoyed full social acceptance and legitimacy. The core principles of the new constitutional order, civil society independence , and the rule of law, wereare viewed as aspirational rather than realised. Within this perceived fragility of Tunisia’s political culture and post-revolution institutions, some senior Nahdawis continued to regard Ennahda as a necessary bulwark against the erosion of the country’s Arab-Islamic identity.0 This lingering sense of mission was echoed by one of the movement’s founders, who downplayed the significance of Ennahda’s political specialisation by describing it as a change of ‘small dimension’, arguing that:
We [Nahdawis] are now interested in the relations with state power based on a legal system and an Islamic regime that is democratic, and what concerns us is ensuring that no one can establish an anti-Islamic system.0
These words suggest that, for some members, Ennahda continueds after 2016 to function as a moral safeguard, whose very presence prevents the emergence of policies or regimes that might undermine Islamic norms and valuesisions in a Muslim society. This understanding reaffirms the party’s historical image as a defender of Tunisia’s religious and cultural identity, without explicitly denyingrejecting the significance of political specialisation or the organisational transformation it entailed.
This group of identity targets is notably heterogeneous. It includes senior daʿwa figures, Nahdawis in party leadership roles, and members from Ennahda’s exile community, ranging in age from their mid-fifties to their mid-seventies. What unites them is the formative experience of having joined Ennahda well before the Arab Uprisings, under the rule of Habib Bourguiba or Zine El Abidine Ben Ali. Regardless of their current roles within the party or civil society, many remain deeply attached to memories of Ennahda as a persecuted, tightly knit, family-like movement for which they sacrificed their youth and part of their lives. They often look back on the former Islamist movement with nostalgia and view the process of specialisation and the resulting refashioned identity as Muslim Democrats with mixed feelings.
Within this group, problematic identification with athe rebranded party of Muslim Democrats manifests in the discrediting of Ennahda’s new practices, its post-specialisation conduct, and the outcomes of its transformationthe organisational change. Some express a longing for the movement’s earlier social and educational mission.0 They firmly believeargue that the party’s retreat from its broader social project has created a vacuum in religious and ethical guidance, leaving Tunisians in ‘a period of disarray in terms of religious identity […], thereby ’ and allowingenabling ‘a more dangerous interpretation of Islam to prevail among the youth’.0 Others draw a direct link between Ennahda’s departure from political Islam and what they describe as a rise in amrad ijtimaʿiyya (‘societalal illspathologies’), including drug abuse, crime, and moral disorientation.0 Such discursive practices subtly undermine Ennahda’s envisagedplanned transformation and implicitly call for a re-anchoring of its organisational identity in its traditional Islamist traditionroots.
In this regard, one senior member, now active exclusively in civil society, gently rejects the Muslim Democrats label by describing Ennahda in terms that recall the pre-2011 movement:
There is no doubt that the Ennahda movement is an Islamic party with a specific perspective and vision that renews and develops the Islamic thought and the religious practice by opening up to human experience.0
Members who hold similar viewsMembers  do not fully acceptendorse the ideanotion that Ennahda should operate as a political party detached from the Islamist tradition and mission. Instead, they maintain that ‘Ennahda abandoned the advocacy field, but not the Islamic daʿwa’.0 In an indirect challenge to the party’s political specialisation, they express frustration over the decline of religious and educational activities in Tunisia, contending that such initiatives could have enhanced the effectiveness of counter-terrorism efforts more than the securitisation policies adopted after the summer of 2013.0 They also criticise the prolonged cross-ideological cooperation with secular forces and figures associated with the former regimeelite, as well as the political concessions made to them, which they view as corrosive to having eroded Ennahda’s moral compass and as marginaliseding of its grassroots base.0
UltimatelyIn conclusion, this group of identity targets articulates a quiet yet potent form of resistance to Ennahda’s recast identity as a civil party of Muslim Democrats. Their attachment toidentification with the organisational identity of the former Islamist movement is neither openly oppositional nor wholly incompatible with the post-2016 specialised political party. Rather, it takes the form of a subtle and conditional dissent that continues to question the costs of Ennahda’s transformation.
Recrafting Ennahda’s organisational identity: Muslim Democrats, Islamists, or Seculars?
Following an ineffective theorisation of the need for change (Chapter 4), identity targets within Ennahda hindered the change process in the post-specialisation period (2016–2021) by resisting alignment with the party’s new organisational identity as Muslim Democrats. n the post-specialisation period  The absence of a homogenousneous identification with this organisational identity not only stalled Ennahda’s process of change but also redirected it. Identity targets rerouted the trajectory of change by crafting divergent group identities as alternative endpoints, conditioned by ‘their self-perception based on how they perceived themselves in relation to their affiliation to Ennahda’.0
From the institutional perspective prevalent in organisation studies, the recrafting and reconstruction of organisational identities and group ideas constitute a form of ‘institutional work’: a purposeful and creative act through which institutional arrangements are established, disrupted or maintained (Chapter 1). In Ennahda’s case, this processwork affectedconcerned Ennahda’s the rebranded post-specialisation identity in the post-specialisation period.0 The focus on how individual and collective actors resist, accommodate or overhaul a processes of change process﻿ attributes significant power to agency in influencingshaping institutional continuity and transformation (Chapter 1).
In 2020 and 2021, when Ennahda members were asked to define the party, dissonant voices emerged from within. Some long-term members across the organisational spectrum continued to refer to Ennahda in the post-specialisation period ‘as a political party that still frames its vision in those intellectual roots that promote the Arab-Islamic identity’0 or as a ‘party that preserves its Islamic roots’.0 By contrast, most high- and middle-ranking leaders close to the party leadership defined Ennahda as ‘a civil party of Muslim Ddemocrats’, explicitly endorsing Ghannouchi’s proposed label.
Direct challenges to this label came from non-devotee conservative members who could not identify as Muslim Democrats:
Ennahda’s way of doing politics is completely secularised; I can’t see anything related to religion with the bills that we propose in the parliament. De facto, we are a party of national conservatives.0
Similarly, some younger members, who do not share the same religious and emotional ties to Ennahda as their parents’ generation, described it as a secular party. They argued that ‘Ennahda is a secular party that only upholds religious values such as freedom, equality and respect—values common to all national and conservative parties […] and that should become more inclusive and diverse in its membership’.0
Across interview excerpts expressingreflecting similarthese views, a clear tendency emerges to downplay explicit Islamic references and to recastframe Ennahda’sthe transformation as a shift process towards becoming a national conservative party, ‘not in the ideological sense, but in the social one, to attract broader segments of the Tunisian society, which includes socially conservative people’.0 Likewise, as noted earlier, younger newcomers view Ennahda as ‘a national party based on coalition and dialogue’.0
In theory, organisational identity recrafting operates as a ‘sense-giving strategy’ designed to render organisational change meaningful and intelligible.0 In Ennahda’s case, however, this agentic process also functions as a means of resisting change from multiple standpoints. Moreover, this identity recrafting process highlights the difficulty of drawing a clear distinction between social identities, understood here as ithendividuals’ self-perceptionsconceptions individuals derive from or construct through their affiliation with Ennahda based on party affiliation, and organisational identity, which addresses theorganisational identity, which addresses the question ‘Who are we as an organisation?’ as an organisation?’.0 Following the specialisation in political activities and the ensuing changes in membership and recruitment, the former inevitably shaped the latter.
On the eve of President Saied’s unilateral takeover of state institutions, Ennahda heldsignified different meaningsthings forto different members. For some, membership meant belonging to a civil party of Muslim Democrats that ‘slots the political and the religious in two different compartments’ and no longer attemptsseeks to enforce religion through state power, seeking instead to integrateing Islamic ethics and cultural identity into a broader civic and political platform.0 For others, representing or voting for Ennahda amounted to supporting a Tunisian secular conservative party, in sharp contrast to those Nahdawis who continue to view it as firmly rooted in the Islamic tradition. For this latter group, despite the division of labour between politics and the associative sphere, Ennahda remains attached to a horizontal, transnational identity and Muslim consciousness embodied in the Ikhwani tradition, which is deeply entrenched in Muslim Brotherhood-like movements that emerged fromshaped by specific historical conditions.
The uneasy coexistence of these three group identities has compromised both Ennahda’s ijmaʿ (internal consensus) and its wihda (unity). At the same time, the foundations of internal consensus have shifted. After the approval of the specialisation motion in 2016, Ennahda’s shared history of persecutionrepression, Islam as an emotional bond, and the former ‘dissident subculture built around identity, faith and behaviour’ can no longer homogenise the party’s cadresrank and file. Nevertheless, these elements remain salient identity markers and sources of intragroup solidarity for some long-term members whose bonds with fellow Nahdawis were forged throughshared ‘blood and tears’.0
A decade after the Uprisings that ousted Ben Ali, the uneasy coexistence of discordant group identities produced through organisational identity recrafting rendered Ennahda neither clearly distinguishable nor fully trustworthy to its voters, nor to the new electoral constituency it sought to attract prior to Saied’s crackdown on its leadership and the wider Tunisian opposition.0
Discouraging Ennahda’s progressive change: Public opinion, media, and bias in post-revolutionary Tunisia
In the post-Uprisings period, public trust in Ennahda declined sharply, from 40% in 2010–2011 to 16% by 2019.0 Three years after the party specialised in politics, a 2019 Sigma Conseil poll indicated that Ennahda’s president, Rached Ghannouchi, was the least trusted Tunisian political figure, with 67% of respondents expressing unfavourable views.0
Despite its leadership’s efforts to recast Ennahda’s organisational identity and promote inclusive governance, the party’s transformation into a modern political organisation and its contribution to Tunisia’s democratisation received little public recognition. This lack of acknowledgement, coupled with a shrinking electoralIslamist base, discouraged the leadership from advancing and completing its envisaged organisational change.
Even after the fall of Ben Ali’s regime, segments of the Tunisian public continued to derogatorily refer to Nahdawis derogatorily as khwanji, a term in Tunisian dialect term originally denoting membership in the Muslim Brotherhood. Under Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, the term acquired strongly negative connotations and has persisteds as a label for individuals with ties to Ennahda, portrayed as involved in subversive or unlawful activities.
On the eve of Saied’s presidential coup on 25 July 2021, widespread suspicion and mistrust coalesced into public opposition to Ennahda.0 In addition to the aggravating economic crisis, for which much of the public blamed the party due to its prolonged presence in power, resentment was further fuelled by Ben Ali’s long-running smear campaign. For over two decades, the regime had portrayed Ennahda as a shadowy organisation plotting against the state, a stigma that persisted in the post-Uprisings era owing to ineffective media reforms.
In Tunisia, the post-2011 media landscape remained closely entwined with political power, perpetuating narratives forgedestablished under the former regime.0 Despite the ousting of the former rais and Ennahda’s prolongedsustained presence in government, ‘some Tunisians continue to perceive us as a former clandestine group led by dangerous individuals who operate through secrecy, informal structures and invisible networks’, a senior Ennahda member lamented to the author.0
The unreformed media sector contributed to sustaining and amplifying these negative perceptions. Following Ben Ali’s departure, the new political elite failed to democratise the media and online space. Although institutions such as the National Authority for Information and Communication (INRIC) and the High Independent Authority for Audiovisual Communication (HAICA) were established to promote a free, diverse, and professional media sector, meaningful reform proved elusive.0 Provisions on financial transparency, self-regulation of print and electronic outlets, and separation of administrative and editorial functions failed to translate into professional practice. Despite new legal frameworks and professional standards, they did not result in the proper training of editors and journalists,0 nor did they diversify media ownership.0
Between 2011 and 2014, the Tunisian government, in which Ennahda was a key actor, actively hindered the liberalisation of the broadcast sector. Business elites and media executives with ties to Ben Ali or Leila Trabelsi’s family retained control over major outlets.0 The post-revolutionary elite also remained susceptible to lobbying from broadcasters licensed under the former regime who resisted market competition. Consequently, Tunisians continued to consume news in a partisan, often biased, and unprofessional media environment.0
Tunisian media invoked the legacy of Ben Ali’s regimethe ancien régime, reinforcing a narrative of a national ‘rescue mission’ against the Islamist threat.0 In parallel, the sector became a competitive arena for an ambitious new political elite, including Ennahda, which stifled regulations that might have jeopardised its interests.0 Audiovisual platforms, in particular, were used to score political points rather than promote democratic discourse.
As Andrew Bennett notes, Ennahda’s 2011 government faced criticism for delaying reforms of state-run media and the implementation of Decree 116, which sought to diversify ownership, improve professional standards, and break monopolies within the sector. This delay  the party time to establish its own sympathetic television channel, Zitouna TV.0
Throughout the democratic transition, the media continued to frame Tunisian politics within an entrenched secular–Islamist binary. This dichotomy reflected the ideological struggle that had defined the post-independence period, pitting Bourguiba’s vision of a moderncivil, republican and secular Tunisia against an Islamist model that centred onsituates religion as a cultural framework for policymaking and a  poorly defined notion of Islamic governance.0
Even after Ennahda’s departure from political Islam, the media and certain political actors continued to label it as an ‘Islamist party’ and a secret Brotherhood-like organisation allegedly linked to an underground apparatus.0 They deliberately overlooked the party’s long-standing process of ideological revision, initiated as early as 1981, dismissed its political specialisation as disingenuous,0 and seldom acknowledged its contribution to the country’s democratisation process.0
Furthermore, many Tunisian journalists lack the training and qualifications necessary to foster informed and constructive public dialogue or engagement with emerging political concepts.0 ‘Almost overnight, sport commentators began to talk about politics’, a Tunisian scholar remarked in conversation with the author.0 Consequently, recycled narratives and smear campaigns, particularly targeting Ennahda, persisted.0 This  outcom e, however, cannot be attribut ed solely to Ben Ali’s enduring legacy or the ineffective reform of the media sector; it also reflects Ennahda’s failure to communicate its evolution convincingly to the broader public. Although the party reoriented its trajectory towards formal politics, its identity remained too pronounced, limiting perceptions of substantive change beyond its members and core supporters.
Certain aspects of Ennahda’s political conduct further contributed to public distrust. On multiple occasions, political figures initially introduced as independent publicly ‘came out’ in support of Ennahda, a practice widely regarded as unprofessional, which heightened suspicion and reinforced perceptions thatof informal channels and unofficial structures operated within the party.0 Similarly, the mobilisation of Nahdawi-led civil society groups for political purposes fuelled mistrust among secular segments, who perceived the party’s exclusive engagement in Tunisia’s institutional politics as deceitful.
For example, during the 2018 protests against the Individual Freedoms and Equality Committee (COLIBE) report, which proposed constitutional reforms including the decriminalisation of homosexuality and gender equality, some Ennahda leaders and allied organisations took to the streets to defend Tunisia’s Islamic identity. The coordination between party leaders and certain Nahdawi-led associations reinforced critics’ perception that the party had not fully embraced political specialisation.0
Ennahda’s identification with a transnational Muslim consciousness, common among Islamist and Islamist-born movements, also shaped negative public perceptions. During the Troika government (2011–2014), the party sought alignment with Qatar and Turkey, securing financial support from both. Ghannouchi’s involvement in the International Union of Muslim Scholars, historically led by Yusuf al-Qaradawi (d. 2022),0 alongside a series of symbolic and political engagements, including consultations with the Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi and an unannounced visit to Qatar in May 2021,0 reinforced public public associations  between the party and a regional pro-Muslim Brotherhood axis.0
These actions fuelled scepticism regarding the party’s transformation and undermined its credibility as an agent of democratisation. In the summer of 2021, amid anti-Ennahda mass mobilisation, many Tunisians the party was widely perceived Ennahda as irresponsible and untrustworthy. On this occasion, some Tunisian political figures actively sought to ‘defame the party’s reputation and exclude it from the political scene’.0 On the eve of President Saied’s invocation of a state of emergency, media posts from the representatives of certain political partiesactors unleashed scathing accusations against Ennahda, holding it solely responsible for the institutional paralysis that enabledfacilitated Saied’s coup. The party was denounced for allegedly exploiting the COVID-19 crisis to retain power and for normalising corruption as a defining feature of Tunisia’s post-Uprisings political order.0
Following Saied’s presidential coup, the new legal framework effectively rendered the High Independent Authority for Audiovisual Communication (HAICA) a dormant institution, stripping it of its constitutional status and placing it under direct government control. Alongside a series of ad hoc decree-laws restricting freedom of expression, most notably Decree Law No. 2022-54, authorities revived and weaponised repressive legal instruments from the Ben Ali era, including the outdated Telecommunications Code and the controversial 2015 anti-terrorism law. These measures have facilitated a comprehensive campaign of slander against Ennahda leaders and other critical voices critical of the President, culminating in the familiar alarming practice of branding political opponents as ‘terrorists’.0
Ten years on: Ennahda’s waning cohesion and growing exclusion
Since its legalisation and  entryre-emergence into the Tunisian political sceneTunisian politics, Ennahda has not only experienced a gradual contraction of its constituency but has also witnessed more alarming internal challenges. During preparations for the Eleventh Congress, initially scheduled for May 2021 and repeatedly postponed, Ennahda’s unity succumbed to the formation of competing power cliques and growing discontent towards its president.0
As early as September 2020, Ennahda affiliates hailed the preparations for the Eleventh Congress as a decisive moment that would redefine the party’s direction. Yet beneath this surface of enthusiasm and apparent unity, unresolved tensions and competing expectations loomed. A key agenda item for the Congress was the potential amendment or revocation of Article 31 of Ennahda’s statute, which limits the party president to two consecutive terms. This possibility alarmed senior party figures, resulting in a direct challenge to Rached Ghannouchi’s leadership when a group of 100 senior members demanded that he publicly commit not to seek re-election, a condition they regarded as essential for convening the Congress.0
Internal dissatisfaction with the potential revocation of Article 31 was expressed through a written correspondence deliberately leaked to the media between September and October 2020.0 Confronted with mounting pressure and the threat of party fragmentation, Ghannouchi ultimately conceded, pledging neither to amend the statute to extend his tenure nor to undermine the principle of tadawul (leadership rotation).0
This confrontation represented not onlymerely a power struggle driven by the ambitions of some senior Ennahda leadersfigures such as Abdellatiful Latif Meal-Makki, former Minister of Public Health, senior Ennahda leader, and Shura Council member,0 but also revealed deeper fractures and a broken consensus within the party. As the leaked correspondence shows, the controversy underscored the need for a generational transition in leadership, a firm rejection of the ‘personalisation of power’, and the urgency of advancing the party’s transformation into a modern and transparent political organisation.0
The ‘100 leaders’ supporting the preservation of Article 31 argued that ‘Tunisia needs a renewed and re-united Ennahda’ to enhance its conduct, with leadership rotation constituting a prerequisite. They maintained that such rotation should function both as an institutional ‘value and a mechanism’ to renew Ennahda’s project, strengthen its collective vision, and reinforce commitment to restoring internal cohesion.0
In the leaked correspondence, the 100 leaders explicitly stated that ‘affirming that the president is the guarantee of the party’s unity implies a sophism’. In their view, extending the president’s mandate exacerbates division and discord at a critical moment for both the party and Tunisia. The letter further contended that revoking Article 31 ‘destroys Ennahda’s moral credibility through the violation of the party’s statute […]—a move reminiscent of the authoritarian and personalistic regime against which people revolted on the 14 ofin January [2011]’.0
Initially, Ghannouchi responded to the demand to respect Article 31 as a precondition for participation in the Eleventh Congress by accusing its proponents of pursuing exclusioniaryst objectives and of downplaying the national interest during a delicate period of political, economic, and health crises.0 In an effort to mediate the dispute, Ghannouchi’s brother-in-law, Rafiq Abdessalam, and the former president of Ennahda’s Shura Council, Abdelkarim Harouni, both aligned with the pro-Ghannouchi bloc, authored a third letter proposing to delay the Congress to prevent factionalism, establish a ‘strategic council’ under the party president’s leadership, and include a provision in the internal bylaws designating the president as the official candidate for top state positions.0
As Larbi Sadiki rightly observed, the pro-Ghannouchi initiative was intendedserved to prepare the ground for endorsing his candidacy in the 2024 presidential elections.0 Notably, the initiative also demonstrated a misreading of the trajectory of Saied’s Tunisia.
The latest organisational developments within Ennahda, coupled with publicly expressed grievances from its members and the troubled process of leadership alternation﻿, indicate that the party lacks internal mechanisms to deliberate perspectives that diverge from Ghannouchi’s views.0 These developments also suggest that leadership changes within Ennahda isare neither motivated by a commitment to alternation as an organisational principle nor by a willingness to facilitate generational transition in the party’s upper ranks, despite widespread calls for such reform. Instead, changes it appears to result from mounting pressure on Ghannouchi and his risk-averse approach in the face of potential party fragmentation.0 A considerable number of signatories to the open letter criticising Ghannouchi’s leadership later left the party, with some of them joining Mekki’s newly formed Party of Work and Achievement, which appealed to a socially conservative electorate.0
On 25 July 2021, amid political deadlock, institutional paralysis, and worsening economic and health crises, widespread protests erupted against the short-lived government of Hichem Mechichi (September 2020–July 2021).0 In response, President Kais Saied invoked Article 80 of the Constitution, assuminggranting him exceptional powers for up to 30 days in circumstances posing an imminent threat to the nation. In the absence of a Constitutional Court to determine the crisis’s legitimacy of this move,0 Saied proceeded to suspended parliament, dismissed the prime minister, and revoked parliamentary immunity.0 Although his decisive measures were initially welcomed by thousands of Tunisians as a means of rescuing the country from political gridlock and economic collapse, public enthusiasm soon waned.
In this delicate political context, Ghannouchi implemented an arbitrary reshuffling of Ennahda’s Executive Bureau.0 More than 100 leaders from the party’s Shura Council, as well as from regional and local offices, submitted their collective resignation in a joint statement, drawing further criticism during what was arguably the most critical phase in the country’s young democracy.0
Following Saied’s unilateral takeover of state institutions, Ennahda emerged as both itsthe main principal victim and a key actor held nd the principal political actor blamed for the events precipitating his actions.0 Widespread dissatisfaction with Ennahda’s performance on the eve of Saied’s power grab led to the party’s political isolation. Ennahda’s initial attempt to mobilise public support against the suspension of parliamentary activities by organising protests outside the military-guarded Bardo Palace attracted only limited participation.0 After failing to initiate dialogue with the uncompromising President, in February 2022 Ennahda shifted its strategy in mid-February 2022 by aligning with emerging anti-coup grassroots movements0 in an effort to overcome isolation and remain politically relevant.0
However, pervasive anti-Ennahda sentiment among Tunisians and across much of the political spectrum helped legitimise Saied’s actions in public debate and delayedhindered the formation of an effective, broad, cross-ideological coalition capable of challenging his consolidation of power.0 The slow formation of a united  front against Saied further contributed to Tunisia’s democratic backsliding. In the aftermath of Saied’s coup, deep mistrust of Ennahda obstructed theany revival of the political consensus that had previously characterised Tunisian politics.0 Instead, the period leading up to and the immediately following the President's power grabpost-July 2021 period saw the resurfacing of the ‘Islamist–secular’ divide, driving new ideological and opportunistic alliances primarily aimed at excluding Ennahda and delaying the formation of cross-ideological opposition fronts.0
Amid an intensifying crackdown on opposition figures, more than a decade after their celebrated return to Tunisia, much of Ennahda’s leadership has once again been imprisoned, most notably Rached Ghannouchi, detained on charges of alleged involvement in terrorist activities and endangering state security, while other members continue to operate under severe pressure.0
Following Ben Ali’s departure, Ennahda had demonstrated a remarkable capacity to revive its organisational machinery and reconstruct internal structures. However, after President Saied’s crackdown on the opposition, and with some members fleeing abroad, Ennahda has yet to reorganise as a movement in exile. Amid deep-rooted disagreements and a fractured consensus, the only binding force sustainingmaintaining Ennahda’s residual unity is the shared plight of its political prisoners, a powerful symbol of collective injustice that Nahdawis have long endured in the past and that continues to carry mobilising potential.

Conclusion
Conclusion
Conclusion
More than a decade has passed since chants of ‘bread, freedom, and justice’ filled the streets of Cairo and Tunis. For the Islamist movements that rose to power in the immediate post-revolutionary period, these years marked both an opening and a reckoning, testing whether long-standing organisations could reinvent themselves in the face of power, disillusionment, and the weight of their own histories. Yet much of the scholarship remains locked within the interpretive confines of Social Movement Theory and externally oriented analyses of change in behaviour, discourse, and ideology. This book advances a different premise. The most revealing transformations occurred not primarily at the level of ideology, discourse, or mobilisation, but within the internal organisational worlds of these movements. Accordingly, it approaches Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers not as ideological vessels or actorssocial movements responding exclusively to incentives, but as long-standing organisations and institutions.
The book demonstrates how intra-organisational dynamics help explain these movements’ capacity for change and the lasting imprint of a decade of internal developments. It departs from earlier scholarship by proposing a multi-explicative lens that captures organisational constraints on, and enablers of, change. To this end, it develops an integrated institutional framework that brings together the Institutional Logics Perspective with concepts drawn from Institutional Work.
As the empirical chapters show, in the aftermath of the Arab Uprisings the Muslim Brotherhoods established the Freedom and Justice Party (FJP) through a process of coercive modelling, or isomorphic change, defined as a ‘constraining process that forces one unit to resemble the other’, within a political environment marked by uncertainty , suspicion, and the absence of models of modern political organisations.2 As Chapter 2  demonstrates, this coercive form of change stemmed from the assertion of the movement’s socio-reformist logic over its political wing. The prospect of a distinct political party logic threatened the quasi century-old conception of the organisation as a ‘Brotherhood in faith’ and as the incubator of comprehensive social transformation.0 The Brotherhood’s socio-reformist mission presupposed the preservation of both the purity of its group idea as an ideal society and of﻿ the organisation,0 which was conceived as instrumental to fulfilling its transformational role.0 These interrelated objectives led its old guard to intervene and to activate a coercive mode of institutional change during the formation of the FJP.
By contrast, in Ennahda, fear of exclusion from the Tunisian political arena,0 rooted in the logic of the pre-2011 clandestine and persecuted grouporganisation, acted as a catalyst for change. This dynamic paved the way for a ‘non-isomorphic change’, a gradual process of variation in organisational identity, practices, and discourse that characterised Ennahda after 2011.0 As Chapters 4 and 5  show, Ennahda underwent visible changes in organisational practices and identity, moving towards a more open and modern political partyorganisation, particularly after the Tenth Congress in 2016. This trajectory was facilitated by the predominance of the political party logic within the pre-2011 Ennahda Movement (Chap ter 1) and by the organisation’s weakened state on the eve of the Arab Uprisings (Chapter 4 ). 
Nevertheless, following Ennahda’s Tenth Congress in 2016, the leadership’s justification for the need to specialise in political activities did not secure uncritical endorsement of this transformation (Chapter 4 ). Problematic identification with the new organisational identity of the ‘Muslim Democrats’, both among cadres and within the support base, constrained the change process.0 Limited public recognition of Ennahda’s transformation, combined with a pre-existing negative bias towards the Islamist-born party among segments of the Tunisian public, further inhibited the leadership from advancing the change process towards a national conservative party (Chapter 5). 
The cumulative analysis of the organisational dynamics of the Muslim Brothers and Ennahda points to mediating variables that affected their respective capacities for change.0 Organisational transformation was hindered by institutional agents’ fixation on preserving a certain group idea, along with its mission, organisational vision, and practices, as illustrated by the Brotherhood. In Ennahda’s case, constraints stemmed from the ineffective theorisation of the need for change and the resulting non-homogeneous identification of change recipients with a new organisational identity.
The integrated institutional framework underpinning this book (Chapter 1 ) responds to the need to move beyond myopic and quasi-deterministic approaches that portray Islamist movements’ trajectories as linear, structure- or incentive-driven, or assess them through exclusively external categories. The adoption of this less epistemically burdened framework, together with the treatment of these movements as organisations and institutions, contributes to de-ideologising and ‘de-sacralising’ the literature on Islamist movements. More importantly, the multilevel perspective on change advanced here, which foregrounds intra-party developments, contributes to ‘de-ikhwanising’ the field. It shifts attention towards context specificity and organisational culture and history, rather than continuing to treat the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood as the primary influence on kindred movements.0 In doing so, this approach counterbalances the overstretched generalisations derived from macro-comparative studies of Muslim Brotherhoods-like movements.
Multilevel perspective on change: Meanings, direction, and intentionality
This book introduces a multi-explicative perspective on change that comprises three interdependent levels: meanings (maintaining or altering institutions), direction, and intentionality. Together, these levels constitute a new analytical lens (Chapter 1 ). Through their interaction in the cases of the Egyptian Muslim Brothers and Ennahda, change can be understood as follows:
  1. a controlled, and thus intentional, coercive mechanism through which a strong organisation replicates its prevailing logic in another entity, driven by exclusive institutional agents;
  2. a stalled process of variation involving practices, structures, and identity, theorised by a local entrepreneur on pragmatic grounds and contested internally.
In the cases of the Brotherhood and Ennahda, change assumes opposing meaningsthe meanings attributed to change are antonymous. For the Brotherhood, change implies the replication of the movement’s prevailing logic, namely its socio-reformist logic, in another organisational format to protect its original group idea and mission as an all-encompassing movement. By contrast, Ennahda conceives change as a process of altering existing institutional arrangements.
Moreover, Ennahda and the Muslim Brothers conceptualise change in contrasting ways: as an opportunity versus a threat. Ennahda viewed the prospects of organisational change as an opportunity to consolidate a firm and secure position in Tunisia’s post-2011 political scene,0 to the extent that, in 2020, a senior member naively claimed that ‘it is impossible to even think about a ruling coalition in Tunisia without Ennahda’.0 By contrast, the Muslim Brothers’ old guard framed change as an attack on the group idea of the peaceful ‘Brotherhood in faith’ and, in the post-2013 period, justified this fear by emphasising the threat that substantial ve change could pose to organisational survival. Despite these divergent meanings, the initiation of both types of change was deliberate.
A closer examination of the Muslim Brothers’ case also shows that the partial and temporary changes adopted after 2013 lacked any clear direction, as they were not conceived as steps towards long-term variation. These reconfigurations emerged out of necessity and were soon reversed once new leading personalities sought to exploit the brief decentralisation of the vertical chain of command by transforming them into permanent reforms.0 Meaningful organisational change within the Brotherhood thus appears to occur only temporarily and partially when the organisation’s activities and survival are at risk and its vertical structure is compelled to decentralise. In this sense, such changes function as patterned survival mechanisms . For the old guard, the enduring clandestine condition of the organisation, combined with a deeply embedded fear of endangering the almost century-old group idea and the movement’s survival, renders resistance to change a perpetual strategy, reinforcing the perception of change as an adversity to be countered.
Despite long-standing ambitions to specialise in political activities, Ennahda’s stalled internal transition towards a modern political organisation illustrates that moving towards the end direction of change is particularly difficult and costly when ithe endpoint of a transformation culminates in a new organisational identity.0 As Chapter  5 demonstrates, when non-homogeneous identification follows the rebranding of a new organisational identity, identity targets may recast change directions based on their social identities, thereby blurring the image the party seeks to project. Furthermore, Ennahda’s lackThis dynamic, combined with the absence of a a credible and distinctive economic vision, led Tunisian voters and the partyEnnahda’s core supporters to perceive the Islamist-born party and its secular rivals as largely indistinguishable. In turn, this perception indirectly sustained President Saied’s populist rhetoric, which, on the eve of the 2019 presidential elections, delegitimised party politics as a whole.0
Contrasting models of party formation
The Party of Ennahda Movement Party and the FJP emerged from contrasting models of party formation. Ennahda originated in the transposition of a key segment of the pre-2011 movement, namely the Executive Bureau Abroad, into the party’s founding body, followed by a gradual process of transformation (Chapte r 4).0 During this phase, Ennahda’s leadership pursued the de-institutionalisation of established organisational practices and values and introduced new organisational norms deemed more appropriate to the party’s role in national democratisation and its engagement in prolonged ‘pacted politics’.0
By contrast, the Muslim Brotherhood adopted a hybrid formula that preserved the close hizb-haraka (party-movement) relationship and culminated in a process of coercive modelling initiated by a financially stronger and more successful sponsor organisation (Chapter  2). This trajectory produced an excessively dependent political entity, the FJP, and ultimately inhibited the development of the institutional logic characteristic of an autonomous political party.
Antecedents to party formation and modes of derivation are therefore crucial for explaining the divergent organisational trajectories of parties rooted in religious movements and their capacity for change. Formative and structural conditions, such as low cohesion or organisational weakness, can affect the sustainability of newly established parties.0 The process of party formation undertaken by Ennahda was unlikely to result in organisational mimicry of the pre-existing movement, given the conditions under which the party was legalised. Structurally, Ennahda was organisationally weakened and forcibly disconnected from its base on the eve of the Jasmine Revolution. As shown in Chapter 4 , Ben Ali’s severe repressive measures had left the movement with a limited presence and social reach within Tunisian society. Compared with the rigid and complex hierarchical apparatus of the Muslim Brothers in the pre-Uprisings period, Ennahda’s organisational chart exhibited a degree of decentralisation and flexibility. In the years immediately preceding the Jasmine Revolution, the movement relied on two power bases, one in Tunisia and the official leadership in London.0 Consequently, even its vertical command structure was partially stretched and less rigid, rendering it more receptive to change.
The formative conditions under which the FJP emerged were markedly different. As discussed in Chapter 2,  the FJP’s organisational dynamics were shaped by a leadership determined to reassert itself as the exclusive agent and guardian of the Brotherhood’s gradual reformist logic and associated group mission, particularly after facing internal challenges during the movement’s internal elections (2009–2010).0 The old guard, therefore, imposed its organisational vision, modes of thinking, and positions on the newly formed party through coercive modelling. In addition, the movement’s sense of organisational exemplarity and deep societal rootedness reinforced the decision to adopt a hybrid sponsor movement–party model. The old guard’s awareness of the Brotherhood’s organisational success and self-perception as an original model to be emulated encouraged coercive modelling as a mechanism of party derivation at a time of profound uncertainty and in the absence of alternative models of political organisation.0
In Ennahda’s case, organisational flexibility, its limited reach as an Islamist movement, and the pre-2011 movement’s political logic (C hapter 1) facilitated its transformation into a modern political organisation. By contrast, in the case of the Muslim Brothers, societal rootedness, self-perception as an exemplary organisation, and an entrenched fear of change fostered the coercive modelling of the FJP in the image of the Brotherhood. This less sustainable model of party derivation denied the new organisation any prospect of future autonomy0  and ultimately contributed to the delegitimisation of both. Accordingly, alongside structural weakness and low cohesion, a sponsor organisation’s perception of itself as a model to be reproduced should be regarded as a key antecedent of party formation that is likely tocan undermine the sustainability of a newly established political party.
On legitimacy and agency
To varying degrees, both Ennahda’s and the Muslim Brotherhoods’ models of party formation produced ‘externally legitimated’ parties.0 In the case of the FJP, the hybrid model fostered indirect loyalty among affiliates and supporters, thereby constraining prospects for the party’s future emancipation.0 As illustrated in Chapter 2 , coercive modelling also functioned as a mechanism for transferring external legitimacy from a deeply socially rooted sponsor movement to a new political entity, compensating for the latter’s limited vision during an unsettled political period.
Within the Brotherhood, the presence of a sanctified and largely unquestionable elite of self-legitimated power holders meant that coercive modelling of the FJP on the template of its sponsor organisation only required passive acceptance from the rank and file rather than active identification with either new or pre-existing organisationalinstitutional configurationsarrangements. The historical leadership’s moral legitimacy, rooted in decades of survival and endurance through repeated waves of repression, remains a powerful organisational resource.0 Although the Muslim Brothers’ old guard has largely lost credibility and trust since 2013, being a small circle of powerful actors with full control over the movement’s financial capital has enabled them to reassert their authority and fix the organisation in line with their preferences. In some interviewees’ accounts, the movement’s ongoing ordeal and its likely future glorification, may further reinforce the old guard’s moral legitimacy for having shielded the Muslim Brothers from dissolution.0
In Ennahda’s case, some recipients of change, or  ‘identity targets’, developed only indirect loyalty to the post-specialisation party and remained attached to the Islamist movement’s former organisational identity. Despite formally endorsing the hybrid identity of ‘Muslim Democrats’, segments of Ennahda’s older generation subtly resisted it, largely owing to the inadequate theorisation of the need for specialisation in politics.0 This points to the limitations of framing change primarily as necessary and functional for a specific domestic context rather than as intrinsically valuable and meaningful. The diffusion of new practices and organisational values presented as ‘pragmatically legitimate’ does not, in itself, ensure their full institutionalisation.0 On the contrary, it may generate resistance or even a redirection of change once members perceive organisational transformation as contingent upon unstable and unpredictable circumstances that may soon shift again. For planned change to gain ‘cognitive legitimacy’, organisations should therefore avoid presenting the need for organisational transformation as merely ‘pragmatic’. Instead, they should devise theorisation strategies that emphasise the long-term advantages of the proposed change and provide enduring meanings capable of securing full endorsement (Chapter  5)﻿.
Finally, Ennahda’s post-specialisation experience invites a re-evaluation of agentive behaviour by underscoring the importance of identification and change recipients in analysing dynamics of organisational change. Beyond mediating acceptance or rejection of change and a new identity, internal ‘identity targets’ may recast the change process on different directions and recraft new group identities. In this sense, they can themselves act as agents of change.0
Lasting imprint of a decade-long quest for change
A decade after the Arab Uprisings, which sought to overturn long-standing political orders, Ennahda and the Egyptian Muslim Brothers experienced complex organisational developments shaped by their encounters with governencounters with governance and subsequent removal from power. These experiences left a lasting imprint on their system-ness, understood here as a combination of cohesion and coherence, along with the credibility once granted to them by supporters and the broader public.0
In the case of post-specialisation Ennahda, its shaken disrupted value system and the coexistence of distinct group identities, resulting from the recrafting of its organisational identity, have undermined the party’s unity. Members, supporters, and leadership no longer share a common vision of the party’s core values, policy positions, or strategic direction. Low discipline, growing discontent over Ghannouchi’s monopolisation of leadership, and waves of defections further indicate the party’s diminished system-ness.0
Since President Saied’s unilateral takeover of state institutions on 25 July 2021, Ennahda has ceased to be part of Tunisia’s success story. The party faces renewed repression, with some high-profile members imprisoned or forced into exile. Amid a new struggle for relevance and survival, Ennahda has not yet reorganised as a movement in exile but has reoriented its priorities towards pro-democracy and human rights advocacy, collaborating with other Tunisia-based civil society actors and opposition figures, a strategy reminiscent of its organisational past (Chapter 1 ).0
A decade after the military coup that ousted President Morsi, the Egyptian Muslim Brothers have become a smaller, more elitist, and inward-looking movement. Largely inactive, wiWith its membership scattered across multiple countries,0 the organisation has been hollowed out by mass disillusionment, waves of defections, and two internal leadership disputescontestations.0 It now survives in exile, clinging to its name and history but exhibiting low cohesion and detachment from its base. The Brotherhood’s survival as a politically relevant actor appears to be a lesser organisational priority. While Rrestoring the organisation’s effectiveness across all domains, formed the long-term vision of the former acting General Guide Ibrahim Munir (d. 2022), re-engaging former and inactive members, including specialised cadres from the FJP and disengaged youth, and bridging repairing internal divisions within the downsized organisation were central prioritiesconstituted the long-term vision of former acting General Guide Ibrahim Munir (d. 2022). After more than a decade of exile and displacement, the Brotherhood’s old guard continues to prioritise rebuilding internal cohesion and fostering consensus, especially regarding whether to normalise relations with the Egyptian regime in exchange for the release of political prisoners, a prospect that remains deeply contested.0
Having transformed into fully fledged public actors at the forefront of institutional politics, both Ennahda and the Brotherhood faced unprecedented public scrutiny. This exposure demonstrated that, even after sharing ‘blood and tears’ with fellow members, Islamist and Islamist-inspired movements are not immune to the corrupting effects of power, including organisational rifts and internal struggles over leadership positions. Moreover, although both movements have retreated from the public eye, their intra-organisational dynamics, once kept secret and far from indiscreet eyes, have now become increasingly visible and accessible. Paradoxically, the Brotherhood has become more noticeable in the public sphere; during the organisational rifts discussed in Chapter 3 , leaders exchanged statements and counter-statements via social media, while members and supporters circulated memes satirising what was once regarded as a ‘sacred leadership’.0
With respect to Ennahda, the purposeful leaking of party correspondence in 2020, intended to pressure Rached Ghannouchi into avoiding an extension of his tenure, revealed a broken consensus within the party’s leadership and highlighted deficiencies in its deliberative mechanisms and rules for leadership alternation (Chapter 5) .0 The leak also brought internal affairs into the public domain. Ten years on from the Arab Uprisings, in-group partitioning (or the threat thereof) can serve an agentive function, servingintended to ‘warn and discipline a longstanding, monopolising leadership’, as exemplified by the ‘letter from 100 leaders’ (Chapter 5 ).0 Consequently, post-specialisation Ennahda challenges scholars to reconsider low system-ness, not merely as a static organisational property or an indicator of compromised stability,0 but as a purposeful and dynamic process through which leadership is contested instrumental in contesting leadership from within.39
Rethinking change within and beyond the Organised Islamiyyun 
Ennahda’s longer experience in power and its process of party transformation offer valuable lessons, prompting scholars to reconsider how ‘change’ is conceptualised in religiously oriented parties, both within and beyond the Organised Islamiyyun introduced in this book (see Introductio n). The complexity of organisational change should not be viewed myopically as a linear process culminating inevitably in a finite outcome, nor reduced to a purely reactive response to opportunity.0 Instead, change is better understood as a partial and often stalled process, continually (re)negotiated and contested internally by identity targets, and difficult and costly to sustain to completion.0
Future analyses of change in Islamist-born parties should recognise that their organisational dynamics carry specific meanings. They are not incidental, nor are they merely reactive phenomena. These dynamics tend to align with the cultural-symbolic elements constitutive of their institutions. Islamic references, such as the emphasis on a comprehensive reformist project or the protection of a country’s Islamic repertoire of values, have historically imbued the material components of these organisations with meaning. The role of defender or representative of a Muslim country’s Islamic identity can persist as an entrenched group idea or a pronounced identity marker, even in organisations inclined toward change, such as Ennahda. This persistence may serve not only as a form of resistance to internal change but also as a strategy ‘to assert a Muslim subjectivity’ in Islamist-born movements compelled to dilute their value systems to gain political legitimacy or to survive.0
As institutions, the material components of the Organised Islamiyyun (structures and practices) reflect their capacity for change. In the case of the Muslim Brotherhood, the hierarchical organisational vision and the apparatus have been instrumental in carrying out the movement’s historical mission of reforming the individual and , society, and the state, thereby constraining organisational change. By contrast, Ennahda’s organisational flexibility and limited social extension facilitated the initiation of a transformative process towards a modern political organisation. Nevertheless, despite these differing capacities for change, both movements’ organisational dynamics remain largely coherent with pre-existing meanings constructed around identity markers and group ideas: the cultural-symbolic elements drawn from the Islamic tradition that historically shaped their material structures and practices.
The book concludes with a final reflection that cautions against a common Western assumption underpinning studies of contemporary Islamism. Long-lived clandestine movements do not necessarily seek comprehensive organisational change, particularly when their culture, practices, and structures have safeguarded their survival for decades. As the case of the Brotherhood demonstrates, if an organisational culture and group idea are deemed essential to fulfilling a movement’s mission, why change them at all?
Postscript 
I embarked on this project a decade after the Arab Uprisings, driven by the urgency to move beyond the epistemic stagnation in which the field of Islamism studies has sunk. I bring this work to a close with images of destruction wrought by Israel’s war oin Gaza since October 2023  vividly imprinted onin my mind. Amid the increasing securitisation of media narratives and of political and academic discourse on Hamas, and, by extension, the Muslim Brotherhood, many of the premises that initially underpinned this study have inevitably been unsettledshifted.
As academic discourse on Islamism risks moving from epistemic stagnation toward epistemic degradation, scholars will increasingly face a familiar yet reconfigured set of dilemmas. Echoing the effects of the War on Terror, when Islamist actors were primarily reframed through a security and counter-terrorismextremism lens, the post-October 7 contextcontext raises similar questions for scholars of contemporary Islamism: How can the risk of depoliticising Islamism through terrorist labelling be mitigated?43 How can the ontological ‘flattening’ of this multifaceted phenomenon be avoided? How can the ongoing degradation of these groups’ interpretive frameworks be challenged rather than reproduced? And how can the integrity and rigour of knowledge production about these groups be safeguarded?
I conclude this book with these pressing questions in mind, in the hope that they will not only guide future research but also serve as a stark reminder of the challenges the post-October 7 context poses to Islamism studies as a field and scholarly community.
